Source: [S93] Deloitte LLP Consolidated and LLP Financial Statements 2026, signed 25 September 2026 Confirmed; percentages Inferred. The cost lines and operating profit sum to £5,817m, about £8m more than revenue; the difference sits in small items the summary does not show.

Four things to take from this table:

  1. Half of every pound goes on people. Employee costs were 50.3% of revenue. Note that this line includes salaried partners, who are employees [S88][S93].
  2. About a quarter is pass-through. Sub-contractors and recoverable expenses were 23.6%. The accounts say revenue includes "recoverable expenses incurred on assignments", including sub-contractor costs [S93] Confirmed. When Deloitte brings in a specialist software firm or a contractor and bills the client for them, both the fee and the cost go through the books.
  3. The network costs money. Each member firm pays subscription fees to Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited (DTTL), the global coordinating company. They sit in "other operating costs" [S93] Confirmed. The amount is not split out.
  4. Equity partners are not a cost line. Their pay is the profit. Distributable profit of £899m across 799 full-time-equivalent equity partners gives the £1.125m average [S84][S88] Inferred (our arithmetic, which matches Deloitte's figure).
KEY TERM

Distributable profit: the profit available to share among equity partners, measured on Deloitte's internal "management accounts" basis. It uses different accounting policies from the statutory accounts, which is why it was £899m while statutory profit for the year was £769m [S93] Confirmed. Press releases quote distributable profit.

The engine underneath: rate card, utilisation, realisation, leverage

The accounts show totals. The mechanism that produces them is the same across all large professional-services firms. Deloitte does not publish its internal targets, so what follows is the standard model Inferred, tied to what the accounts do confirm.

KEY TERM

Charge-out rate (the rate card): the standard price per hour or day for each grade, from analyst to partner. Utilisation: the share of a person's available hours that are chargeable to a client. Realisation: the share of the standard value of those hours that the client actually pays, after discounts and write-offs. Leverage: how many staff work under each partner. Profit rises with all four.

The FY2026 accounts confirm the mechanism in Deloitte's own words. Fixed-fee contracts are recognised "based upon the value of the actual services provided ... determined based on the actual inputs of time at charge-out rates, via timesheet reporting" [S93] Confirmed. In plain English: even when the client pays a fixed price, Deloitte measures progress by hours times rates. Your timesheet is how the firm knows how much revenue it has earned.

Figure 1, on the next page, traces the whole flow from fee to partner on one page.

The operating model in layers

Money is one flow. Figure 2 shows the others: what moves between clients, the four client-facing businesses, the firm's own centre, and the global network. The key point for a beginner: the client-facing businesses do not work alone. Before any work starts, the centre checks conflicts. During the work, the centre supplies people, tools and delivery capacity. Above the firm, the network supplies the brand and the rules, and charges a fee for them.

Fixed fee or time and materials?

Pricing typeHow it worksWho carries the risk
Time and materialsThe client pays for hours worked at agreed rates, plus expenses. Revenue is "time charged to date" [S93] Confirmed.Mostly the client. If the work takes longer, the bill goes up.
Fixed feeAn agreed price for a defined scope. Revenue recognised by inputs of time at charge-out rates [S93] Confirmed.Mostly the firm. Overruns cut realisation, so the partner earns less per hour.
Contingent feePaid only if something happens (for example, a deal completes). Not recognised until the contingency resolves [S93] Confirmed.The firm, fully, until the event.
Per unit / transactionA price per item processed, for example in data processing [S93] Confirmed.Shared. Volume risk sits with the firm.
Risk and rewardPart of the fee depends on outcomes. Allowed under the UK government's Management Consultancy Framework Four alongside time and materials and fixed price [S117] Confirmed.Shared, by design.
SOURCE UNCERTAIN

No verified Deloitte day rate exists in our sources. Supplier rate cards for the government framework sit in a tool we could not open [S117]. Historic Test and Trace rates disclosed in 2021 were about £1,000 a day per person [S332]. Do not quote a current day rate in interview. Deloitte also publishes no utilisation or realisation targets.

Leverage: how many people per partner?

Leverage is the shape of the pyramid. The more juniors each partner leads, the more chargeable hours feed each partner's share. Using Deloitte's own numbers [S88][S93] and our arithmetic Inferred:

  • UK group FY2026: 23,970 FTE employees across 1,453 partners is about 16.5 staff per partner. Per equity partner it is about 30.
  • Counting only fee-earners (20,346 FTE), it is about 14 per partner.
  • Deloitte global FY2025: 473,050 people across 21,183 partners, principals and managing directors is about 22 per partner [S81].
  • Revenue per head, UK group FY2026: about £235k per person (employees plus equity partners) Inferred. Average employee cost: about £122k per FTE including employer pension and social security, bonuses and salaried partners. That is not a typical salary; senior grades and Swiss pay pull it up [S93] Inferred.

The most important number in the FY2026 accounts is easy to miss. Average fee-earning employees fell from 21,471 to 20,346 FTE, down about 5%, while revenue rose 2% [S93] Confirmed. More revenue from fewer people pushed distributable profit up 14%. That is leverage and productivity working in the partners' favour, likely helped by delivery centres, AI tools and lower hiring Inferred. Section E and Figure 41 come back to this.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Profit up 14% on revenue up 2% with fewer staff. Is that good news for someone joining?"
For: a profitable firm can invest (technology spend rose to £180m [S407]) and the bonus pool rose 14% [S407]. Against: the same arithmetic means fewer junior seats per pound of revenue; entry-level hiring has fallen since FY2023 [S89]. Suggested stance: "It is good for the firm's resilience and it raises the bar for juniors. The analysts who thrive will be the ones who use AI tools to do higher-value work, not the ones competing with them on volume."

Anatomy of one engagement

Figure 4 zooms into one engagement team. The grade ladder in Deloitte consulting runs roughly analyst or consultant, senior consultant, manager, senior manager, director, partner (charge-out rates by grade: [S93]; the ladder itself is standard practice Inferred). A team rarely works only with its own members. It draws on the account team that owns the client relationship, the Quality, Risk & Security function that runs conflict and independence checks [S330], specialists from other offerings, alliance partners such as SAP or Salesforce [S319], the UK delivery centres [S323], and firm-wide AI tools [S85][S116].

RoleWhat they do on the engagementHow they affect the economics Inferred
PartnerWins the work, signs the contract, owns quality and risk, manages the client's senior people.Mostly not chargeable; their value is the sale and the relationship.
DirectorRuns delivery day to day across workstreams; often leads the proposal.Protects realisation by keeping scope under control.
Manager / senior managerPlans the work, manages the team, reviews outputs, handles client meetings.Decides staffing mix, so drives leverage.
Consultant / senior consultantBuilds the analysis, configures the system, writes the deliverables.Expected to be highly chargeable.
Analyst (your likely entry role)Research, data work, slides, testing, meeting notes, first drafts.Most chargeable time per pound of salary. The base of the pyramid.

C. The contracts: what partners, staff and clients each give and get

A professional partnership runs on three unwritten bargains. Only some of the terms are published. We label which parts are documented and which are norms.

PartyGivesGetsEvidence
Equity partnersCapital (£296m in total at 31 May 2026); unlimited effort; personal reputation; their vote on leadersA share of distributable profit (average £1.125m, FY2026); a say in who leads; capital repaid after retirement[S93][S407] Confirmed
Salaried partnersPartner-level work and sellingPartner title, salary and bonus; a chance of conversion to equity[S88][S95] Confirmed
StaffChargeable hours, mobility, willingness to learn fastSalary, bonus, training (£64.2m L&D spend in FY2025, about 35 hours per FTE), promotion, a brand on the CV[S89] Confirmed; "up or out" is a norm Inferred
ClientsFees; access to their people, systems and data; decisionsExpertise, extra capacity, a brand that reassures boards and regulators, someone accountable for deliveryFee types [S93] Confirmed; the rest Inferred

The partner deal, from the accounts

  • Capital. Each member's capital is set by their profit "units" and is repayable after retirement. Total members' capital was £296m at 31 May 2026 (2025: £293m) [S93] Confirmed. Across 809 members that averages about £366k, though individual amounts vary Inferred (our arithmetic).
  • Profit share. In Deloitte's words: "Members' share of profits is based upon a comprehensive evaluation of their individual and team contribution to, among others, quality, risk, performance, and leadership" [S93] Confirmed. The UK Executive allocates units with oversight from the Partnership Council. For audit partners, the Audit Non-Executives observe the process to test the link to audit quality [S93].
  • Cash. Partners draw monthly advances against expected profit. The firm holds back tax and pays it to HMRC for them. The average effective tax rate on equity partners was 49% in FY2026 [S88] Confirmed.
  • Annuities. A partner annuity scheme pays retired partners. It was closed to new entrants on 1 June 2021. Liabilities are £1,545m. In Deloitte's words: "The annual payments are mainly capped at 8% of applicable Group operating profit before annuity charges in any financial year" [S93] Confirmed. In effect, today's partners fund past partners' retirement out of today's profit Inferred.
  • Voting. The Senior Partner and Chief Executive is elected by partner vote, after soundings by the Partnership Council [S93][S96] Confirmed.
  • Conversion. Salaried partners become equity partners in a separate step: 29 in 2024, 77 in 2025, 68 on 1 June 2026 [S84][S85][S95] Confirmed.
KEY TERM

Partner annuity: a retirement income paid by the firm to former partners, funded from current profits rather than a separate pension pot. Deloitte UK closed its scheme to new partners in 2021 and caps the annual cost at mainly 8% of operating profit before annuity charges [S93]. Why you care: it is a cost the current partners carry, so it shapes how hard they push for profit.

The staff deal: promotion, pay and the narrowing pyramid

  • On 1 June 2026, over 6,000 people were promoted out of about 25,000, average in-grade salary rose 4.2%, and the bonus pool rose 14% [S95][S407] Confirmed.
  • A year earlier the mood was different. In May 2025 UK staff were reportedly told the firm would "promote fewer people and reduce average salary rises" because profits were "below our original plan" [S101] Reported.
  • New partners: 48 promoted on 1 June 2026, after 60 in 2025 and 80-81 in 2024 [S95][S85] Confirmed.
  • Promotions to partner and director fell from 501 (FY2023) to 485 (FY2024) to 341 (FY2025) [S89] Confirmed. The top of the pyramid is narrowing.
  • Voluntary attrition (people choosing to leave) was 10.0% in FY2025, after 9.4% in FY2024 and 11.1% in FY2023 [S89] Confirmed.
  • Low attrition has a cost. In FY2026 Deloitte offered voluntary redundancy on enhanced terms to "less than 3% of our A&A business" because too few people were leaving [S407] Confirmed.
KEY TERM

Up or out: the norm in big professional firms that people are expected to move up through the grades on a rough timetable, or leave. Deloitte does not publish an up-or-out policy. Treat it as an industry norm Inferred, visible in the promotion numbers above. Low voluntary attrition breaks the model, because the pyramid only works if people leave the lower grades at a steady rate.

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

Partner counts differ by definition. The promotions release says "1,308 partners overall" on 1 June 2026 [S95]. The FY2026 metrics say 1,453 partners as a full-year FTE average including Switzerland [S88]. The results release says equity partners rose 6.5% to a record 784 (a year-end headcount), while the accounts use 799 (an FTE average) [S407][S88]. Quote 784 as "record equity partners" and 799 only when you explain the £1.125m average.

DON'T SAY THIS

"Partners earn £1.1m each." That is an average across 799 FTE equity partners, before the 49% average tax rate, and it hides a wide spread [S88][S407]. Salaried partners are not in it at all.

D. The risk and control architecture

Deloitte's biggest asset is trust in one brand. Its biggest liability is that thousands of partners in separately owned firms around the world can damage that brand. The firm manages this with three layers of control: legal separation between firms, governance inside the UK firm, and gates on every engagement.

Layer 1: the network is a brand, not one company

The UK firm's legal position, verbatim from Deloitte's FY2026 release:

"Deloitte LLP is a limited liability partnership registered in England and Wales with registered number OC303675 and its registered office at 1 New Street Square, London EC4A 3HQ ... Deloitte LLP's affiliate (Deloitte Management Services Limited) is a shareholder in Deloitte EMEA BV (Deloitte EMEA). Deloitte EMEA is a member firm of Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited (DTTL). DTTL and Deloitte EMEA do not provide services to clients." [S407] Confirmed

DTTL is "a private company limited by guarantee incorporated in England and Wales" [S83] Confirmed. The network's own legal language explains the logic. DTTL and each member firm "are legally separate and independent entities, which cannot obligate or bind each other in respect of third parties", and are "liable only for their own acts and omissions, and not those of each other" [S83] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Member firm: a separate legal business, owned by its own local partners, that has signed up to use the Deloitte brand and follow DTTL's standards. Company limited by guarantee: a company with no share capital, owned by members who guarantee a nominal sum; common for coordinating bodies that do not trade.

Why this matters to you Inferred: a failure in Deloitte China or Deloitte Australia does not legally bind Deloitte UK. But it lands on the same brand and the same search results. Section I shows that this is not theoretical.

Layer 2: UK governance after 1 June 2026

From 1 June 2026, Deloitte LLP and its Swiss practice combined with 14 other participating member firms to form Deloitte EMEA. Deloitte NSE LLP (North and South Europe), the previous parent, ceased to be the parent [S93] Confirmed. Inside the UK firm, governance changed the same day [S93][S407] Confirmed:

BodyRole from 1 June 2026Who / note
Senior Partner and Chief ExecutiveLeads the firm; elected by partnersDarren Graves, from 1 June 2026 [S96][S407]
UK ExecutiveRuns the firm day to day; allocates partner profit unitsIncludes Hayley McKelvey, Chief AI Officer [S407]
UK Board (replaced the UK Oversight Board)Sets long-term strategy with the Executive; oversees risk, reputation, public interest, quality and ethicsChair: Jane Whitlock [S407]
Board committeesAudit and Risk; Remuneration; Nomination; Partnership Council[S93]
Partnership CouncilFairness between partners; soundings for leadership elections[S93][S94]
Audit Governance BoardOversees the ring-fenced audit practice; majority independentContinues unchanged [S93][S94]
Designated membersLegal signatories of the LLPDarren Graves, Heather Bygrave; Martin Reilly from 1 Sep 2026 [S93]

Layer 3: gates on every engagement

This is where consultants meet the control system. The Audit Transparency Report describes the gates [S94] Confirmed:

  1. Conflict check before acceptance. "All proposed engagements and business and financial relationships go through a conflict check before they are accepted." The audit partner is always consulted if a potential conflict touches an audit client. "Where potential conflicts cannot be eliminated or reduced to an acceptable level, we decline the engagement."
  2. Public Interest Review Group (PIRG). Reviews engagements with high public-interest or reputational risk. It has looked at more than 800 matters over its history. In FY2025 it formally considered 32 matters and declined 9%; in FY2024, 38 matters with 19% declined.
  3. Tax Review Panel. Considers reputational risk in complex tax work.
  4. Consulting forum. For SR&T and T&T, a "Consultative Forum" and a "globally aligned client portfolio management process".
32Matters formally reviewed by the PIRG, FY2025 (38 in FY2024) [S94]
9%Of those declined, FY2025 (19% in FY2024) [S94]
800+Matters reviewed by the PIRG in its history [S94]
95%FRC-sampled audits rated good or limited improvements, 2025 report [S94]
KEY TERM

Conflict of interest: a situation where the firm's duty to one client clashes with its interest or its duty to another, for example advising a bidder while auditing the target. Independence: the rules that stop an auditor having financial or business ties with its audit client. For a consultant, independence decides which clients you are allowed to work for at all. Part 3 covers the UK rules that limit consulting for audit clients.

How Deloitte rates its own risks

The firm publishes a principal risks register. Two entries matter for consulting [S94] Confirmed:

  • "Our reputation, role and future public interest impact": Very High residual risk. Threats listed include "Increased government focus on the reputation and role and public sector use of professional services organisations" and "Increasing breadth and depth of non-audit offerings (including Operate)".
  • "Client Portfolio": High. It cites "Reputational risks associated with client selection" and notes that "Reputation is at risk from the 'company we choose to keep' and the projects we choose to deliver".

"Operate" means running services for clients on an ongoing basis, such as a benefits system or a finance function, rather than advising and leaving. The firm itself flags it as a source of risk. Rhode Island, in Section I, shows why.

Quality management

Audit firms must run a system of quality management under the standard ISQM (UK) 1. Deloitte UK's evaluation at 31 May 2025 found "two deficiencies identified (neither severe nor pervasive)" and concluded the system gives reasonable assurance; one was fixed by the report date [S94] Confirmed. The FRC rated 95% of sampled Deloitte audits "good or limited improvements required" (94% the year before) [S94]. The audit practice is "operationally separated" from the rest of the firm, an FRC requirement for the Big Four, and the transition period ended during FY2025 [S94] Confirmed. Deloitte UK also uses an offshore audit delivery centre, Global Audit India [S94].

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"I noticed the Public Interest Review Group declined 9% of the 32 matters it formally reviewed last year, and the firm rates its own reputation risk as Very High, partly because of Operate work. How does that gate show up for a consultant day to day?" [S94] It shows you read the Transparency Report, and it is a real question.

E. Business mix and growth over time

Global: doubled in eleven years

Deloitte's global revenue grew from US$35.2bn in FY2015 to US$74.5bn in FY2026, about 7% a year compounded [S80][S70] Inferred (our arithmetic). The fastest years were FY2022 (+19.6% in local currency) and FY2023 (+14.9%), the post-COVID boom in digital and consulting work [S74][S73] Confirmed. Growth then slowed to 3-5% a year [S70][S71][S72]. Headcount roughly doubled too, from over 225,000 to nearly 500,000 [S80][S70].

The business mix changed too. On 1 October 2024 Deloitte globally cut its five businesses to four, folding Consulting, Risk Advisory and Financial Advisory into T&T and SR&T [S94][S72] Confirmed. Global CEO Joe Ucuzoglu announced it in the FY2024 release: "over the course of FY2025, we are aligning our capabilities into the following business units: Audit & Assurance, Tax & Legal, and two units housing our Consulting services: Strategy, Risk & Transactions and Technology & Transformation" [S72] Confirmed. This breaks the UK time series in FY2024, so compare old and new numbers with care.

Consulting9661,0811,1891,3701,596

Audit & Assurance585636665723869

Sources: old structure [S90][S91][S92]; new structure [S88][S89] Confirmed. Old Consulting is not the same perimeter as new T&T, so do not compute a growth rate across the break.

Fewer staff, more equity partners

UK group FTE employees rose from 18,405 in FY2019 to a peak of 26,824 in FY2024, then fell to 23,970 in FY2026, down about 11% in two years [S92][S89][S88] Confirmed (percentage Inferred). Over the same two years, FTE equity partners rose from 749 to 799 [S88] Confirmed. Fewer staff, more owners, higher profit per owner: that is the shape of the last two years.

There are two ways to read this, and you should be able to hold both Inferred. The optimistic reading: the firm over-hired in the FY2023 boom (6,800 hires and 4,109 experienced hires that year [S87][S89]), then corrected, and new technology lets fewer people deliver more. The cautious reading: if AI and delivery centres keep raising output per head, the firm needs fewer juniors per partner for good. Entry-level hiring fell from 2,767 in FY2023 to 1,908 in FY2025 [S89] Confirmed, with "more than 1,950" in FY2026 [S407]. Part 4 turns this into how you stand out.

UK: steady revenue, rising profit, one dip

Deloitte UK (with Switzerland) grew from £3,950m in FY2019 to £5,809m in FY2026, about 5.7% a year [S92][S88] Inferred (our arithmetic). FY2025 was the exception: revenue fell 1% to £5,676m, the first fall in about 15 years [S101] Reported. T&T fell 10%. UK government and public services revenue fell 14%, from £761m to £652m. Deloitte's footnote gives the reason: "The reduction in FY25 revenue was primarily due to the early announcement of the general election which resulted in delays to procurement decision making, contract award decisions and start dates of projects" [S89] Confirmed. Even in that year, distributable profit rose 4% to £789m [S85] Confirmed. That is the multidisciplinary model doing its job: tax and legal grew 7% while T&T shrank.

F. What "private partnership" means for your research

Deloitte UK has no shares on a stock market. That changes where the numbers come from.

What you cannot get

  • No share price, no analyst forecasts, no quarterly results Inferred.
  • No margin by business. You cannot tell whether T&T is more profitable than audit [S93].
  • No day rates, utilisation or realisation targets.
  • No client names in the accounts and no individual partner pay.

What is public, and where

  • LLP accounts at Companies House (OC303675), audited by BDO: income statement, costs, partners, capital, annuities, governance [S93].
  • Business and ESG performance metrics PDF each September: revenue by business and industry, profit per partner, FTEs, attrition, promotions [S88][S89][S90][S91][S92].
  • Audit Transparency Report: governance, quality, PIRG, risk register [S94].
  • Global revenue release and Global Impact Report each September [S70][S71][S81].

Three traps sit in these sources [S93][S88][S407] Confirmed:

  1. The UK headline includes Switzerland. Business-line figures do not.
  2. The fiscal year ends 31 May, so FY2026 is mostly calendar 2025.
  3. Partner and people numbers come in headcount and FTE-average versions. Always say which.
KEY TERM

FTE (full-time equivalent): a way of counting staff where two half-time people count as one. An "FTE average" is the average over the year, so it differs from the headcount on a single day. Deloitte UK's "25,000 people" is a rounded headcount; 23,970 is the FTE average [S88][S407].

What leaders say

  • Joe Ucuzoglu, Deloitte Global CEO, FY2026: "In a time of rapid change and technology-fueled disruption, organizations around the world continue to place their trust in Deloitte to successfully navigate this historic reshaping of markets and industries" [S70] Confirmed. As quoted by City AM: "Deloitte is unlocking AI's potential through a people-led, AI-powered approach grounded in trust, integrity, and professional excellence" [S100] Reported.
  • Darren Graves, UK Senior Partner and CEO from 1 June 2026. He joined Deloitte as a Business Tax graduate in 2001, made partner in 2012, led UK Transactions Tax, and from 2022 was Managing Partner for NSE Tax & Legal [S96] Confirmed. He was confirmed by partner vote around 31 March 2026, reportedly unopposed [S96][S97] ("unopposed" is Reported). He has said he wants to "reinvent our firm for the next generation" [S97] Reported. On results day: "As AI makes intelligence increasingly abundant, the role our people play will matter more, not less. AI can't replace lived experience or replicate the judgement and unwritten know-how built..." [S407] Confirmed.
  • Richard Houston, UK CEO since 2019, became CEO of Deloitte EMEA from 1 June 2026 [S94][S407] Confirmed.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Will AI shrink the consulting pyramid?"
Yes: fee-earners fell 5% while revenue rose 2% [S93]; junior hiring is down a third from FY2023 [S89]; the firm has a Chief AI Officer and a firm-wide Claude roll-out [S407][S116]. No: the FY2023 peak was exceptional by Deloitte's own footnote [S89]; T&T returned to growth in FY2026 [S407]; the CEO says people "will matter more, not less" [S407]. Suggested stance: "The pyramid gets narrower at the bottom but not flatter. Analysts will spend less time producing first drafts and more time checking and explaining them. I want to join a firm that is building the checks, not just buying the tools."

I. The skeletons, told straight

Every big firm has a list. Interviewers do not expect you to defend Deloitte. They do notice whether you know the facts, keep them in proportion, and can say what the firm learned. Only verified matters are listed. Each line ends with why it matters to a consulting candidate Inferred.

MatterWhat happenedWhy it matters to you
Autonomy (UK audit), 17 Sep 2020Record £15m FRC fine and severe reprimand for audits of Autonomy covering 2009-2011; two former partners fined; about £5.6m of FRC costs. The tribunal cited "wholesale nature of the failure of professional scepticism" [S105] Confirmed.Shows why independence and scepticism are taken seriously firm-wide, including in consulting.
Serco, 16 Jul 2019£4.2m FRC fine (after discount) over audits of Serco's electronic tagging division, 2011-12 [S106] Reported.A government contract scandal touched the auditor too. Public-sector work carries reputational risk on every side.
Mitie, 21 Apr 2022£2m fine, reduced to £1.45m, over 2016 goodwill testing; the FRC said there was "no suggestion that breaches were intentional, dishonest or reckless" [S107] Reported.Most failures are about judgement and evidence, not fraud. That is true in consulting too.
SIG, 22 Dec 2022£1.25m fine, discounted to £906,250, for 2015-16 audits [S108] Reported.Pattern: repeat sanctions keep audit quality on the board agenda.

China's Ministry of Finance fined 211.9m yuan (about US$31m) and suspended the Beijing office for three months (17 Mar 2023) [S112] Reported.A separate legal firm, but the same brand. This is the "liable only for their own acts" structure at work.
Australia AI report, Oct 2025Deloitte Australia refunded the final instalment of an AU$440,000 government review after an academic found fabricated references and a misquoted court judgment. The corrected report disclosed use of "a generative AI large language model (Azure OpenAI GPT-4o)" [S113] Reported.The live cautionary tale for AI-assisted consulting. It broke the same week as the Anthropic deal.
US federal cuts (DOGE), 2025At least 129 Deloitte contracts terminated or cut, more than any other consultancy; Deloitte US made "modest personnel actions" in April 2025 [S114] Reported (the DOGE data itself was questioned).Public-sector consulting carries political risk. The UK saw a milder version in FY2025 [S89].
Rhode Island, 2024-26Deloitte ran the state's RIBridges benefits system. A ransomware attack discovered in December 2024 affected more than 650,000 people. A May 2026 settlement brought the state's total recovery to US$12m, plus about US$6m of system support. Deloitte denied wrongdoing [S115] Reported.In "Operate" work the firm owns operational and cyber risk, not just advice. This is why the risk register rates Operate as a threat [S94].

For proportion: over the five years to June 2025, pre-discount FRC fines totalled KPMG £81.8m, PwC £34m, Deloitte £19m and EY £18m [S110] Reported. Deloitte is not the outlier among the Big Four.

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

The detail that the Rhode Island attackers used a Deloitte employee's stolen credentials rests on a search snippet, not a page we read (the settlement itself is from [S115]). Kier, Ted Baker and Patisserie Valerie are sometimes mentioned in Big Four lists; we could not verify they were Deloitte audits, so they are excluded.

DON'T SAY THIS

"I don't think that was really Deloitte's fault." Or the opposite: "Big Four firms can't be trusted." Both close the conversation. Don't attribute other firms' scandals to Deloitte, and don't describe Glencore as a finding while it is still an investigation.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW, IF ASKED ABOUT THE FIRM'S PROBLEMS

"The ones I would take most seriously for consulting are the Australian AI report and Rhode Island. The first shows what happens when AI output is not checked properly. The second shows that when you run a service rather than advise on it, you own the operational risk. Deloitte's own risk register rates reputation risk as Very High and names Operate work as a driver [S94], so the firm clearly sees it. As a junior, the practical lesson for me is simple: check every source and every output before it reaches a client, however good the tool is." [S113][S115]

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Should Deloitte keep doing public-sector Operate work, given Rhode Island and DOGE?"
Keep: government is a large, sticky market; UK government and public services revenue was £679m in FY2026 [S88]. Retreat: political and cyber risk is concentrated there, and the risk register flags government scrutiny [S94][S114][S115]. Suggested stance: "Keep it, but price and staff it as a risk business: tighter cyber controls, clearer exit terms, and explicit acceptance through the public interest review."

ONE-PARAGRAPH SUMMARY OF THIS PART

Deloitte is a brand shared by legally separate firms. The UK firm is an LLP owned by about 800 equity partners. It turned £5.81bn of FY2026 fees (UK and Switzerland) into £899m of distributable profit: half of each pound pays staff, about a quarter passes through to sub-contractors and expenses, and about 15p is left for the owners. Revenue grew 2% while fee-earning staff fell 5%. Since 1 June 2026 it sits inside Deloitte EMEA under a new CEO and a new Chief AI Officer. Its biggest risk, by its own rating, is reputation, and the cases that matter most for a consultant are about AI quality and Operate work [S93][S88][S407][S94].

Part 3

Why Deloitte is built this way

The mechanism behind the firm: why audit, tax, advisory and technology sit in one partnership, how the pieces work together and where the rules force them apart, what clients really pay for, and the support machine behind the client teams. This is the raw material for a "why Deloitte" answer that nobody else in the room will give.

The short answer

Deloitte is a set of partner-owned firms that share one brand. Inside each country firm, four businesses with different economic rhythms share one profit pool. Audit is steady and regulated. Tax is steady. Technology consulting swings with clients' appetite for large programmes. Put together, they behave like an investment portfolio: when one falls, the others hold the firm up, and the shared profit pays for the next round of investment (today, mostly AI and delivery centres) Inferred.

The price of that design is friction. Independence rules stop the consulting side selling most services to the companies the audit side audits. The UK regulator has ring-fenced audit inside the firm. A scandal in one country lands on every firm that carries the name. Deloitte's leaders have looked at this trade and decided, repeatedly and publicly, that it is worth it.

£5.81bnRevenue FY26, UK and Switzerland consolidated; UK alone £5,014m [S407] [S88]
£1,746mUK Technology & Transformation revenue FY26, +4%; about 35% of UK revenue [S88]
-10% vs -1%FY25: UK T&T fell 10%; UK and Swiss firm revenue fell 1% [S88] [S85]
£899mDistributable profit FY26, +14%, shared by 784 equity partners [S407]
KEY TERM

Multidisciplinary partnership (MDP): a firm that combines several professions (here audit, tax, legal, strategy, risk, deals and technology consulting) under one ownership and one brand. Academics who studied the big accounting firms found this form "was vigorously contested" from the start, because regulators worried that auditors who also sell consulting may be conflicted [S315] Reported.

What the structure actually is

"Deloitte" is a brand, not a single company. Deloitte describes itself as the brand under which "nearly 500,000" people "in independent firms throughout the world come together" [S302] Confirmed. Three layers matter.

Layer 1: the global umbrella (DTTL)

At the top is Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited (DTTL), a private company limited by guarantee incorporated in England and Wales. It sets brand and quality rules. In Deloitte's words, "DTTL does not provide services to clients" [S302] Confirmed. Member firms pay DTTL subscription fees, which show up in the UK accounts as an operating cost [S93] Confirmed. The key legal line is that DTTL and each member firm "are liable only for their own acts and omissions, and not those of each other" [S302] Confirmed.

Layer 2: the region (new in 2026: Deloitte EMEA)

Until 31 May 2026 the UK firm sat under Deloitte NSE LLP (North and South Europe), a holding entity that served no clients [S93] Confirmed. From 1 June 2026, Deloitte LLP and its Swiss practice combined with other member firms to form Deloitte EMEA: 16 firms, more than 80 countries, about €20bn of revenue, 6,000 partners and 132,000 people, with more than €1.5bn of planned extra investment over four years in generative AI, sovereign cloud and sector solutions [S124] Confirmed. Richard Houston, previously UK CEO, runs it [S124] Confirmed. The UK accounts give the reason: "strategic alignment across participating firms, thereby enhancing the ability to invest in innovation, technology platforms, and talent development at a regional level" [S93] Confirmed. The legal chain, verbatim from the UK results: Deloitte LLP's affiliate "is a shareholder in Deloitte EMEA BV (Deloitte EMEA). Deloitte EMEA is a member firm of Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited (DTTL). DTTL and Deloitte EMEA do not provide services to clients" [S407] Confirmed.

Layer 3: the UK firm and its four businesses

Deloitte LLP is a limited liability partnership registered in England and Wales, number OC303675, at 1 New Street Square, London EC4A 3HQ [S407] Confirmed. Since a global simplification that took effect on 1 October 2024, it runs four businesses: Audit & Assurance (A&A); Tax & Legal (T&L); Strategy, Risk & Transactions Advisory (SR&T-A); and Technology & Transformation (T&T) [S94] [S72] Confirmed. The old Consulting, Risk Advisory and Financial Advisory units were folded into the last two [S89] Confirmed. Deloitte calls T&T and SR&T together its "advisory businesses" [S407] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Limited liability partnership (LLP) and equity partner: an LLP is a partnership whose owners ("members") are not personally liable for the firm's debts. Equity partners own the firm. They are not paid a salary; they share what is left after staff and costs are paid. That residual is distributable profit: £899m in FY26, or £1.125m per equity partner on average [S407] Confirmed. Salaried partners carry the title but are employees [S88] Confirmed.

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte UK made £5.81bn and T&T is 30% of it." The £5.81bn includes Switzerland. Deloitte's own footnote: "All revenue numbers presented herein, unless otherwise noted, represent UK and Switzerland consolidated" [S407]. UK-only revenue was £5,014m and the Swiss practice £795m [S88] Confirmed. The four business lines are UK-only, so T&T is about 35% of the UK firm Inferred (arithmetic).

Why one partnership: the theory and the numbers

There are six mechanisms that explain why the firm is built like this. Each is stated as a theory, then tested against evidence.

1. A portfolio of businesses that peak at different times

Audit is recurring and required by law: a listed company must have one every year. Tax work follows the tax calendar and changes in tax rules. Consulting depends on whether clients feel confident enough to start large programmes. These cycles do not line up, so combining them smooths partner income Inferred.

The UK numbers for the last two years are the clearest live test. In FY25 (the year to 31 May 2025), UK T&T revenue fell 10% to £1,675m. Tax & Legal rose 7%, Audit & Assurance 3% and SR&T Advisory 3% [S88] [S85] Confirmed. The firm's total fell only 1%, its first fall in about 15 years [S101] Reported. The reason given was that "Clients delayed large-scale investment programmes amid economic uncertainty" [S305] Reported. Distributable profit still rose 4% [S85] Confirmed. In FY26, T&T recovered by 4% and profit jumped 14% on revenue growth of 2% [S407] Confirmed.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"I looked at the last two years of UK results. In FY25, Technology & Transformation fell 10%, but tax grew 7% and audit 3%, so the firm only dipped about 1% and profit still went up. In FY26 T&T came back with 4% growth. To me that is the case for the multidisciplinary model in two numbers: it lets the firm keep investing through a weak consulting year."

2. Brand trust from audit, sold across the firm

Audit puts Deloitte inside the finance function of large companies and makes the name a signal of reliability. Deloitte's own framing: "Our multidisciplinary model, deep domain and industry knowledge, and commitment to upholding quality and trust in the corporate reporting ecosystem allow us to provide integrated solutions" [S300] Confirmed. The firm's origin story is the same idea: William Welch Deloitte, who set up in London in 1845, is described as the first person appointed independent auditor of a public company, the Great Western Railway [S103] Reported. Inferred The trust earned in audit helps every other business win work, even where the rules stop the audit team itself from passing on leads.

3. Partner capital and a long horizon

Partners own the firm and are paid out of distributable profit [S407]. Each equity partner puts in capital; total members' capital was £296m at 31 May 2026 [S93] Confirmed. There are no outside shareholders and no quarterly results Inferred. That let the firm ride out FY25 without a share-price shock, and it means investment comes out of partners' pockets. Deloitte globally has committed US$3bn to AI through 2030 [S300] Confirmed; the UK spent £180m on technology in FY26, up from £158m [S407] Confirmed.

4. Liability containment

Because each member firm is "liable only for their own acts" [S302], a failure in one country should not bankrupt the others Inferred. This is the lesson of Arthur Andersen, which collapsed after Enron in 2001-02. Andersen's UK practice joined Deloitte UK in 2002 [S103] Reported.

5. Scale for alliances and investment

Big technology vendors want partners who can put thousands of certified people on their platforms. A pooled network can do that; a single country firm cannot Inferred. Global CEO Joe Ucuzoglu, on the EMEA combination: "Our clients expect leading expertise wherever it is based, alongside seamless cross-border and technology-enabled delivery at speed" [S306] Reported.

6. Breadth for careers

Ucuzoglu's own list of reasons for keeping the model (March 2023, in a video after EY's split collapsed) was that clients value the breadth, people value "the diversity of career paths", markets value the quality and communities value the impact. He called the decision "not even a close call" and said previous separations had "never once played out as intended" [S308] Reported. In June 2022 Deloitte had already called media reports of a split "categorically untrue", adding "we remain committed to our current business model" [S309] Reported.

KEY TERM

Local currency growth: growth with exchange-rate effects stripped out. Deloitte's global revenue rose 5.7% in US dollars but 3.8% in local currency in FY26 [S300]. The local-currency figure is the "real" growth.

The decision that made Deloitte different: 2002-03

After Enron, regulators worried that auditors selling consulting were conflicted. The other big firms sold or spun off their consulting arms: Ernst & Young sold to Cap Gemini (2000), KPMG Consulting floated and became BearingPoint, and PwC Consulting was sold to IBM (2002) [S104] Reported. Deloitte announced in February 2002 that it would separate Deloitte Consulting as "Braxton". On 31 March 2003 it abandoned the plan, citing a "tight credit market and the uncertain state of the economy", and kept consulting "focused on nonaudit clients" [S104] Reported. That left Deloitte the only one of the big firms that still owned a large consulting practice [S104] Reported. By FY25, consulting (SR&T plus T&T) was US$43.7bn of Deloitte's US$70.5bn global revenue, about 62% [S81] Confirmed. Inferred Deloitte today is, by revenue, a technology and strategy consultancy attached to an audit firm.

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

The "only Big Four that kept consulting" history rests on one contemporary press report (InfoWorld, April 2003) [S104] and background knowledge; peer details are Reported, not checked against each firm's own records. PwC, EY and KPMG have all rebuilt large consulting businesses since. Say "Deloitte did not complete its planned spin-off, while the others sold theirs", not "Deloitte is the only firm with consulting".

What the structure costs

Cost 1: independence blocks selling

An auditor must be independent of the company it audits, or its opinion is worthless. UK rules turn that principle into hard limits. Under the FRC Revised Ethical Standard 2019 (effective 15 March 2020), auditors of UK public interest entities (PIEs: broadly listed companies, banks and insurers) may only provide a short "whitelist" of non-audit services, mostly work required by law or closely linked to the audit [S180] Confirmed. Non-audit fees from such clients are capped at 70% of the average audit fee of the previous three years [S182] [S180] Confirmed. Internal audit, secondments and contingent fees are banned for all audit clients [S180] [S181] Confirmed. The rules reach the whole network: services to a UK PIE's parent and worldwide subsidiaries are caught [S180] Confirmed. The current version is the Revised Ethical Standard 2024, effective 15 December 2024 [S178] Confirmed.

Inferred In practice, if Deloitte audits a FTSE company, Deloitte's T&T team generally cannot sell it an ERP implementation. Every large Deloitte audit client is a client the consulting side must largely leave to Accenture, PwC, EY or KPMG, and the reverse is true for them.

Cost 2: the regulator has ring-fenced audit inside the firm

On 6 July 2020 the FRC published principles requiring the Big Four to operationally separate their UK audit practices, with full implementation by 30 June 2024 [S183] Confirmed. The required outcomes include audit governance that protects auditors from the rest of the firm, and audit partners' profit share not persistently exceeding what the audit practice itself contributes, so there is no cross-subsidy [S183] Confirmed. Press reports of the approved plans add that dealings between audit and the rest of the firm must be at arm's length, and the audit practice may not receive fees for introducing work to other parts of the firm [S312] Reported. On 10 October 2024 the FRC said all four firms had completed the transition, with independent audit boards and more transparency on transactions between audit and non-audit businesses [S184] Confirmed. Deloitte UK's Audit Governance Board said ring-fencing "has undoubtedly played an important part" in better audit quality [S94] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Operational separation: the audit practice stays inside the same LLP (one legal firm, one brand) but has its own board, its own financial accounting and limits on what money and work can flow to and from the rest of the firm [S183] [S184]. It is separation inside the firm, not a legal split Inferred.

Cost 3: slow decisions across many partner-owned firms

Any structural change needs agreement across many partnerships. EY's attempt to split (below) failed partly for this reason [S310] Reported. Inferred A partnership can be patient, but it is rarely fast.

Cost 4: one brand, so one firm's mistake travels

In 2025 Deloitte Australia agreed to repay the final instalment of an AU$440,000 contract with Australia's Department of Employment and Workplace Relations, after a report on its welfare compliance framework was found to contain fabricated citations and an invented quote from a Federal Court judgment [S316] Confirmed. The revised report disclosed use of "a generative AI large language model (Azure OpenAI GPT-4o)" [S316]. It happened in a legally separate firm, yet the story ran worldwide under the Deloitte name, in the same week Deloitte announced its Claude deployment to 470,000+ people [S325] [S326]. Other cases make the same point: the US SEC fined Deloitte China US$20m in 2022 over audit failings [S111] Confirmed, and Deloitte UK has its own FRC record, including the record £15m Autonomy fine in 2020 [S105] Confirmed.

Deloitte UK's own risk register rates "Our reputation, role and future public interest impact" as a Very High residual risk, and lists "Increasing breadth and depth of non-audit offerings (including Operate)" as one of the threats [S94] Confirmed. In other words, the firm itself names the multidisciplinary model as a source of its top risk.

The natural experiment: EY's Project Everest

EY is the only one of the four to have seriously tried the alternative. Its plan, known as Project Everest, was to split audit from consulting and list the consulting side on the stock market. Its stated rationale was to address "conflicts of interest often associated with audit and advisory firms" and capture consulting growth [S310] Reported. It was abandoned on 12 April 2023 after the US executive committee withdrew, following a dispute over how much of the tax business should stay with audit, and opposition from member firms in China and Israel [S141] [S310] Reported. The reported cost was about US$600m [S141] Reported.

What the experiment shows Inferred: the split had real attractions (freedom to sell to audit clients, outside capital), but unpicking a multidisciplinary partnership is very hard. Tax sits naturally on both sides. Partners in each country have a vote. Deloitte's response has been to go the other way: a larger combined regional firm, Deloitte EMEA, funded by partners rather than by outside investors [S124] Confirmed.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Should the Big Four split audit from consulting?"

For a split: independence rules wall off the biggest clients from consulting; the UK regulator has already ring-fenced audit [S183]; Deloitte's own risk register rates its reputation as a Very High risk and names the breadth of non-audit work as a threat [S94]; a listed consultancy could raise capital without partners' pockets.

Against: FY25 showed the portfolio absorbing a 10% consulting fall [S88]; EY spent about US$600m and still could not agree the split [S141]; tax and risk work sit naturally with both sides; private capital in mid-tier firms (Grant Thornton) is a recent, unproven experiment [S144] [S145].

Suggested stance: "For Deloitte, the portfolio benefit and the investment capacity outweigh the lost access to audit clients today. The test I would watch is whether AI shrinks the hours on big implementation projects enough that consulting stops being the growth engine. Then the logic of keeping it tied to audit would weaken."

How the businesses work together

The matrix: offering by industry

Every Deloitte professional sits in an offering (what they do) and usually aligns to an industry (who they do it for). The six global industries are Consumer; Energy, Resources & Industrials; Financial Services; Government & Public Services; Life Sciences & Health Care; and Technology, Media & Telecommunications [S301] Confirmed. In the UK, Financial Services is the biggest industry at £1,735m of FY26 revenue, with Government & Public Services at £679m [S88] Confirmed.

UK T&T offerings named on Deloitte's careers page are Enterprise, Technology & Performance; Engineering, AI & Data; Cyber; Customer; Human Capital; and Defence & Security [S320] Confirmed. FY26 demand was for "enterprise technology support, including ERP implementation, Cyber and Human Capital services" [S303] Confirmed. Deloitte's own summary of the idea: "Our multidisciplinary model allows us to bring together technology, tools, insights, and deep industry experience across all businesses to provide integrated solutions" [S301] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Offering: a practice built around a skill, such as Cyber or Human Capital (people and organisation). ERP (enterprise resource planning): the core software that runs a company's finance, supply chain and HR, for example SAP, Oracle or Workday. ERP implementations are long, large programmes, which is why they drive T&T revenue.

Account teams: where collaboration lives

For large clients Deloitte appoints a Lead Client Service Partner (LCSP). Deloitte US profiles and postings describe the role as leveraging Deloitte's networks to support major relationships, making sure account plans are "developed, monitored", and that pursuit processes are run "consistently ... across the account" [S322] Reported. These sources are from the US member firm; the UK term and practice are assumed similar but not verified. Inferred Cross-selling is organised around the client, not the offering: the LCSP sees the whole wallet and offering partners bring specialists.

Alliances: the vendor sells the licence, Deloitte sells the implementation

Deloitte UK lists 14 alliance partners: Adobe, Anaplan, Apple, AWS, Google, Informatica, MuleSoft, Oracle, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UiPath, Workday and Workiva [S319] Confirmed. Its own description: "We combine our award-winning consulting services, market sensing data and trusted relationships with some of the largest technology firms to help solve your most complex challenges" [S319] Confirmed. Globally, Deloitte was named NVIDIA Global Consulting Partner of the Year 2026 for the fifth year running and won six Google Cloud Partner of the Year awards [S300] Confirmed. On 6 October 2025 Deloitte and Anthropic announced Claude for more than 470,000 Deloitte people, a Claude Center of Excellence and certification for 15,000 professionals [S325] Confirmed.

Delivery centres: where the building happens

Deloitte UK opened onshore technology centres in Belfast, Cardiff, Manchester and Newcastle from 2025, starting with 750 technologists and aiming for 1,500 within three years [S323] Reported. T&T managing partner Rob Cullen said the investment "accelerates our ambition to become the largest onshore technology capability in UK" [S323]. The FY26 results say the centres were "fully operational in FY26" [S407] Confirmed. Deloitte's US-India delivery organisation (USI) is reported at more than 100,000 people [S324] Reported, but it belongs to the US firm and its role on UK engagements is not established. Deloitte UK audit uses an offshore audit delivery centre, Global Audit India [S94] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Delivery centre: a lower-cost location where teams build, test and run technology for engagements led elsewhere. Onshore means inside the client's country (useful for security-cleared public sector work); offshore means abroad, often India.

Where independence blocks collaboration

Deloitte's own rule, from its Audit Transparency Report: "All proposed engagements and business and financial relationships go through a conflict check before they are accepted." If conflicts cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, "we decline the engagement" [S94] Confirmed. The audit partner is always consulted where a potential conflict touches an audit client [S94] Confirmed. A Public Interest Review Group reviews engagements with high reputational risk: 32 matters in FY25, of which 9% were declined [S94] Confirmed.

Inferred (from [S180] [S183] [S94]) So truly integrated, multi-business work happens mostly at clients that Deloitte does not audit (often audited by another Big Four firm), in the public sector, and in private companies below the PIE threshold.

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte can offer its audit clients the full package, from audit to tech implementation." For UK listed and other PIE audit clients, that is exactly what the rules forbid [S180]. Say instead: "The integrated model works best at clients Deloitte doesn't audit, which is why the conflict check comes before everything else."

What clients actually buy

Who the clients are

Deloitte serves "nearly 90% of the Fortune Global 500" [S300] Confirmed. Gartner ranks Deloitte the No. 1 consulting services provider worldwide by revenue; Deloitte's 2026 release says this is the ninth consecutive year [S125] Reported (Deloitte's release, Gartner report paywalled). In UK public procurement, Tussell data reported by Consultancy.uk shows UK public sector consulting spend at a record £3.7bn in 2024/25, up 6%, and Deloitte as the top supplier of key consulting contracts for five years running, with £400m+ in fees, about four times the next firm [S335] Reported. In late June 2026 Deloitte won a four-year Home Office data and analytics deal worth up to £200m [S233] Reported. "Up to" is a ceiling, not guaranteed spend Inferred.

What they are buying

  1. Scale at short notice. On NHS Test and Trace in 2020-21, Deloitte had around 900 to 1,035 consultants working at peak [S332] [S333] Confirmed. Few organisations can find a thousand people in weeks.
  2. Certified platform skills. 14 UK alliances [S319] and, globally, 15,000 people to be certified on Claude [S325]. Deloitte US cites more than 36,000 SAP-focused professionals [S146] Confirmed.
  3. Sector depth from the industry side of the matrix [S301].
  4. A defensible choice. A board or minister can justify hiring the firm Gartner ranks No. 1 [S125] Inferred.
  5. Risk transfer. A contract with a large balance sheet behind it. The Australian refund shows the mechanism working in reverse: the client got money back [S316] Inferred.

Why they accept the price

Rates disclosed to Parliament: Deloitte staff on Test and Trace cost about £1,000 a day each, close to £1m a day in total, with some senior consultants up to £6,624 a day [S332] [S333] Confirmed. Deloitte's contracts were worth £298m, with £174m spent by end-March 2021 [S332] [S333]. The government's explanation was "skills shortages in certain areas of the civil service" and "comparatively low salaries in the civil service" [S333] Reported. The National Audit Office (NAO, Parliament's spending watchdog) found in November 2025 that 86% of survey respondents said consultants made valuable contributions [S334] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Day rate: the price a client pays per consultant per day. It covers salary, the firm's overheads, time between projects and partner profit, which is why it is far higher than the consultant's own daily pay. Deloitte recognises revenue on time-and-materials or on fixed fees managed internally through "actual inputs of time at charge-out rates" [S93] Confirmed.

The counter-case, with numbers

  • Performance. During heavy consultant use on Test and Trace, only 17% of people got test results within 24 hours against a 90% target [S332] Reported.
  • Dependence. In April 2021 Test and Trace had 2,239 external workers; consultants were still 45% of central staff [S333] Reported.
  • Visibility. The NAO said "Government does not have consistent data on how much individual departments are spending on external consultants" [S334] Confirmed. HM Treasury estimated central government spend at about £1.36bn in 2022-23; the government targeted £550m of savings in 2024-25 and £700m by 2028-29 [S334] Confirmed. Yet Tussell measured wider public sector consulting at a record £3.7bn in 2024/25 [S335] Reported. The two figures use different scopes, so do not compare them directly.
  • Ideas. Mariana Mazzucato and Rosie Collington's book The Big Con (2023) argues that over-reliance on consultancies weakens state capability, charges well above equivalent public staff and creates conflicts of interest, naming the Big Four including Deloitte [S337] Reported (summary only, book not read). Critics said its idea of public value is loosely defined [S337].
  • Quality failure. The Australian AI report [S316].
YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Is the government right to keep buying from firms like Deloitte?"

Yes: the civil service cannot hire a thousand people in weeks; the NAO found most users valued the work [S334]; data and digital skills are scarce, which is why the Home Office still bought up to £200m of data work after pledging cuts [S233].

No: £1,000+ a day per person on Test and Trace, 45% of central staff from outside, and weak results against targets [S332] [S333]; the state cannot even count what it spends [S334]; The Big Con argues it hollows out capability [S337].

Suggested stance: "Short, sharp capacity in a crisis is good value. Long-term dependence is not. The best engagements leave the client able to do it themselves, and I'd want to work on ones that are designed to hand over."

The non-core side: the centre and internal AI

Enabling Functions

Deloitte UK calls its internal support business "Enabling Functions". Its own line: "In Enabling Functions we support our colleagues to do that well, so the firm can continue to make a positive impact" [S330] Confirmed. Two early-careers routes are named on Deloitte's pages. The Leadership Support Centre in Cardiff supports senior leaders. Quality, Risk & Security Services (Cardiff and London) covers client vetting, conflict checks, anti-money laundering and cyber security, with sub-teams for Financial Crime, Independence, Deloitte Business and Security, Strategy and Operations, and Contentious Matters [S330] Confirmed. Search results also name People and Performance (HR), Growth, IT Services, Finance, Administration and Corporate Responsibility, with Cardiff described as the centre for centralised business operations [S331] Reported (snippet only). No headcount for Enabling Functions was found.

Inferred The Independence team is where the rules in Figure 7 are enforced day to day. Before T&T can start work, Quality, Risk & Security checks whether the client is an audit client and whether there is a conflict. The friction point of the multidisciplinary model has been turned into a job.

Internal AI

  • PairD. Deloitte's own generative AI assistant, built by its AI Institute, rolled out in the UK from October 2023 and to 75,000 people across Europe and the Middle East by January 2024 [S328] Confirmed. Staff had to complete training and were warned output may be inaccurate [S328]. UK staff were sending it 1 million prompts a month in FY25 [S85] Confirmed, and new graduates were introduced to it at induction in 2025 [S232] Confirmed.
  • Claude. Made available to more than 470,000 Deloitte people globally from October 2025, with 15,000 certifications planned [S325] [S326] Confirmed.
  • Zora AI. A set of AI agents sold to clients on subscription, launched March 2025. Deloitte said it would use Zora AI for Finance internally for expenses, targeting 25% lower costs and 40% higher productivity [S327] Reported (targets, not outcomes).
  • Governance. From 1 June 2026, Hayley McKelvey joined the UK Executive as Chief AI Officer, "responsible for driving the firm's AI strategy across client services and internal operations" [S407] Confirmed. Deloitte US's equivalent assistant, Sidekick, reports "about two hours saved per user each week" [S329], but that is a US tool, not established in the UK.
SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"What struck me is that the UK made AI an executive job this year: a Chief AI Officer covering both client work and internal operations. Staff were already sending PairD a million prompts a month, and Claude went to 470,000 people globally. I'd like to understand how that changes an analyst's first year, and what checks sit around AI-assisted deliverables after the Australian report."

Putting it together: how a client team is wired into the firm

Figure 13 pulls the pieces into one picture of where a graduate actually sits. There are three kinds of role around every engagement. Embedded roles do the client work every day. Connective roles link the team to the rest of the firm and to vendors. Utility roles are shared services the team draws on without thinking about them, until something goes wrong (the pack's own framing) Inferred.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"As I understand it, collaboration at Deloitte is organised around the client: a lead client partner sees the whole relationship and pulls in specialists from other offerings, and the alliances with platforms like SAP and Workday supply the technology. The limit is independence. At audit clients most of that is off the table, so the integrated model really shows up at non-audit and public sector clients."

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte's culture is really collaborative." Everyone says it and it tells the interviewer nothing. Name the mechanism instead: the offering-by-industry matrix, the LCSP, alliances, and the conflict check that decides where collaboration is even allowed [S301] [S94].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Will AI break the consulting pyramid?"

It will: UK fee-earning staff fell 5% in FY26 while revenue rose 2% and profit 14% [S93] [S407]; the firm offered voluntary redundancy in audit because too few people were leaving [S407]; T&T was the slowest-growing business globally at 2.5% [S300].

It won't, yet: Deloitte still hired 1,950+ graduates, apprentices and interns in FY26 [S407]; the UK CEO's line is that "the role our people play will matter more, not less" [S407]; large ERP and cyber programmes still need many people.

Suggested stance: "The base of the pyramid gets narrower and the work at the base changes from producing to checking and judging. That is why I'd want a firm that trains people on the tools early."

Part 4

How Deloitte stands out, and what only it can claim

Deloitte against nine rivals on size, shape and design choices; the handful of things only Deloitte can honestly claim; and, just as useful in an interview, where it does not lead.

The field at a glance

Deloitte competes with three kinds of firm. The other Big Four (PwC, EY, KPMG) have the same shape: audit plus tax plus consulting, owned by partners. Listed technology services firms (Accenture, IBM Consulting, Capgemini) have no audit and are owned by shareholders. Strategy houses (McKinsey, BCG, Bain) are partner-owned, much smaller and focused on advice. Each latest year is different, because the firms' financial years end in different months. Read the "period" column before comparing.
