KEY TERM

Managed services (Deloitte calls its version "Operate"): running part of a client's operations or technology for years at a time, for a recurring fee, rather than doing a project and leaving. It brings steadier revenue. Half of Accenture's revenue is managed services [S129]; Deloitte's FY26 release named Operate as an area of "significant growth" without giving a number [S120] Confirmed.

Six design choices, and where each firm sits

Size is the least interesting difference. The more useful comparison is design: six choices each firm has made, and what each choice costs. Figure 8 places each firm on each choice. Positions on five axes are approximate judgements from the evidence in this Part; axis 4 is calculated.

1. Audit inside the firm, or independent of audit?

The Big Four keep audit. That gives them a trust brand and board-level access, and costs them most consulting at their own audit clients (Part 3, Figure 7). Everyone else is free of that limit. EY's failed split [S141] and KPMG's new US law firm, which may not serve KPMG audit clients [S142], show how much the constraint bites. A newer UK challenger, Unity Advisory, launched in April 2025 with up to US$300m from Warburg Pincus and no audit at all; its co-founder Steve Varley pitches a firm that "crucially, has no conflicts" [S167] Confirmed.

2. Strategy to operations, or specialism?

Deloitte spans strategy (Monitor Deloitte, bought in 2013 [S134]), technology delivery (T&T), risk, deals, tax, audit and Operate [S120]. Accenture spans strategy to managed services, without audit or tax [S129]. Strategy houses are narrower, though BCG now earns over 40% of revenue from AI and tech-focused work [S133].

3. Partnership or listed company?

Partnerships fund investment from partners' profits and can take a long view. Listed firms raise capital easily but answer to shareholders every quarter: Accenture returned a record US$11.5bn to shareholders in FY26 [S129] Confirmed. Private equity is a middle path in the mid-tier: New Mountain Capital took about 60% of Grant Thornton US's non-audit business in 2024 [S144] and Cinven bought into Grant Thornton UK in 2025 [S145] Reported. None of the Big Four has done this.

4. Pyramid shape

Revenue per head is a rough measure of the pyramid. Low revenue per head means big delivery teams and heavy offshore use; high means small teams of expensive experts. By the pack's arithmetic: BCG about US$430k, McKinsey about US$375-400k, PwC about US$156k, Deloitte about US$149k, KPMG about US$144k, EY about US$131k, Accenture about US$91k, Capgemini about €53k Inferred (from [S120] [S126] [S127] [S128] [S129] [S132] [S133] [S135]).

5. Alliance-led or vendor-neutral?

Deloitte and Accenture are built around platform alliances; Deloitte US cites "over 36,000 SAP-focused professionals" [S146] Confirmed. Strategy houses were traditionally neutral, though Bain now describes "a vibrant ecosystem of technology partners" [S406].

6. Time-and-materials or managed services?

Accenture is half managed services and reports bookings (signed future work) [S129]. Deloitte is mostly project work with Operate growing [S120]. Strategy houses are mostly project fees.

What only Deloitte can claim

These are the claims that survive checking. Each comes with the evidence, the safe wording, and why it matters to you.

1. The largest of the Big Four by a wide margin, level with Accenture

Evidence: US$74.5bn in FY26, against PwC US$56.9bn, EY US$53.2bn and KPMG US$39.8bn (their latest years) [S120] [S126] [S127] [S128] Confirmed. Accenture reported US$74.18bn for a year ending three months later [S129]. Safe wording: "the largest of the Big Four by a wide margin, and roughly level with Accenture as the largest professional services firm." Why it matters: scale funds investment such as the US$3bn AI programme [S120] and gives graduates exposure to more sectors.

2. No. 1 in Gartner's consulting services market share, nine years running

Evidence: Deloitte's release says it is the "No. 1 consulting services provider by revenue" for "the ninth consecutive year and 14th time in total" [S125] Reported (Deloitte's own release; the Gartner report is paywalled). Why it matters: an outside analyst measures it, and it covers consulting only, not audit.

3. It kept consulting when the others sold theirs

Evidence: after Enron, EY sold its consulting arm to Cap Gemini (2000), KPMG Consulting floated as BearingPoint and PwC Consulting went to IBM (2002). Deloitte planned to spin off "Braxton" and abandoned the plan on 31 March 2003 [S104] Reported. Safe wording: "Deloitte did not complete its planned consulting spin-off, while EY, KPMG and PwC sold theirs." Why it matters: a twenty-year head start in running audit and consulting as one firm; consulting is now about 62% of global revenue [S81] Confirmed. The peer details rest on one contemporary report, and all three rivals have since rebuilt consulting arms.

4. Strategy through Operate, plus audit, under one brand

Evidence: Monitor Deloitte (strategy, acquired 2013) [S134], T&T and SR&T [S120], Operate [S120] and Audit & Assurance. Accenture has no audit; strategy houses have no audit or large-scale implementation; PwC, EY and KPMG have the same shape but smaller consulting businesses [S126] [S127] [S128]. Confirmed for each part; the "only one" claim is Inferred. Why it matters: a graduate can see a problem from diagnosis to running the fix.

5. The largest single Big Four regional firm in Europe

Evidence: Deloitte EMEA: 16 firms, 132,000 people, 6,000 partners, €20bn, from 1 June 2026, with more than €1.5bn of planned extra investment [S124] Confirmed. KPMG's UK-Swiss combination is much smaller [S140]. Houston: "Deloitte EMEA uniquely strengthens our ability to invest at scale across borders" [S124]. ["Largest" and "first" are Inferred; verify before saying either.] Why it matters: a London graduate joins a firm that can staff and invest across 80+ countries.

6. The UK government's top consulting supplier five years running

Evidence: Tussell data: Deloitte top supplier of key consulting contracts for five years, £400m+ in fees, about four times the next firm [S335] Reported. A separate City AM analysis of Tussell data found £431m of UK government consultancy contracts to Deloitte in Labour's first year, ahead of PA Consulting (£310m) and KPMG (£301m) [S174] Reported. Why it matters: many T&T analysts start on public sector work, and some of it needs security clearance. It also means Deloitte is the first name critics reach for (Part 3).

7. The biggest enterprise AI rollout of its kind, at announcement

Evidence: Claude made available to more than 470,000 Deloitte people in October 2025, with 15,000 certifications [S325]; CNBC called it Anthropic's "biggest enterprise deployment ever" [S326] Confirmed. Deloitte was also NVIDIA's Global Consulting Partner of the Year for the fifth year running [S300] Confirmed. Why it matters: the tools you would use day to day, and the skills you could be certified in.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"Deloitte and Accenture are now almost exactly the same size, around US$74bn. The difference is that half of Accenture is managed services, while Deloitte also has audit and tax. What draws me is the breadth: strategy, technology and the Operate side in one firm, with the portfolio holding steady when consulting dips."

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte is the biggest consulting firm in the world on every measure." Accenture matches it on revenue, has about 300,000 more people and is far bigger in managed services [S129]. Gartner's ranking is by consulting revenue only [S125].

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte is the only Big Four firm with a consulting business." PwC Advisory is US$24.3bn and EY Consulting US$16.4bn [S126] [S127]. The defensible point is historical: Deloitte did not complete its 2002-03 spin-off [S104].

DON'T SAY THIS

"Deloitte EMEA is the first firm of its kind." That is an inference, not something Deloitte or our sources state. Say "16 firms, 132,000 people, €20bn" and let the numbers do the work [S124].

Where Deloitte does not lead

Saying this plainly is a sign you have done the work. Interviewers trust candidates who know the weak spots.

  • Growth. Deloitte grew 3.8% in local currency in FY26 [S120]. Accenture grew 5% [S129], BCG 7% [S133] and KPMG 5.1% in its FY25 [S128]. Deloitte's T&T grew only 2.5%, the slowest of its four businesses [S120] Confirmed.
  • UK consulting in FY25. Deloitte UK T&T fell 10%, the worst of the Big Four UK consulting falls found: EY UK consulting -6% [S139], KPMG UK Advisory -3% [S140], PwC UK consulting -3% [S401] Reported.
  • Strategy prestige. McKinsey, BCG and Bain own the top-strategy brand. BCG's revenue per head is nearly three times Deloitte's Inferred (from [S120] [S133]).
  • Managed services scale and visibility. Accenture's managed services alone are US$37.3bn, and it reports bookings that show future work [S129]. Deloitte does not report bookings.
  • UK audit quality, 2026. In the FRC's July 2026 inspections, KPMG scored 95% of audits good or needing only limited improvement, Deloitte 90%, EY 90% and PwC 89% [S137] Reported (one secondary outlet). Deloitte ties for second.
  • UK headline size. Deloitte's £5.81bn includes Switzerland [S407]; PwC's UK group (with the Middle East) reported £6.155bn [S138]. On UK-only figures Deloitte (£5,014m) is bigger than PwC UK (£4.365bn), but the scopes differ [S88] [S138].
  • Reputation. No rival had the Australian AI report [S316], though every Big Four firm has FRC fines; KPMG's five-year total was the largest [S110] Reported.
YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Why Deloitte and not Accenture?" (expect this if you mention technology).

Accenture's case: bigger technology and managed services business [S129], no audit independence limits, faster growth, and a published graduate salary of £35,190 plus a signing bonus on one listing [S402] Reported.

Deloitte's case: breadth beyond technology (tax, deals, risk, strategy) [S120]; a partnership that kept investing through a 10% consulting fall [S88]; UK onshore technology centres [S323]; the UK's top government consulting supplier [S335].

Suggested stance: "If I only wanted to build systems at scale, Accenture would be a fair choice. I want to see the business problem as well as the system, and Deloitte's mix of strategy, risk and technology in one partnership gives a graduate that view."

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Is the slow T&T growth a warning sign?"

Yes: global T&T grew 2.5%, slowest of the four [S120]; City AM framed it as "industry-wide pressure from artificial intelligence" [S222]; small UK firms are cutting consulting spend while paying AI companies [S239].

No: UK T&T grew 4%, the fastest UK business [S407]; MCA members forecast UK consulting growth of 5.7% for 2026 [S241]; clients are turning to consultants for AI transformation help [S240].

Suggested stance: "It is a signal that the work is changing, from big programmes measured in hours to AI-enabled delivery measured in outcomes. The firms that win will be the ones that change how they price."

Part 5

The industry from zero

What consulting sells, who buys it, how a firm turns a working day into profit, how big the market is, and the forces reshaping it. Read this before any of the opinion sections: every argument later in the pack rests on the mechanics here.

What consulting sells, and who buys it

A consultancy sells people's time and judgement to an organisation with a problem it cannot, or will not, solve alone. Strip away the branding and a client is buying one or more of five things Inferred:

What the client buysWhat it means in practiceExample
ExpertiseKnowledge the client does not have in house.How to move a bank's core systems to the cloud; how to meet a new regulation.
CapacityExtra hands for a fixed period. The client may know what to do but lack the people. A lot of "consulting" spend is this.Around 900 to 1,035 Deloitte consultants worked on Test and Trace at peak [S332][S333] Reported.
IndependenceAn outside view not tied to internal politics.A CEO quoted in HBR: when unsure of the question, "I'm more tempted to use a big brand" [S160] Confirmed.
LegitimacyA known firm's name helps a board or minister defend a decision."No. 1 consulting provider by revenue" is a ranking a buyer can cite [S125] Reported.
ImplementationBuilding and running the change: systems, processes, training. This is where most of the money now flows.Source says global technology consulting will pass $400bn in 2026 [S157] Reported.

Who signs the cheque. In large companies the buyer is usually a C-suite executive: the chief financial officer (CFO) for finance and cost work, the chief information or technology officer (CIO, CTO) for technology, the chief operating officer (COO) for operations Inferred. Source Global Research, a consulting market analyst, says digital transformation projects "are most likely to be commissioned by CxOs, so companies are prepared to pay more for them" [S157] Reported. Banks and insurers buy heavily because regulation forces change on them (Part 6). The public sector (central government, the NHS, local government, defence) is the other big buyer. Old MCA data put financial services at about a third of UK fee income and the public sector at about a fifth, but that data set dates from around 2016 to 2018, so treat the shares as indicative only [S159] Reported.

KEY TERM

Engagement (or project): one piece of paid work for one client, with a start, an end and a contract. SOW (statement of work): the contract document that sets out what will be delivered, by when, by whom and for how much. When a Deloitte analyst says "I'm on an engagement", this is what they mean.

The five kinds of firm, and how they differ

"Consulting" covers very different businesses. The useful split is by what each type mainly sells and to whom. The taxonomy below is an analyst's grouping Inferred; the named examples come from the sources shown.

TypeUK examplesWhat they mainly sellTypical buyerScale signal
Strategy houses ("MBB")McKinsey, BCG, BainBoard-level strategy, M&A strategy, more and more AI-led transformationCEO, board, private equity fundsBCG: US$14.4bn revenue, 33,500 people (2025) [S133] Confirmed
Big Four consulting armsDeloitte, PwC, EY, KPMGStrategy through to delivery: technology, finance, risk, regulation, people, operations. They also audit, which limits who they can advise.CFO, CIO, COO, chief risk officer, governmentDeloitte global US$74.5bn (FY26), all businesses [S120] Confirmed
Tech and IT services firmsAccenture, IBM, Capgemini, Indian IT majorsLarge technology builds, enterprise software, cloud, long-term managed services, offshore deliveryCIO, CTOAccenture US$74.18bn, half of it managed services (FY26) [S129] Confirmed
Mid-tier and boutiquesPA Consulting, Grant Thornton, BDO, Baringa; challengers Unity Advisory, Queen's Tower Advisory, Eden McCallumSpecialist or mid-market work; some pitch senior-heavy, AI-heavy or "no conflicts" teamsMid-sized firms, PE-backed companies, public sectorPA won £310m of UK government consultancy contracts in Labour's first year [S174] Reported
In-house teams (and AI labs)Corporate strategy units and "transformation offices" staffed by ex-consultants; OpenAI and Anthropic consulting venturesThe work clients used to buy from outsiden/a (they are the client)OpenAI bought UK consultancy Tomoro AI, about 150 staff [S166] Reported

Size concentrates. In MCA data, large firms take 77% of UK consulting fee income, medium firms 20% and small firms 3% [S150] Reported. Deloitte sits at the intersection of two columns: it is a Big Four firm, and its Technology & Transformation business competes head-on with Accenture and IBM for technology delivery.

How consulting differs from its neighbours

Interviewers test whether you know what you are applying for. Many applicants blur consulting with audit, deal work or banking. The table below is the cleanest way to keep them apart. Definitions are general knowledge Inferred except where a source is shown.

BusinessWhat it deliversHow it is paidRegulated byTypical graduate taskLink to Deloitte consulting
ConsultingAdvice and delivery of change: strategy, technology, operations, riskMostly time (day rates) or fixed fee; some outcome-linked feesNo licence or statutory regulator for consulting itselfResearch, data analysis, slides, testing, workshop notesThis is the role.
AuditA legally required opinion on whether financial statements give a "true and fair view"Annual audit feeFRC; the auditor must be independentTesting transactions and controlsIf Deloitte audits a company, Deloitte consulting is heavily restricted there [S180] Confirmed
TaxCompliance (filing returns) and tax adviceFees by time or fixedProfessional bodies; tax lawPreparing computations, researchSeparate business line (Tax & Legal, £1.36bn UK, FY26) [S407]
Deal advisory (transaction services)Due diligence, valuation, restructuring around one transactionTime-bound fees tied to the dealProfessional rulesFinancial models, data roomsSits in Deloitte's SR&T business with strategy and risk
Investment bankingRaising capital; advising on mergers and acquisitionsMostly success fees when a deal completesFCAPitch books, valuation modelsA neighbour, not a competitor for most consulting work

DON'T SAY THIS

"Consulting is basically like investment banking but for operations." The payment model is the giveaway: banks earn mainly when a deal completes; consultancies earn mainly for time or a defined deliverable, and the hard part is getting change to stick after the deal or decision.

How a consulting firm makes money

Every consulting firm runs on the same four levers. Learn them and the industry's news makes sense: AI, graduate cuts, offshore centres and outcome pricing all act on one or more of them.

KEY TERM

Day rate (rate card): the price per day the firm charges for one person of a given grade. A rate card is the list of rates by grade agreed with a client. Rates disclosed to Parliament for Deloitte's Test and Trace work averaged about £1,000 a day per person, with some senior consultants up to £6,624 a day [S332] Confirmed.

KEY TERM

Utilisation: the share of a person's available working time that is billed to clients. Chargeable hours are the hours actually billed. Juniors are expected to be highly chargeable; partners spend more time selling and managing [S93] Inferred. Deloitte does not publish its utilisation targets.

KEY TERM

Leverage: how many staff work under each partner. More juniors per partner means each partner's profit share draws on more billed hours. At Deloitte UK in FY26 that was roughly 30 staff per equity partner and about 16.5 per partner of any kind (my arithmetic from 23,970 average FTE staff, 799 FTE equity partners and 1,453 partners) [S88][S93] Inferred. Realisation: the share of the standard value of time that is actually billed and collected after discounts and write-offs [S93].

KEY TERM

The pyramid: the staffing shape that leverage produces. A few partners and directors at the top; more managers; many consultants and analysts at the base. Equity partner: an owner of the partnership who shares the profit. Deloitte UK had 784 equity partners at year end FY26 [S407] Confirmed.

Put together, the arithmetic is simple. Revenue per person is billed days times day rate. Billed days are available days times utilisation. Leverage multiplies that across the team under each partner. What is left after pay, offices, technology and network fees is the profit pool that equity partners share. Deloitte's own accounts show that even fixed-fee work is tracked "via timesheet reporting" at charge-out rates [S93] Confirmed, so these levers still govern a project priced as a lump sum.

Two live numbers show the levers at work. Deloitte UK's average fee-earning staff fell about 5% (21,471 to 20,346 FTE) in FY26 while revenue rose 2% and distributable profit rose 14% to £899m [S93][S407] Confirmed. More revenue from fewer fee-earners is leverage and productivity moving in partners' favour Inferred. That is also exactly why AI is such a sensitive topic: it acts on the base of the pyramid.

Core vocabulary in one place

Bench: consultants not currently on a client project. Long bench time hurts utilisation.

Pitch / RFP: the competitive bid to win work. RFP means "request for proposal", the buyer's formal invitation to bid.

Framework agreement: a pre-approved list of suppliers a buyer (often government) can call work off without a full tender each time. Example: the UK government's Management Consultancy Framework Four (MCF4), with 219 suppliers across 10 lots [S117] Confirmed.

Managed services: the consultancy runs a process or system for the client for years. Revenue recurs. Deloitte calls its offer "Operate" [S120].

Time and materials (T&M): the client pays for days worked. Fixed fee: one price for a defined deliverable. Outcome-based (risk and reward): some fee depends on results. MCF4 allows all three [S117] Confirmed.

Offshore / nearshore delivery: doing work in lower-cost locations (India, Malaysia, the Philippines are named in reporting on the Big Four) or nearby cheaper countries [S162] Reported. Onshore regional centres: lower-cost UK cities. Deloitte opened centres in Belfast, Cardiff, Manchester and Newcastle from June 2025 [S254] Confirmed.

Alliance partners: software vendors (SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, AWS and others) whose products the consultancy implements. Deloitte UK lists 14 [S319] Confirmed.

Systems integrator (SI): a firm that makes several software products work together inside a client. ERP (enterprise resource planning): core finance, HR and supply chain software such as SAP S/4HANA. Big, long and risky projects.

PMO (programme management office): the team that runs plans, governance and reporting on a large programme. TOM (target operating model): a design of how an organisation should work in future. Change management: helping people actually adopt the new way of working.

How big is the market?

Two respected bodies measure the UK market and get very different answers. Neither is wrong. They count different things.

£21.8bnUK consulting fee income 2025, +3% (MCA / Oxford Economics, July 2026) [S150][S151]
£14.9bnUK market 2024 on Source Global Research's narrower definition [S154]
$275bnGlobal consulting market 2025, +6% (Source, "big consulting") [S156]
>$400bnGlobal technology consulting, 2026 forecast, broader definition (Source) [S157]

MCA. The Management Consultancies Association, the UK trade body, publishes an annual report with Oxford Economics. It estimates the whole UK industry. Fee income rose 3% to £21.8bn in 2025; MCA members alone earned £10.9bn; exports rose 9% and are now 31% of fee income [S150][S151] Confirmed. The headline hides a split: 52% of firms grew and 46% shrank. The report says the 3% "masks a mixed performance across the sector" [S151] Reported. Forecasts have been cut again and again: 2026 growth was predicted at 8.7% (January 2025), then 7.8% (mid-2025), then 5.7% (early 2026); the July 2026 report says 6% for 2026 and 8% for 2027 [S154][S150] Reported.

Source Global Research. Source counts only "big consulting": firms with 50 or more consultants, and it excludes outsourcing and managed services [S157] Reported. On that basis the UK market was £14.9bn in 2024, down from £15.4bn [S154][S241] Reported. Source forecasts 6% UK growth in 2026 from a survey of 200 senior UK buyers. Its head of market trends, Nick Jotischky: "There's a cautious optimism that there's going to be growth in the market" [S155] Confirmed.

Global. Source sized global consulting at $275bn in 2025, 6% growth after "a disappointing 2024". Cybersecurity was the fastest-growing service at about 9% (about $36bn); technology and innovation was $69.2bn (+5%); strategy just over $60bn (+6%); risk and financial management $58.7bn (+7%) [S156] Reported. Its separate $400bn+ figure for technology consulting uses a broader definition. Do not add the two together [S157].

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

The MCA's 2025 report gave £20.4bn for 2024 [S152][S153]. The 2026 report says 2025 grew 3% to £21.8bn [S150]. £21.8bn is about 7% above £20.4bn, so the 2024 base was probably revised upward to around £21.2bn Inferred. If you quote growth, quote the MCA's own 3%, not a figure computed across the two reports.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"The UK market is roughly £22bn on the MCA's measure and grew only 3% last year, with nearly half of firms shrinking. The forecast recovery, 6% then 8%, depends on clients moving from planning to implementation. That suits a firm that can deliver, not only advise."

The forces reshaping the industry now

Eight forces are pushing on the consulting model at once. Figure 24 maps each force to what it changes and who gains or loses. The text below gives the numbers.

1. Generative and agentic AI, and the pyramid

If AI drafts research, slides and code, firms need fewer analysts at the base. A recruiter told City AM: "The Big Four are looking at AI very seriously to replicate junior work more cost-effectively" [S162] Reported. A summary of a May 2026 FT Big Read (paywalled, not read) quotes KPMG UK's advisory head Lisa Fernihough: "I want this organisation, us, to still exist … That's how disruptive I believe AI will be" [S164] Reported. Mark Bunker, formerly of Deloitte, who founded Queen's Tower Advisory, reportedly targets teams that are "20 per cent humans, 80 per cent AI agents" [S164] Reported. Agentic AI means AI systems that take actions (book, file, update records) rather than only answer questions. Deloitte's own Tech Trends 2026 says only 11% of organisations have such systems in production [S244] Confirmed.

2. Pricing moves from days to outcomes

McKinsey is reported to link about a quarter to a third of fees to outcomes; sources disagree on the figure [S163][S164] Reported. In 2013 a partner quoted in HBR expected value-based pricing to go "from the high single digits to a third of the business within 20 years" [S160] Confirmed. A commentator writing in January 2026 called the shift "sluggish" [S163] Reported.

3. Graduate intake cuts and low attrition

Reported UK graduate intakes fell at all of the Big Four between 2023 and 2024: KPMG 1,399 to 942 (-29%), Deloitte about 1,700 to 1,400 (-18%), EY -11%, PwC -6% [S162][S143] Reported. Graduate accountancy adverts fell 44% year on year [S162] Reported. Attrition is the share of staff who leave each year. Big Four firms rely on it to make room for promotions. When fewer leave, firms pay people to go: Deloitte offered voluntary redundancy to up to about 175 audit staff in June 2026, citing "low rates of attrition" [S227] Confirmed. The wider market is mixed: MCA members raised graduate hiring 10% in 2025 [S150] Reported.

4. New entrants

OpenAI and Anthropic launched consulting ventures in May 2026, and OpenAI bought UK consultancy Tomoro AI (about 150 staff, clients including Tesco and Virgin Atlantic). An industry insider called it "definitely a direct play against the traditional consulting firms" [S166] Reported. Unity Advisory launched in April 2025 with up to $300m from private equity firm Warburg Pincus, led by ex-EY UK chair Steve Varley. It offers no audit, so it has no audit conflicts [S167] Confirmed.

5. Private equity enters professional services

Private equity (PE) firms buy companies with investors' money and sell them later. Cinven completed a buyout of Grant Thornton UK in 2025, reportedly valuing it around £1.5bn; the average partner payout was reported at £682,000 [S168] Reported. In the US, New Mountain Capital took about 60% of Grant Thornton's non-audit business in 2024 [S144] Reported. None of the Big Four has taken outside capital [S144][S120] Inferred.

6. UK government spend controls

In October 2023 Rachel Reeves, then shadow Chancellor, said Labour "will aim to cut consultancy spending in half over the next parliament" [S176] Confirmed. In government the target became: stop non-essential consultancy, halve it in 2025-26, save £550m in 2024-25 rising to £700m a year by 2028-29 [S173][S177] Confirmed. The data conflict sharply; Part 6 sets them side by side. Deloitte matters here because it was the largest UK government consultancy supplier by contract value in Labour's first year, at £431m [S174] Reported.

7. The US DOGE cuts

In 2025 the US Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) drive cancelled federal contracts. The Pentagon cancelled $5.1bn of contracts in April 2025 (claimed savings $4bn), naming Accenture, Booz Allen Hamilton and Deloitte [S169] Confirmed. Fortune reported more than 120 Deloitte contracts eliminated, more than twice any other consultancy [S170] Reported. This hit Deloitte's US firm, a legally separate member firm from Deloitte UK, but it shows the risk of depending on government buyers Inferred.

8. AI quality failure: Deloitte Australia

In October 2025 Deloitte Australia agreed to partially refund the A$440,000 paid for a 237-page government report that contained a fabricated court quote and references to non-existent papers. The revised version disclosed use of "a generative AI large language model (Azure OpenAI GPT-4o)" [S316][S171] Confirmed. It happened in a separate member firm, yet the story ran worldwide under the Deloitte name [S316] Inferred. It is the clearest public example of why human review of AI output is now part of the product.

Where it goes in the next three to five years: five competing views

Serious people disagree. Know at least three positions and who holds them, then pick your own.

ViewWho holds itThe argument
"Disruption comes slowly, then suddenly"Christensen, Wang and van Bever, HBR, Oct 2013 [S160] ConfirmedConsulting moves from integrated "solution shops" to modular providers. Knowledge is "democratized". The story "will begin with smaller clients". "The steady invasion of hard analytics and technology (big data) is a certainty". Closing line: "there may be nothing as vulnerable as entrenched success". AI is the strongest version yet of the force they described Inferred.
"AI breaks the pyramid and the scale advantage"FT Big Read and City AM (May 2026, as summarised); The Telegraph (26 May 2026) [S164][S166] ReportedAI-native boutiques and AI labs take work. The Big Four's leverage model weakens. Graduate intakes fall. KPMG's Fernihough frames the threat as existential.
"Cautious recovery, driven by implementation"Source Global Research; MCA [S155][S150][S157]"Clients are embarking on a year of implementation and execution, and that will often lead to a need for external support" (Nick Jotischky) [S155]. UK growth of about 6% in 2026 and 8% in 2027. 81% of tech buyers intend to rely more on external consultants [S157] Reported.
"Conflict-free, PE-funded, outcome-priced challengers win share"Steve Varley, Unity Advisory [S167]; Cinven / Grant Thornton [S168]"People are looking for a proposition that is super client-centric, has really low administrative cost, is AI-led rather than based on legacy infrastructure and, crucially, has no conflicts" [S167] Confirmed.
"The old pyramid persists"Marin Ivezic, January 2026 (single commentator) [S163] ReportedFirms have spent billions on AI yet still staff and bill the traditional way. The move to outcome pricing is slow.

Deloitte's own line sits between the third and fifth views. UK CEO Darren Graves, in the FY26 results: "As AI makes intelligence increasingly abundant, the role our people play will matter more, not less" [S407] Confirmed. Global CEO Joe Ucuzoglu describes "a people-led, AI-powered approach that is grounded in trust" [S120] Confirmed.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Where will consulting be in five years?" Pick a side and give a mechanism.

Case for disruption: AI removes the junior hours that pay for the pyramid; AI labs and PE-backed challengers attack on price; SME card data already show consulting spend falling 1.9% while AI subscriptions rise [S239] Reported.

Case for resilience: clients' main AI barriers are data security (40%), skills (34%) and governance (28%), which are human and organisational problems [S240] Reported; MCA and Source both forecast growth [S150][S155].

Suggested stance: "I think demand for implementation grows while demand for junior analytical hours shrinks. The winners will be firms with delivery depth, trusted brands in regulated sectors and AI alliances, provided they change how they price and how they train juniors. So the pyramid becomes narrower at the base, not flat." Then name one fact: Deloitte UK grew profit 14% on 2% revenue growth while fee-earners fell about 5% [S407][S93].

Part 6

The role's own industry and its regulation

Consulting needs no licence. A Deloitte consultant is still boxed in by four sets of rules: audit independence, public procurement, data and AI law, and the financial-services rules that clients hire consultants to implement. This part gives each rule with its exact date, then the competitive map.

Why a lightly regulated industry still has rules that bite

Consulting itself has no statutory regulator and no licence to practise [Inferred from S180, S205]. Anyone can call themselves a management consultant. The voluntary standards come from the Management Consultancies Association (MCA), which runs the "Consulting Excellence" quality hallmark and the Chartered Management Consultant (ChMC) title, held by 2,800+ people in its 2026 report [S205][S150] Reported.

A consultant at Deloitte faces a different reality, for one reason: Deloitte also audits. Audit is tightly regulated, and the rules that protect auditor independence reach into what the consulting side may sell. Add the government's own buying rules, data and AI law, and the regulation that drives bank and insurer spending, and you have the rulebook that shapes a graduate's day-to-day work.

Rule set 1: auditor independence

KEY TERM

Auditor independence: the principle that an auditor must be, and be seen to be, free of interests that could bias its opinion. Selling large consulting projects to a company you audit creates a self-review threat (you would audit your own work) and a financial interest in keeping the client happy. Public interest entity (PIE): broadly, a company with securities listed on a regulated market, a bank or an insurer.

The EU Audit Regulation (applies from 17 June 2016)

Regulation (EU) No 537/2014 was adopted on 16 April 2014 and applied from 17 June 2016 [S182] Confirmed. It did three things that still matter [S182][S180] Confirmed:

  • A 70% fee cap. Non-audit fees from a PIE audit client cannot exceed 70% of the average statutory audit fee over the previous three years.
  • A list of banned non-audit services (Article 5).
  • Mandatory audit firm rotation (Article 17): PIEs must change auditor after a set period.

The rules are retained in UK law after Brexit [Inferred; not separately verified]. The FRC's Revised Ethical Standard 2016 gave effect to them in the UK [S179][S180] Confirmed.

FRC Revised Ethical Standard 2019 (issued 17 December 2019, in force 15 March 2020)

The FRC (Financial Reporting Council) is the UK audit regulator. Its 2019 standard was released on 17 December 2019 and took effect on 15 March 2020 [S180] Confirmed. Per Deloitte's own February 2020 briefing, the key changes were [S180][S181] Confirmed:

  • Blacklist to whitelist. Instead of listing what is banned, the FRC now lists what is allowed for UK PIE audit clients. Permitted services are largely those required by law and regulation, loan covenant reporting, other assurance closely linked to the audit, and reporting accountant work.
  • Bans for all audited entities (not only PIEs) on internal audit services, secondments of staff, and contingent fees.
  • Reach across the network. All services by the firm and its network to UK PIEs, their UK parents and their worldwide subsidiaries fall under the whitelist.
  • A new category, Other Entities of Public Interest (OEPI): large AIM companies, Lloyd's syndicates, the largest pension schemes, and the largest private companies (more than 2,000 employees, or turnover over £200m and balance sheet over £2bn). The whitelist applies to OEPIs for periods from 15 December 2020, but the 70% cap does not.
  • A tougher test: would an "objective, reasonable and informed third party" conclude that independence is compromised?

FRC Revised Ethical Standard 2024 (issued 15 January 2024, in force 15 December 2024)

The current rulebook. Published 15 January 2024, effective 15 December 2024. It simplified the 2019 text, aligned it with the international IESBA Code, and added a restriction on fees from entities related through a single controlling party. The FRC's Mark Babington: "The revised ethical standard has been simplified to ensure auditors are clear as to the high ethical standards expected" [S178] Confirmed.

What this means on a Monday morning. Before a Deloitte consulting team can start work, the firm checks whether any Deloitte network firm audits that company or a related entity. If it is a PIE audit client, most consulting is simply not allowed [S180] [Inferred from Confirmed rules]. Deloitte UK has a whole internal team for this: Quality, Risk & Security Services, with sub-teams for Independence and conflict checks [S330] Confirmed. In practice, Deloitte's T&T business cannot sell an ERP implementation to a FTSE company Deloitte audits; that client's technology work goes to Accenture, PwC, EY or KPMG [S314] Inferred. Challengers such as Unity Advisory sell "no conflicts" as a feature for exactly this reason [S167] Confirmed.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"Because Deloitte audits, the FRC's Ethical Standard means Deloitte consulting can only sell a short whitelist of mostly audit-related services to UK public interest entities it audits, and even those are capped at 70% of the average audit fee. So a large share of the integrated, strategy-to-delivery work happens at clients audited by someone else, in the public sector and in private companies. I'd expect independence checks to be a routine part of starting any engagement."

Rule set 2: operational separation of audit

On 6 July 2020 the FRC published principles requiring the Big Four (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, PwC) to operationally separate their UK audit practices. Implementation plans were due by 23 October 2020 and full implementation by 30 June 2024 [S183] Confirmed. The required outcomes [S183] Confirmed:

  • Audit governance that protects auditors from the rest of the firm.
  • Audit partners' profit share should not persistently exceed the audit practice's own contribution, so no cross-subsidy.
  • A culture of challenge and scepticism, with auditors acting in the public interest.

Press reports of the principles add that dealings between audit and the rest of the firm must be on arm's-length terms, and that the audit practice may not be paid for introducing work to other parts of the firm [S312] Reported. On 10 October 2024 the FRC announced that all four firms had completed the transition, with independent audit boards chaired by Audit Non-Executives [S184] Confirmed. Sarah Rapson of the FRC: "The FRC is pleased with the spirit in which the firms have embraced operational separation and the progress achieved to date" [S184].

The point for you: this is separation inside one firm, not a legal split. Deloitte remains one LLP, registered OC303675 [S407] Confirmed. Consulting must stand on its own economics and cannot lean on audit as a door-opener Inferred.

Rule set 3: audit reform, from white paper to abandonment

For seven years the plan was to replace the FRC with a stronger regulator, ARGA (the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority). That plan is now dead.

DateWhat happenedSource
December 2018Kingman Review recommends replacing the FRC, after the collapses of Carillion, BHS and Patisserie Valerie.[S187] Reported
March 2021Government white paper "Restoring trust in audit and corporate governance" proposes ARGA.[S187] Confirmed
July 2024King's Speech announces a Draft Audit Reform and Corporate Governance Bill.[S185][S186] Confirmed
July 2025A minister tells the Business and Trade Committee that pre-legislative scrutiny will not happen this session.[S186] Reported
20 January 2026Government abandons the Audit Reform Bill. Business Secretary Peter Kyle confirmed; Business Minister Blair McDougall wrote to the select committee. Reason given: growth and lower burdens on large firms. ARGA is dropped. The government still intends to put the FRC on a statutory footing with stronger investigative powers and mandatory industry funding. ICAEW's Alan Vallance called it a "false dawn"; FRC chief executive Richard Moriarty said the FRC would continue its work "regardless".[S185][S186][S235] Confirmed
13 May 2026King's Speech 2026 contains no audit reform bill and no mention of the FRC or ARGA.[S188] Confirmed

What remains, as of October 2026 [Inferred from the above]: the FRC's existing powers, the Ethical Standard 2024 and operational separation. A statutory footing for the FRC is a stated intention with no bill in the 2026 session. No law forces the Big Four to split audit from consulting in the UK. Meanwhile the FRC's July 2026 inspections rated 90% of Deloitte's inspected audits as needing no more than limited improvement (KPMG 95%, EY 90%, PwC 89%) [S236] Reported.

DON'T SAY THIS

"ARGA is coming." It was dropped on 20 January 2026 [S185].

"Consultants at Deloitte are regulated by the FRC." The FRC regulates audit. Consulting is caught only through the independence rules that apply to the firm as auditor.

"Deloitte can't work for any FTSE company." It can work for companies it does not audit, and for audit clients within the whitelist and the cap.

"The UK forced the Big Four to split." Separation is operational, inside each firm. EY's own voluntary attempt to split ("Project Everest") was abandoned on 12 April 2023 [S141] Reported.

"The EU AI Act high-risk rules apply from August 2026." The Digital Omnibus moved them (see below).

Rule set 4: how the government buys consultancy

The Procurement Act 2023

The Procurement Act 2023 and the Procurement Regulations 2024 came into force on 24 February 2025, after a delay from October 2024. Procurements started before that date stay under the old Public Contracts Regulations 2015. A new National Procurement Policy Statement was laid on 13 February 2025 [S190] Confirmed. The Act brings more transparency, including published notices and contract information [S175] Reported. Note: a September 2024 City AM article still gives the original October 2024 start date [S175]; the delayed date is the correct one.

On 1 April 2026 the Crown Commercial Service (CCS) became the Government Commercial Agency (GCA) [S190] Confirmed. Use the new name.

MCF4: the main route to central government consulting

The Management Consultancy Framework Four (MCF4, reference RM6309) runs from 29 July 2025 to 28 July 2027, with 219 suppliers across 10 lots. It allows time-and-materials, fixed-price or risk-and-reward pricing [S117] Confirmed. It replaces MCF3 (RM6187) and the restructuring and insolvency framework (RM6269), and is valued at around £1.7bn. The lots: business; strategy and policy; complex and transformation; finance; HR; procurement and supply chain; health, social care and community; infrastructure; environment and sustainability; restructuring and insolvency [S191] Reported. Whether Deloitte holds a place on each lot was not verified.

Consultancy spend controls, and the data that conflict

The policy is clear. The evidence on whether it is working is not. Different sources measure different things: planned versus actual spend, central departments versus the whole public sector, contracts awarded versus money paid.

The two Tussell-based analyses disagree on who ranks second after Deloitte (PA Consulting at £310m in one, Palladium at £102m in the other) [S174][S335]. They use different date ranges and definitions of "key" consulting contracts. Quote "Deloitte is the largest supplier" (both agree) and avoid naming the runner-up. The civil service's chief operating officer Cat Little also warned that cuts should not "simply lead to an increase in 'professional services' or 'contingent labour'" [S172], which is one reason headline consultancy figures can fall while total outside spend does not.

Rule set 5: data and AI

UK data protection

The base regime is the UK GDPR plus the Data Protection Act 2018 Inferred. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amends it. Timeline [S194][S195] [Reported, two sources agree on Royal Assent]:

  • 19 June 2025: Royal Assent; some provisions in force immediately.
  • 20 August 2025: first commencement regulations.
  • 5 February 2026: most data protection changes in force.
  • 19 June 2026: new complaints duty (organisations must acknowledge data protection complaints within 30 days).

The EU AI Act, and the Digital Omnibus delay

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the EU's law on AI, with tighter rules for "high-risk" uses such as hiring, credit scoring, education and biometrics. It matters to UK consultants because UK clients that sell into the EU are caught, and because it creates advisory work. Original timeline [S193] Confirmed: in force 1 August 2024; prohibitions and AI-literacy duties from 2 February 2025; general-purpose AI (GPAI) obligations from 2 August 2025; most other provisions from 2 August 2026.

The Digital Omnibus on AI then delayed the high-risk rules. Provisional agreement 7 May 2026; Parliament approval 16 June 2026; Council adoption 29 June 2026; published in the Official Journal in late July 2026 [S192] Reported. New deadlines per Orrick [S192] and Morgan Lewis [S234]:

  • 2 December 2026: Article 50 transparency for synthetic (AI-generated) content; new bans on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material [S192] Reported.
  • 2 December 2027: stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III) [S192][S234] Reported.
  • 2 August 2028: AI built into regulated products (Annex I) [S192][S234].
  • 2 August 2030: public authority systems [S192]. Relief for "small mid-caps" with under 750 staff [S192].
SOURCE UNCERTAIN

Annex III high-risk date. Orrick (written after publication) and Morgan Lewis say 2 December 2027 [S192][S234]. The artificialintelligenceact.eu timeline lists 2 August 2027 [S193]. Entry into force of the omnibus: Orrick says 29 July 2026; another summary says 27 July 2026 [S192]. Neither was checked against the Official Journal. In an interview, say "the high-risk deadline moved into late 2027" and, if pressed, "2 December 2027 on the law-firm readings".

The UK's own approach to AI

The UK has no AI bill. The AI Opportunities Action Plan (13 January 2025, 50 recommendations) set a pro-innovation stance [S203] Reported. The King's Speech on 13 May 2026 had no AI bill. It did include a Regulating for Growth Bill, with a stronger statutory growth duty for regulators and "cross-cutting AI sandboxes", and a Cyber Security and Resilience Bill [S188] Confirmed. A sandbox is a controlled space where firms test new products under a regulator's eye with some rules relaxed. So a client operating in both the UK and the EU faces two very different AI regimes, which is exactly where advisers add value Inferred.

Rule set 6: the client-side regulation consultants are hired to implement

Regulation is a demand engine. Financial services firms in particular buy consulting to meet hard legal deadlines. Know these six.

The competitive map of UK suppliers

Who Deloitte competes with depends on the job. On a bank's Basel 3.1 programme it faces PwC, EY, KPMG and specialists. On an SAP rollout it faces Accenture, IBM and Capgemini. On a government framework it faces PA Consulting and the mid-tier. On a board strategy question it faces McKinsey, BCG and Bain. The UK figures available are on different bases, so compare with care.

What clients value today

  • Help with AI that works safely. In an MCA client survey of 350+ leaders (May 2026), two in five organisations sought consulting help with digital and technology transformation. Top AI barriers: data security and privacy (40%), lack of skilled internal teams (34%), governance and roadmap problems (28%) [S240] Reported.
  • Judgement and trust. MCA chief executive Tamzen Isacsson: "The competitive edge now lies in being able to provide judgment, sector knowledge and trust that is earned through outcomes" [S240].
  • Expertise plus partnerships. Source's 2026 outlook says expertise paired with strategic partnerships can be decisive in winning work, and that firms must address client worries about AI to build trust [S158] Reported.
  • Cyber. The fastest-growing service globally (about 9%) and the top area where clients say they will bring in outside help [S156] Reported.
  • More outside help, not less, in technology. 84% of tech buyers plan upgrades in the next year and 81% intend to rely more on external consultants [S157] Reported.
  • Value for money, provably. Government buyers must "demonstrate the value-for-money case" (Reeves) [S176] Confirmed; challengers sell low cost and no conflicts [S167].
Part 7

What is happening right now

The eleven stories from April to early October 2026 that a Deloitte Consulting or Technology interviewer is most likely to know, each explained from scratch, with why it matters to the firm and to you, and one question or opinion you could raise. Then the latest CFO Survey and Tech Trends in brief.

How to use this part

"Tell me about something in the news" is a near-certain question. The interviewer is testing three things: that you follow the business, that you can explain it simply, and that you can say what it means. Each story below is built in that order. Pick three you find genuinely interesting and practise them out loud. The first two (the results) are the ones you must know cold.
