The results: Deloitte UK and Deloitte global, FY2026

Story 1 · Deloitte UK FY26: revenue +2% to £5.81bn, profit +14%30 Sep 2026
Outlet and source

Deloitte UK press release, "Deloitte UK publishes 2026 financial results", 30 September 2026 [S407][S220]; FY26 metrics document [S88]. Bloomberg's "Deloitte UK Partner Pay Grows to $1.5 Million on AI Demand" (29 Sep) is paywalled and was not read [S223].

In plain English

Deloitte UK's year ends on 31 May. In the year to 31 May 2026 revenue rose 2% to £5.81bn (FY25 £5.68bn) [S407] Confirmed. Careful: that headline is UK and Switzerland consolidated. Deloitte's footnote says "All revenue numbers presented herein, unless otherwise noted, represent UK and Switzerland consolidated" [S407]. The split is UK £5,014m and Switzerland £795m [S88] Confirmed. The four UK businesses: Technology & Transformation (T&T) £1.75bn (+4%), Tax & Legal £1.36bn (+2%), Audit & Assurance £998m (+3%), Strategy, Risk & Transactions (SR&T) Advisory £913m (+1%) [S407] Confirmed. Distributable profit, the pool shared by the owning partners, rose 14% to £899m. Average profit per equity partner rose to £1.125m (FY25 £1.051m). Equity partners rose 6.5% to a record 784 [S407] Confirmed. Context: FY25 had been the first revenue fall in about 15 years, with UK consulting down 10% [S123][S305] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

Profit grew seven times faster than revenue. Average fee-earning staff fell about 5% while revenue rose 2% [S93] Confirmed, so the gain came from efficiency and leverage, not volume Inferred. The firm says its advisory businesses "returned to profitable growth", led by enterprise technology, ERP, cyber and human capital work [S407][S303] Confirmed. Technology investment rose to £180m from £158m [S407].

Why it matters to the role

T&T, the business you are most likely applying to, is the largest UK business and grew fastest. The firm hired 3,500 people including more than 1,950 graduates, apprentices and interns; over 6,000 of 25,000 people were promoted; the bonus pool rose 14% and average in-grade pay rose over 4% [S407] Confirmed.

Raise this

"Profit rose 14% on 2% revenue growth while fee-earners fell about 5%. How much of that margin came from AI-enabled delivery, and does it change how T&T staffs a typical project?"

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"£5.81bn is the UK and Switzerland figure. The UK alone was about £5.0bn, and UK T&T was £1.75bn, up 4%." Getting this precision right signals you read the release itself, not a headline.

Story 2 · Deloitte global FY26: US$74.5bn, but T&T grew only 2.5%24 Sep 2026
Outlet and source

Deloitte Global press release, "Deloitte reports FY2026 revenue", 24 September 2026 [S221][S120]; City AM, "Deloitte's tech consulting division weighs on growth", 24 September 2026 [S222].

In plain English

The whole network (independent firms in about 150 countries under Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited) reported US$74.5bn for the year to 31 May 2026. That is +5.7% in US dollars and +3.8% in local currency, which strips out exchange-rate effects [S221] [Confirmed; the local-currency total comes from a secondary summary, Reported]. By business, in local currency: Tax & Legal +5.8%, Audit & Assurance +5%, SR&T +4.4%, T&T +2.5%. By region: Asia Pacific +7.5%, EMEA +3.5%, Americas +3.2% [S221] Confirmed. Headcount is "nearly 500,000", and Deloitte committed US$3bn through 2030 to modernise operations and build AI-enabled products [S221] Confirmed.

Why it matters to Deloitte

City AM framed slow T&T growth as a sign of "industry-wide pressure from artificial intelligence" [S222] Reported. The irony: the business that should gain most from AI grew slowest, plausibly because AI lets clients do more themselves and compresses hours on big implementations Inferred. Accenture, now almost the same size at US$74.18bn, grew 5% in local currency [S129] Confirmed.

Why it matters to the role

Globally T&T was the slowest business; in the UK it was the fastest. That contrast is a sharp, specific talking point few applicants will have.

Raise this

"Globally T&T grew slowest, but in the UK it grew fastest. Is that the ERP and cyber mix, the public sector, or the regional technology centres?"

Leadership, people and the pyramid

Story 3 · Darren Graves becomes UK CEO; Deloitte UK appoints its first Chief AI Officer1 Jun 2026
Outlet and source

Deloitte UK press release, "Deloitte UK appoints first Chief AI Officer", 1 June 2026 [S226]; FY26 results [S407]; Accountancy Today, 1 April 2026 (headline only) [S251].

In plain English

Darren Graves became CEO and senior partner of Deloitte UK on 1 June 2026. His predecessor Richard Houston became CEO of the new Deloitte EMEA firm. Jane Whitlock became Chair of the UK Board [S407] Confirmed. Graves joined as a tax graduate in 2001 [S251] Reported. Hayley McKelvey joined the UK Executive as the first Chief AI Officer, "responsible for driving the firm's AI strategy across client services and internal operations" [S407] Confirmed. Hammad Rafique was named managing partner of T&T and Dave Sharman of SR&T [S226] Confirmed.

Why it matters to Deloitte

Putting AI on the executive committee makes it a whole-firm question, not one service line. A CEO from tax rather than consulting is also worth noticing.

Why it matters to the role

Hammad Rafique leads the business you are applying to. Graves's official line on AI and jobs is "As AI makes intelligence increasingly abundant, the role our people play will matter more, not less" [S407]. McKelvey: "Harnessing the power of AI responsibly and strategically, both for our clients and in our own operations, is my priority" [S226].

Raise this

"The Chief AI Officer covers both client work and internal operations. In practice, which moves first: changing how Deloitte delivers, or selling AI to clients?"

Story 4 · Deloitte UK offers voluntary redundancy to up to 175 auditors16 Jun 2026
Outlet and source

City AM, "More Big Four blues as Deloitte plans to slash UK audit roles", 16 June 2026 [S227]; Bloomberg the same day (paywalled, headline only) [S228].

In plain English

Deloitte offered voluntary redundancy on enhanced terms to up to about 175 auditors, under 3% of Audit & Assurance and under 1% of the UK firm. The reason given was "low rates of attrition" [S227][S407] Confirmed. Big Four firms rely on people leaving each year to make room for promotions and new graduates. When fewer leave in a weak job market, the pyramid clogs, so firms pay people to go Inferred. KPMG cut about 600 UK roles in March 2026 [S227] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

It shows how the FY26 profit jump was achieved, and that the people model is under strain.

Why it matters to the role

Low attrition means fewer entry seats, more competition for promotion and a more selective intake.

Raise this

"If attrition stays low, does the classic pyramid still work, or does the shape move toward a diamond, with fewer juniors and more mid-level specialists?"

Story 5 · 1,353 early-career starters at Deloitte; Big Four overhaul graduate training for AI10 and 23 Sep 2026
Outlet and source

Consultancy.uk, "2026 intake of early-career staff to hit 1,500 at Deloitte", 10 September 2026 [S231]; Resultsense summary of City AM, "How AI is changing Big Four graduate training in the UK", 23 September 2026 [S229]; Deloitte UK, 1 September 2025 (prior year) [S232].

In plain English

Deloitte UK said 1,353 graduates, apprentices and industrial placement students would join across 21 UK offices, 44% outside London, including 182 BrightStart apprentices (the headline says 1,500; the body says 1,353) [S231] Reported. In 2025 the intake was about 1,400 across 17 locations, and starters met Deloitte's GenAI platform PairD in induction [S232] Confirmed. The Big Four told City AM they are front-loading exams, pushing trainees into judgement work earlier and coaching communication and teamwork, because AI now does much of the data work juniors used to do [S229] Reported. KPMG's chief people officer: "Graduates will become more involved in reviewing and exercising judgement rather than simply producing outputs" [S229].

Why it matters to Deloitte

It must keep a pipeline of future managers while AI absorbs junior tasks. Cut too hard now and there are no seniors in eight years Inferred.

Why it matters to the role

Entry is flat, not growing. Year-one work will be more judgement-based and client-facing than for past cohorts, so communication and critical thinking weigh more in assessment.

Raise this

"If AI handles first drafts and data work, how does Deloitte make sure analysts still learn the fundamentals the drafts are built on?"

Clients, government and the market

Story 6 · Deloitte wins a Home Office data deal worth up to £200m despite the spend pledge1 Jul 2026
Outlet and source

The Register, "UK.gov vows to cut consultancy spending, then hands up to £350M to consultancies", 1 July 2026 [S233].

In plain English

Deloitte won a four-year Home Office data and analytics deal worth up to £200m, and PA Consulting one worth up to £150m [S233] Reported. "Up to" means a ceiling, not guaranteed spend Inferred. It came despite the government's pledge to cut consultancy spend (Part 6 sets out the conflicting data).

Why it matters to Deloitte

Government is one of Deloitte UK's largest client sectors, and Deloitte is the largest UK government consultancy supplier [S174][S335] Reported. Government says "fewer consultants" but still needs data, digital and AI skills it cannot hire fast enough Inferred.

Why it matters to the role

Many T&T analysts start on public sector work; some programmes need security clearance.

Raise this

"Is the real trend 'less advice, more delivery'? And how does Deloitte help departments build their own capability so they need it less over time?"

Story 7 · UK firms cut consulting spend as they buy AI tools directly9 Sep 2026
Outlet and source

City AM, "UK firms slash consulting spend amid rising AI adoption" (Business Spend Pulse), 9 September 2026 [S239].

In plain English

Card-spend data from fintech Capital on Tap (mostly small firms) showed median consulting fees down 1.9% year on year in August 2026 while total corporate spending rose 2.2%. About one in seven firms now pays AI companies such as Anthropic and ElevenLabs, up from one in thirteen a year earlier. The share of businesses paying professional services firms fell to 18.6%, "the steepest drop in any category" [S239] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

This is the AI substitution risk in numbers. Caveat: it is small-business data; Deloitte's clients are mostly large companies and government, so read it as direction of travel Inferred.

Why it matters to the role

The work that survives is the work AI cannot easily do: complex integration, change management, regulated and high-trust decisions.

Raise this

"If small firms substitute AI tools for consultants, which parts of a large T&T engagement are most and least exposed?"

Story 8 · MCA: 2025 growth only 3%; clients want help making AI work23 Jan, 6 May, 6 Jul 2026
Outlet and source

Consultancy.uk on MCA data: 23 January 2026 [S241], 6 May 2026 [S240] and 6 July 2026 [S150].

In plain English

The MCA cut its 2026 forecast to 5.7% in January, then reported in July that UK fee income grew 3% to £21.8bn in 2025, with 6% forecast for 2026 and 8% for 2027 [S241][S150] Reported. Its May client survey of 350+ leaders found two in five organisations seeking help with digital and technology transformation; top AI barriers were data security and privacy (40%), lack of skilled internal teams (34%) and governance problems (28%) [S240] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

The barriers clients name map onto Deloitte's offer: data engineering, cyber, risk and change management.

Why it matters to the role

"AI" alone is not the product. Getting data, security and governance right is.

Raise this

"If clients' biggest AI barrier is data security, are cyber and data teams now the front door to AI work?"

Story 9 · Accenture FY26 US$74.2bn; PwC UK revenue +2%1 Oct and Sep 2026
Outlet and source

Accenture Q4 FY26 results (SEC filing), 1 October 2026 [S238]; PwC UK results via Accountancy Today, 21 September 2026 [S246][S138]; Irish Times headline, 16 September 2026 [S247].

In plain English

Accenture reported FY26 revenue of US$74.2bn (+5% local currency), split almost evenly between consulting (US$36.9bn) and managed services (US$37.3bn), with about 814,000 people, and guided 3% to 6% growth for FY27 [S238] Confirmed. Managed services means running clients' systems for years. PwC UK revenue rose 2% to £4.365bn and profit per partner 8% to £935,000; its wider UK and Middle East group fell 3% to £6.155bn [S246] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

Accenture and Deloitte are now almost the same size (US$74.2bn vs US$74.5bn), but Accenture grows faster and half its revenue recurs [S221][S238] [Inferred comparison].

Why it matters to the role

"Why Deloitte, not Accenture?" is a classic question. One honest answer: Deloitte combines technology delivery with audit, tax, risk and deals expertise in one firm Inferred.

Raise this

"Accenture earns half its revenue from managed services. Should Deloitte push harder into that, given independence rules limit it at audit clients?"

Rules and reputation

Story 10 · EU delays AI Act high-risk deadlines; UK drops its Audit Reform Bill24 Jun 2026 / Jan 2026
Outlet and source

Morgan Lewis, "EU Approves Delays and Other Amendments to Certain EU AI Act Obligations", 24 June 2026 [S234]; ICAEW, "Government abandons Audit Reform Bill", January 2026 [S235]; Scottish Financial News, 20 January 2026 [S185].

In plain English

Through the "Digital Omnibus", the EU moved stand-alone high-risk AI duties from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and AI in regulated products to 2 August 2028; bans and AI-literacy duties still apply [S234] [Confirmed by several law-firm summaries]. One tracker gives 2 August 2027 for the high-risk date (see Part 6) [S193]. In the UK, the government confirmed on 20 January 2026 that it would not proceed with the Audit Reform and Corporate Governance Bill, so ARGA will not be created [S185][S235] Confirmed. The FRC's July 2026 inspections rated 90% of Deloitte's inspected audits as good or needing limited improvement (KPMG 95%) [S236] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

The AI Act delay may slow urgent compliance work but extends the advisory pipeline into 2027. No audit bill means no forced split of audit and consulting in the UK, which keeps the multidisciplinary model intact Inferred.

Why it matters to the role

Regulation creates consulting work (AI governance, risk, assurance), and independence rules shape which clients you can serve.

Raise this

"Do clients treat the December 2027 deadline as breathing room, or are leaders using it to build AI governance properly?"

Story 11 · Reputation and risk: US settlement, Australian AI refund, FRC investigationsAug 2026 and ongoing
Outlet and source

US Department of Justice, 25 August 2026 [S242]; The Register, 6 October 2025 [S316]; Accountancy Age, 23 July 2025 [S252]; Accountancy Today, 10 July 2025 [S253].

In plain English

Deloitte's US firm agreed to pay US$21.5m to settle allegations that its diversity programmes breached anti-discrimination terms in federal contracts. The DOJ states these "are allegations only and there has been no determination of liability" [S242] Confirmed. In October 2025 Deloitte Australia partly refunded a government department for a report with fabricated references, after disclosing use of a generative AI model [S316] Confirmed. In the UK the FRC is investigating Deloitte's audits of Glencore (2013 to 2020) and of collapsed fintech Stenn [S252][S253] Reported.

Why it matters to Deloitte

Each is a trust risk, and trust is what clients buy. The member firms are legally separate, but the brand is shared [S302] Confirmed.

Why it matters to the role

You will use AI tools as an analyst, and you will be accountable for checking every source and number.

Raise this

Neutrally: "After the Australian report, what quality checks does Deloitte UK apply when GenAI is used in client deliverables?"

The latest Deloitte CFO Survey

The Deloitte UK CFO Survey asks chief financial officers of large UK companies about confidence, risks and plans every quarter. It is the firm's best-known piece of research and a classic interview talking point.

EditionHeadlines
Q2 2026, published 20 July 2026; fieldwork 1 to 13 July; 58 CFOs (10 FTSE 100, 21 FTSE 250) [S224] Confirmed73% report improved optimism about AI's business impact over the past year (59% in Q4 2025, 39% in Q3 2024). 93% expect UK business investment in digital technology to rise in the next 12 months. 78% expect AI to lift productivity within five years; 50% within 12 months. Geopolitics is still the top risk, but its rating fell to 68/100 from 79. Cost control is the biggest dampener on graduate hiring, followed by AI, then outsourcing.
Q1 2026, published 13 April 2026; 79 CFOs [S225] ConfirmedNet confidence fell to -57% from -13% as conflict in the Middle East hit sentiment. Then chief economist Ian Stewart: "The conflict in the Middle East is reshaping business sentiment". 68% said cost control was a strong focus (up from 51%).
NextQ3 2026 is due around mid-October 2026 [Inferred from cadence]. The "Q3 2026 CFO Signals" now in the news is Deloitte's US survey of North American CFOs; do not mix them up [S256].

The story in one line: CFO mood swung from shock in Q1 to recovery in Q2, with AI optimism rising throughout, and cost control weighing on graduate hiring. Debapratim "Debo" De succeeded Ian Stewart as Deloitte UK chief economist from 1 June 2026 and now writes the weekly Monday Briefing [S248] Reported.

Tech Trends 2026 in brief

Deloitte's 17th annual Tech Trends report (10 December 2025) says the question has moved from "what can we do with AI?" to "how do we move from experimentation to impact?" [S244] Confirmed. Five trends:

  1. AI goes physical: AI in robots and autonomous devices that act in the real world.
  2. The agentic workforce: AI agents that take actions. Only 11% of organisations have them in production; the hard part is redesigning processes "agent-first" rather than automating old workflows.
  3. The AI infrastructure reckoning: unit costs fall but total AI bills rise with use; firms mix cloud, on-premises and edge computing.
  4. The great rebuild: AI reshapes how IT functions are organised; leaner teams tied to business outcomes.
  5. The AI dilemma in cyber: AI creates new weaknesses but also stronger defences, such as automated red-teaming (simulated attacks).

Quote to use: Kelly Raskovich, "the distance between emerging and mainstream is collapsing" [S244]. A related September 2026 Deloitte study of 25,000 UK workers estimated they spend about £958m a year of their own money on GenAI tools for work, and nearly a third of users use it without their employer knowing ("shadow AI") [S243] Reported.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: "Which story are you following, and what do you think?" Pick one where you can add a mechanism. Example stance: "Tech Trends says only 11% of organisations have agentic AI in production, and Deloitte's own survey found a third of GenAI users hide it from their employer. Both point the same way: the bottleneck is process redesign and governance, not the models. That is consulting work, and it is why I think T&T's growth depends on change management as much as engineering." Counterpoint to acknowledge: SME data show some clients buying AI tools instead of advisers [S239].

How to stay current between now and the interview

  • Weekly (20 minutes): Consultancy.uk and City AM's professional services coverage for Big Four news; Deloitte's Monday Briefing for the economy.
  • Quarterly: the Deloitte UK CFO Survey (next due mid-October 2026); Accenture's quarterly results as the best public read on tech-consulting demand.
  • Before the interview: re-read the Deloitte UK and global results releases, and check for anything new on the Deloitte UK press room.

The full list, with what each source is good for, cadence and links, is in the separate Reading_List.md file.

Part 8

Forming your own view: both sides of every argument

Nine live debates an interviewer could raise, each with the strongest case on both sides, what Deloitte's own leaders have said, a defensible stance you can adapt, and how to hold it under challenge. Start with the five-step method in Figure 39.

The method: how to build an opinion in 45 seconds

Interviewers do not mark you on whether your view matches theirs. They mark whether you can commit to a position, explain the mechanism, back it with a dated fact, concede the strongest counterpoint and say what it means. A view without a mechanism sounds like a guess. A view without a concession sounds naive.

DON'T SAY THIS

"There are pros and cons on both sides." It is true and it scores nothing. Give both sides, then choose. "It depends" is acceptable only if you immediately say on what, and which way you lean.

Debate 1: Will AI break the consulting pyramid?

Case that it will

AI drafts the research, slides and code that juniors used to produce. Big Four UK graduate intakes fell between 2023 and 2024 (KPMG -29%, Deloitte -18%) [S143] Reported. A recruiter says the Big Four want AI "to replicate junior work more cost-effectively" [S162]. Queen's Tower Advisory, founded by Mark Bunker, formerly of Deloitte, reportedly targets teams of "20 per cent humans, 80 per cent AI agents" [S164] Reported. Deloitte UK's fee-earners fell about 5% in FY26 while revenue rose 2% [S93] Confirmed.

Case that it won't

Clients' main AI barriers are data security (40%), skills (34%) and governance (28%), which need people [S240] Reported. Deloitte still hired more than 1,950 graduates, apprentices and interns in FY26 [S407]. MCA members raised graduate hiring 10% in 2025 [S150]. A commentator found that despite billions spent, firms still staff and bill the old way [S163] Reported. Firms need juniors today to have managers in eight years Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. Darren Graves: "As AI makes intelligence increasingly abundant, the role our people play will matter more, not less. AI can't replace lived experience or replicate the judgement and unwritten know-how built..." [S407] Confirmed. Hayley McKelvey: "The challenge is no longer getting people to use GenAI, it's how businesses meet this growing demand in a way that is secure, responsible and creates lasting value" [S243].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "AI reshapes the pyramid rather than breaking it. The base gets narrower and the junior job changes from producing first drafts to checking and judging them. Deloitte UK grew profit 14% on 2% revenue while fee-earners fell about 5%, which is that shift starting. The risk I'd watch is training: if juniors never build the analysis themselves, where do future managers come from?"

How to hold it if challenged. If told "AI will replace analysts entirely", go back to mechanism: clients pay for accountable judgement and for change that sticks inside their organisation, and Deloitte Australia's refund shows what happens when AI output goes unchecked [S316]. Concede that numbers at the base will probably keep falling.

Debate 2: Should the Big Four split audit from consulting?

Case for splitting

Independence rules block consulting at PIE audit clients: a whitelist and a 70% fee cap [S180] Confirmed. Conflicts are the challengers' main pitch: Unity Advisory sells "no conflicts" [S167]. Regulators already forced operational separation inside the firms by 30 June 2024 [S183][S184]. A split would let consulting raise outside capital for AI, as PE-backed rivals do [S168] Inferred.

Case against

The mix smooths income: in FY25 Deloitte UK consulting fell 10% but total revenue fell only 1% because tax and audit grew [S305] Reported. EY's attempt ("Project Everest") was abandoned on 12 April 2023 after a reported US$600m cost [S141] Reported. The UK dropped the Audit Reform Bill on 20 January 2026, so no law is forcing a split [S185]. Breadth is a recruiting and client selling point [S308].

What Deloitte's leaders have said. Global CEO Joe Ucuzoglu, after EY's split collapsed in 2023, said keeping the model was "not even a close call" and that previous separations had "never once played out as intended" [S308] Reported. In 2022 Deloitte called split reports "categorically untrue" [S309] Reported.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "I'd keep them together, because the portfolio works: FY25 showed audit and tax cushioning a 10% consulting fall. The cost is real, since consulting cannot serve many large audit clients, but operational separation already deals with the quality concern, and EY's failed split shows how hard and expensive unwinding is."

How to hold it if challenged. If pushed on conflicts, accept the cost openly and name it precisely (whitelist, 70% cap, separation). Then argue it is a constraint to manage, not a reason to split. Do not claim the conflict is imaginary.

Debate 3: Is the government right to cut consultancy spend?

Case for cutting

Test and Trace paid Deloitte staff about £1,000 a day each, some seniors up to £6,624 [S332] Confirmed, while only 17% of people got results within 24 hours against a 90% target [S332] Reported. Consultants were still 45% of central staff in April 2021 [S333]. The NAO says government "does not collect data on how it uses consultants" [S173]. Mazzucato and Collington argue over-reliance weakens state capability [S337] Reported.

Case against

The NAO found 86% of survey respondents said consultants made valuable contributions [S334] Confirmed. Government explained use by "skills shortages" and "comparatively low salaries in the civil service" [S333]. Cuts may shift spend into "professional services" or "contingent labour" (Cat Little) [S172]. Spend did not actually fall on some measures: £1.44bn of contracts in Labour's first year [S174]; £3.7bn record public sector spend in 2024/25 [S335] Reported.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. No direct Deloitte UK leadership comment on the spend controls was found in the research. Use the firm's results framing instead: growth came from technology delivery, ERP and cyber [S407].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Right aim, blunt tool. Cutting advice that civil servants could do is sensible. But departments still need data and digital delivery they cannot hire fast enough, which is why the Home Office still bought up to £200m of data work from Deloitte. The better test is whether each contract leaves capability behind. I'd want Deloitte to be measured on that."

How to hold it if challenged. If told "you would say that, applying to Deloitte", agree that the incentive exists, and point to the evidence on both sides, including Test and Trace's poor 24-hour figure. Credibility comes from conceding the bad example.

Debate 4: Is outcome-based pricing good for clients?

Case for

It aligns incentives: the firm earns when the client gains. McKinsey reportedly ties a quarter to a third of fees to outcomes [S163][S164] Reported. Government frameworks already allow risk-and-reward pricing (MCF4) [S117] Confirmed. If AI makes work faster, day rates reward slowness; outcome fees do not Inferred.

Case against

Outcomes are hard to measure and attribute: did revenue rise because of the project or the market? Firms price in risk, so outcome deals can cost more Inferred. Progress is "sluggish" [S163]. Deloitte's accounts show even fixed-fee work is managed by timesheets at charge-out rates [S93] Confirmed, so the internal model is still time-based.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. No public Deloitte UK statement on outcome pricing was found. Deloitte does sell multi-year managed services ("Operate"), named as an area of significant growth [S120] Confirmed.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Good for clients where the outcome is measurable and within the firm's control, such as cost savings on a process Deloitte runs. Risky where outcomes depend on the client's own decisions. So I'd expect a mix: outcome fees on managed services and automation, time-based fees on strategy and complex change."

How to hold it if challenged. If asked "so should all fees be outcome-based?", say no and give a mechanism: a firm cannot accept risk for results it does not control, and if it does, it will charge a premium for that risk.

Debate 5: Offshore delivery centres or UK regional centres?

Case for offshore

Lower cost. Capgemini runs 66% of its staff offshore [S132] Reported. Deloitte's US-India organisation (USI) is reported at over 100,000 people [S324] Reported. Big Four firms are moving more work to India, Malaysia and the Philippines [S162] Reported. Revenue per head shows the effect: Accenture about US$91k vs Deloitte about US$149k globally [S129][S120] Inferred.

Case for UK regional centres

Security clearance and data sovereignty for public sector and defence; same time zone; cheaper than London. Deloitte opened Belfast, Cardiff, Manchester and Newcastle centres from June 2025, starting with 750 technologists and aiming for 1,500 within three years [S254][S323] Confirmed. 44% of the 2026 early-career intake is outside London [S231] Reported. The EU AI Act and data rules raise the value of local delivery Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. Then T&T managing partner Rob Cullen said the centres accelerate "our ambition to become the largest onshore technology capability in UK" [S323] Reported. Whether UK engagements use USI was not established in the research.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Both, by work type. Commodity build and testing will keep going offshore on cost. But Deloitte UK's biggest client is government, where clearance and data location matter, so onshore regional centres are a real competitive advantage, not only a cost move. They also widen who can join, which is good for hiring."

How to hold it if challenged. If told "onshore is just more expensive", accept it on unit cost, then argue total cost: rework, security vetting and time-zone delays. If you are willing to work in a regional centre, say so; it is a credible signal.

Debate 6: Should graduates fear AI?

Case for worry

Fewer seats: Big Four intakes fell [S143]; Deloitte's 2026 early-career intake of 1,353 is flat against about 1,400 in 2025 [S231][S232] Reported. UK CFOs say AI is the second-biggest dampener on graduate hiring after cost control [S224] Confirmed. Accountancy graduate adverts fell 44% [S162].

Case against

Firms are redesigning training, not abolishing it: juniors are pushed into judgement work earlier [S229]. Deloitte promoted over 6,000 of 25,000 people and raised in-grade pay over 4% [S407]. 93% of CFOs expect digital investment to rise [S224], which needs people to deliver it. Graduates who use AI well become more productive earlier Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. Graves: people will "matter more, not less" [S407]. Starters are introduced to the firm's GenAI platform, PairD, during induction [S232] Confirmed.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Not fear, but adjust. The entry bar rises because the first job now starts at checking and judging, not producing. That favours graduates who can question an AI output, explain it to a client and spot what is missing. That's the skill I'm trying to show."

How to hold it if challenged. If asked "why hire you rather than use AI?", answer with accountability and context: AI produces drafts; a client needs someone who understands their organisation and will stand behind the answer.

Debate 7: Is Deloitte's EMEA merger smart?

Case for

Scale to invest: Deloitte EMEA combines 16 firms with 132,000 people, 6,000 partners and €20bn revenue from 1 June 2026, with more than €1.5bn of incremental investment over four years in GenAI, sovereign cloud and sector solutions [S124] Confirmed. Clients want cross-border delivery. KPMG merged its UK and Swiss firms in 2024 [S140], so rivals are consolidating too.

Case against

Bigger partnerships decide more slowly; EY's split failed partly on member-firm opposition [S310] Reported. EMEA growth was only 3.5% in FY26, behind Asia Pacific's 7.5% [S221] Confirmed. Local client relationships could weaken. Integration takes management attention in a difficult market Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. Richard Houston: "Deloitte EMEA uniquely strengthens our ability to invest at scale across borders to accelerate innovation in areas that matter most to our clients" [S124]. Joe Ucuzoglu: "Our clients expect leading expertise wherever it is based, alongside seamless cross-border and technology-enabled delivery at speed" [S306] Reported. Country firms keep "local market responsibility" [S306].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Smart on investment logic. AI and sovereign cloud need spending on a scale no single country firm can fund easily, and a partnership cannot raise outside capital. The test will be whether it can staff cross-border work quickly without losing the local relationships that win it. It's too early to judge results, since it only started on 1 June."

How to hold it if challenged. If told it is "just empire-building", point to the specific investment commitment and the partnership capital constraint. Concede that the benefits are promised, not yet proven.

Debate 8: Partnership or company: which funds AI better?

Case for outside capital

Listed or PE-backed firms can invest ahead of profits. Accenture returned US$11.5bn to shareholders in FY26 and still funds acquisitions [S129] Confirmed. Grant Thornton UK (Cinven) and Unity Advisory (up to $300m from Warburg Pincus) raised outside money [S168][S167]. Partners who retire soon may resist long-term investment that cuts their payouts Inferred.

Case for partnership

No quarterly earnings pressure: the firm absorbed FY25's consulting fall without a share-price shock [S305] Inferred. Deloitte still committed US$3bn through 2030 to AI and modernisation [S221] and raised UK technology investment to £180m [S407] Confirmed. Owners are the people serving clients, which aligns incentives on quality Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. The US$3bn commitment and the EMEA €1.5bn plan are the firm's answer: invest from pooled partner profits at larger scale [S221][S124].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "A large partnership can fund AI, but only by pooling across countries, which is exactly what EMEA does. PE money moves faster, but it comes with an exit date. For a firm whose product is trust and independence, I think the partnership is the better long-term owner, provided partners accept lower payouts in heavy investment years."

How to hold it if challenged. If told "PE firms will out-invest you", compare scales: US$3bn committed globally against up to $300m for Unity. Concede that speed of decision is the partnership's weak point.

Debate 9: Should Deloitte push harder into managed services?

Case for

Recurring revenue: half of Accenture's US$74.18bn is managed services, which grew 6% while its consulting grew 3% [S129] Confirmed. Long contracts smooth the cycle that hurt Deloitte UK consulting in FY25 [S305]. AI makes running processes cheaper, so the margin goes to whoever runs them Inferred. Deloitte already names "Operate" as an area of significant growth [S120].

Case against

Independence rules bar many managed services at audit clients [S180] Inferred. Lower margins and heavy offshore staffing: Accenture's revenue per head is about US$91k against Deloitte's US$149k [S129][S120] Inferred. It ties up capital and people for years, and pulls the brand from advice toward outsourcing Inferred.

What Deloitte's leaders have said. The FY26 global release highlights Operate growth; no UK-specific statement on managed services strategy was found [S120].

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Suggested stance: "Yes, selectively: where Deloitte has built a system, running it afterwards keeps the relationship and the data, and AI will make that work more profitable. But it should not chase Accenture's volume model, because audit independence limits the market and its edge is advice plus delivery."

How to hold it if challenged. If asked "why not copy Accenture outright?", give the structural reason (audit independence limits who you can run services for) and the economic one (different revenue-per-head model).

A one-page cheat sheet

DebateSuggested stance (one line)The one fact to cite
Will AI break the pyramid?Reshape, not break: narrower base, more judgementUK profit +14% on revenue +2%; fee-earners -5% [S407][S93]
Split audit and consulting?Keep together; manage the conflictFY25: consulting -10%, firm -1% [S305]
Cut government consultancy?Right aim, blunt tool; test capability left behindHome Office data deal up to £200m [S233]
Outcome pricing?Where outcomes are measurable and controllableMCF4 allows risk-and-reward pricing [S117]
Offshore or onshore?Both; onshore wins on government and dataFour UK centres, 750 to 1,500 technologists [S254]
Should graduates fear AI?Adjust: the job starts at judgingCFOs: AI second-biggest dampener on grad hiring [S224]
EMEA merger?Smart investment logic; unproven132,000 people, €1.5bn over four years [S124]

Part 9

The interview: process, question bank, questions to ask

How Deloitte UK actually assesses early-careers candidates in 2026/27, what is official and what is hearsay, a dated plan from today to a September 2027 start, how to prepare the Final Stage topic discussion, 56 practice questions with scaffolds, and the questions you should ask them.

The process in one view

Deloitte UK uses one common process for its Graduate, Industrial Placement, Summer Vacation Scheme and BrightStart programmes. It has five stages: an online application, an Immersive Online Assessment, a Job Simulation, a Final Stage Assessment and the outcome [S260] Confirmed. Two independent careers publishers describe the same five stages [S263] [S264].

One warning before anything else. Most English-language prep material describes the US Deloitte Consulting process, which uses group case interviews and several case rounds. Deloitte UK's current official page describes something different: no case interview and no group exercise, but a prepared topic discussion and a long skills and motivation interview [S260]. Where the two disagree, this pack trusts deloitte.com/uk.

5Stages, the same for graduate, placement and summer scheme roles [S260]
4 weeksOfficial maximum gap between each stage [S260]
30-40 minFinal Stage topic discussion, two-way with an assessor [S260]
~50 minFinal Stage skills and motivation interview [S260]

Stage by stage: what happens, what it tests, how sure we are

StageWhat happensTimingWhat it assessesConfidence
1. Online applicationA form of about 15 minutes in one sitting; progress is not saved. Have GCSE and A-level details to hand. You can explain extenuating circumstances [S260].If you meet the criteria you move to stage 2 automatically [S260].Eligibility. Graduate roles need a 2:1 in any discipline and a degree by September 2027 [S260] [S272].Official Confirmed. TargetJobs says results in two weeks [S263]; trust the official “automatic”.
2. Immersive Online AssessmentTwo parts: a behavioural test where you rank responses to workplace scenarios, and a cognitive test of numerical and verbal reasoning [S260].No overall limit, some timed questions; one sitting [S260]. Reported as about 30 [S263] or 40 minutes [S264].Your natural working style and reasoning. You get a strengths report within four weeks; it is not the result [S260].Structure official Confirmed; length Reported. “Game-based, 35 questions” claims come from prep vendors only.
3. Job SimulationOne-way, recorded. Ranking, multiple choice, written responses and video responses, including scenarios that reference AI. All AI information you need is given in the question [S260].Within four weeks of stage 2 [S260]. Reported 40 to 60 minutes, 2 to 4 video questions, 30 to 60 seconds to think, 2 to 3 minutes to answer [S263] [S264] [S288].How you would handle the actual job: emails, prioritising, summarising data, presenting yourself.Components official Confirmed; timings and tasks Reported. Deloitte UK does not name the video platform [S260].
4. Final Stage AssessmentExercise 1: Topic Discussion, a two-way discussion of a topic you were given to research in advance. Exercise 2: Skills and Motivation interview [S260].30 to 40 minutes, then about 50 minutes [S260]. In person at your linked office; virtual and interview-only for the Summer Vacation Scheme [S260].Analysis, communication, judgement under questioning; then your “alignment with the capabilities we look for at Deloitte” [S260].Official Confirmed. TargetJobs reports a choice of four pre-set topics [S263] Reported.
5. OutcomeOffer, then onboarding through Deloitte's Candidate Zone; or feedback and the option to reapply next academic year [S260].Within four weeks, with feedback [S260]. WikiJob reports 1 to 3 weeks [S264].n/aOfficial Confirmed.
KEY TERMS

Job Simulation: Deloitte's name for stage 3, a recorded assessment where you respond to realistic tasks on screen. Nobody watches live. One-way video: you record answers to on-screen prompts; reviewers watch later. Strengths report: an automatically generated summary of your working style, sent after stages 2 and 3. Linked office: the Deloitte office your application is tied to, where the in-person final stage happens.

Official advice worth taking literally

  • On ranking tasks: “go with your gut instinct, don't try to second guess what it is we might be looking for” [S260].
  • Practise on the official Candidate Zone tests. Deloitte warns that paid third-party sites claiming insight “lack Deloitte endorsement” [S260].
  • Read Deloitte's Integrity & AI guidance before any assessment. Breaking it is treated as a breach of process [S260] [S261]. Do not use generative AI to write your answers.
  • “Find a comfortable and quiet place to complete the assessment” [S260].
  • At the final stage: “Our assessors are here to get the best out of you, they are not trying to trip you up or trick you” [S260].
SOURCE UNCERTAIN

Group exercises and partner interviews. Some undated Glassdoor UK reports mention a group exercise, a case study and a partner interview [S289] Reported. US-focused guides say Deloitte “consistently uses a group case interview” [S292]. The current UK official page lists only the topic discussion and the interview [S260]. Expect those two unless your invitation says otherwise Inferred.

Values. WikiJob still says interviews are built around “Integrity, Outstanding value, Commitment, Diversity” [S264]. That is an older Deloitte list. The current Shared Values are in the question bank below [S266].

Blind recruitment. In September 2015 Deloitte UK said recruiters would not see which school or university candidates attended and introduced contextual data [S267] [S268]. Current pages mention extenuating circumstances and inclusive design but do not confirm the 2015 policy is still in use [S260] [S261].

Opening dates. The official timelines page still shows the 2024 cycle (Consulting and Advisory opened 5 October 2024) [S262]. Exact 2027-entry dates were not confirmed.

What happens after an offer

Before you join

  • Personal independence. “You will be required to clear Personal Independence checks before you join us” [S261] Confirmed. Deloitte audits many listed companies, so staff may not hold certain financial interests in audit clients. Expect to declare investments, including shares held in an ISA Inferred.
  • Screening. A Deloitte careers snippet describes an online questionnaire, right-to-work and address checks and a consent declaration, run by an external screening provider [S293] Reported (not seen on a fetched page).
  • Security clearance. No Deloitte source says government clearance (BPSS or SC) is standard for graduates. It is likely only for people staffed on some public sector or defence work Inferred.
  • A Deloitte buddy supports you before you start [S261] Confirmed.

Starting and training

  • Start date. “Our graduate programmes start in September” and you must have your degree result [S261]. The 2027 advert says Autumn 2027 intake [S272].
  • Scale. 1,353 early-careers joiners started in the first week of September 2026; 44% (590) were based outside London across 21 locations [S271] Confirmed.
  • Qualifications. Graduate programmes include professional qualifications [S269] [S272]; technology roles may include certifications such as CISA [S270].
  • Technical academies (12 weeks, paid) in software, cloud, cyber and data are a separate route; 130 people moved from them into technology roles in 2026 [S271].
  • Deloitte University EMEA moved in 2024 from near Brussels to a purpose-built campus east of Paris: up to 500 delegates a day, 22,000 m², 260 bedrooms [S283] [S284]. Whether UK graduates go in year one is not stated.

Your timeline from today (4 October 2026)

You have not applied yet. That is the most urgent fact in this pack. Deloitte says it will “close applications early when we get a very high volume of submissions” [S261], and the 2027 Consulting Graduate advert says roles close “on a rolling basis” [S272]. In the 2024 cycle, Consulting and Advisory opened on 5 October [S262]. You may apply to only one programme per academic year; if you apply to more, only the first counts and you cannot transfer [S261] [S262].

When (estimate)StageWhat to do
This week (5 to 11 Oct 2026)Choose and applyDecide: Graduate (if you graduate by Sept 2027), Summer Vacation Scheme or Industrial Placement. Pick one team (Part 2 and [S320]). Read the Integrity & AI guidance. Submit the 15-minute form.

Dates are an Inferred estimate built from the official “within four weeks” gaps [S260]. Your actual invitations set the real dates.

The Final Stage topic discussion

Deloitte sends you a topic to research and analyse before the day. On the day you discuss it for 30 to 40 minutes with an assessor who “will ask questions throughout” [S260] Confirmed. TargetJobs reports that candidates choose from four pre-selected topics [S263] Reported. Older reports describe a 5-minute presentation followed by questions, with broad topics such as “globalisation” [S264] Reported (older format). A short structured opening works for both formats, so prepare one Inferred.

How a two-way discussion is likely assessed

Deloitte does not publish the scoring grid [S260]. Based on the official format, expect the assessor to look for these things Inferred:

What they watchWhat good looks like
StructureYou frame the question, give two or three points and land a view within the first three minutes.
EvidenceNumbers with a date and a source. Fewer, better facts beat a long list.
JudgementYou commit to a view and name its biggest risk.
ListeningYou answer the question asked, and build on the assessor's points.
Handling challengeYou hold a view when the evidence supports it and change it openly when it does not.
Commercial senseYou say who would act, what it would cost and how a firm like Deloitte could help.

A structure for your opening (about 4 to 5 minutes)

  1. Frame (30 seconds): what the question really is, and who it matters to.
  2. Context (1 minute): two or three facts that set the scene, each dated and sourced.
  3. Analysis (2 minutes): two or three drivers. For each, the mechanism (how it works) and one piece of evidence.
  4. Your view (30 seconds): a clear position.
  5. Risks and what would change your mind (30 seconds).
  6. Hand over: “I'd be interested in your view on X.” This invites the two-way discussion on your ground.

A six-day preparation plan

Day 1. Define the question. List who wins, who loses and who decides.
Day 2. Collect 8 to 10 facts from primary sources (government, regulator, company results). Note dates.
Day 3. Choose your view. Write the strongest counter-argument.

Day 4. Write the 5-minute opening. Cut it to one page of notes.
Day 5. Ask a friend to interrupt you with Q49 to Q52 below.
Day 6. Add one Deloitte link: which team would help a client with this, and how.

Eight practice prompts

These are practice prompts, not reported Deloitte topics, except the first, which WikiJob reports as a past broad topic [S264]. Real 2025/26 topics were not visible in any source read for this pack.

PromptA starting angle and evidenceLabel
Is globalisation reversing, and what should a UK business do about it?Geopolitics topped UK CFOs' risk list in 16 of the last 18 quarters [S224].Reported topic [S264]
Should the UK government cut its use of consultants?Record £3.7bn public sector consulting spend in 2024/25 [S335]; NAO on missing spend data [S334]; The Big Con [S337].Practice
Will AI agents shrink or grow the consulting industry?11% of organisations have agentic AI in production [S244]; SME consulting spend down 1.9% while AI tool spend rises [S239].Practice
How should a large UK employer deal with “shadow AI”?Nearly a third of GenAI users use it without their employer knowing [S243].Practice
Should UK companies wait for AI regulation before scaling AI?EU high-risk AI duties delayed to 2 December 2027 [S234].Practice
What should a board do after a ransomware attack on a competitor?60% of CFOs named cyber-attacks a key risk in Q1 2026 [S225]; Deloitte Cyber's focus areas [S269].Practice
