The question bank

56 questions, grouped by where you are likely to meet them. Each is labelled: (Official) where Deloitte UK describes the question type itself, (Reported [Sxx]) where a candidate or careers publisher reports it, and (Practice) where this pack built it from official categories. These are scaffolds, not scripts. Put your own stories in them.

KEY TERM

STAR: a way to tell a work story. Situation (the context in one or two sentences), Task (what you had to achieve), Action (what you did, the longest part), Result (what changed, ideally with a number).

A. Job Simulation: recorded video and written tasks

Stage 3. You answer on screen to a recorded prompt or type a written reply. Nobody is live. Answer in the first 15 seconds, then give evidence.

Q1. “Introduce yourself to the members of your team and the senior colleagues who haven't met you yet.” (Reported [S264])
Tests: A short, confident self-introduction pitched to a mixed audience. Structure: One-line headline (who you are, what you study, what you bring), one proof point, then what you look forward to working on with them. Aim for about 60 seconds. Weave in: Name the business in Deloitte's own words: Technology & Transformation, one of the four businesses since the 2024 restructure [S307] [S407]. Trap: Reading your CV aloud. The reviewer is picturing a colleague, not a list.
Q2. “What does successful collaboration mean to you?” (Reported [S264])
Tests: The Shared Value “Collaborate for measurable impact”. Structure: Define it in one line (shared goal, clear roles, a result you can measure), give a short example with a number, then say what you would do differently next time. Weave in: Deloitte's wording: teams deliver “tangible, measurable, attributable impact” [S266]. Trap: Describing harmony. Deloitte's value is about outcomes you can measure.
Q3. “Give me an example of a time you've been creative.” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Lead the way; solving problems inside constraints. Structure: STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Make the creative step explicit: what you tried that others had not. Weave in: The Technology careers page asks for people who are “resilient and innovative” and enjoy “solving problems” [S270]. Trap: An art project with no outcome. Choose creativity that solved a problem for someone.
Q4. “What technology do you think could have a big impact on the industrial workplace?” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Curiosity about technology plus commercial sense. Structure: Name one technology. Explain the mechanism (what changes on the shop floor). Say who pays and who gains. Name one risk. Weave in: Deloitte's Tech Trends 2026 lists “AI goes physical” (AI in robots and devices) and says only 11% of organisations have agentic AI in production [S244]. Trap: A list of buzzwords. Pick one technology and explain how it creates value.
Q5. How would you approach being successful in a new team? (Reported [S288], paraphrased)
Tests: Adaptability and a learning mindset. Structure: Weeks one and two: listen and map the people, goals and ways of working. Then deliver one small thing well. Then ask for feedback. Weave in: The Consulting page asks for a “strong learning orientation” [S269]; new joiners get a Deloitte buddy [S261]. Trap: Promising to change things on day one.
Q6. A senior colleague asks for help late in the day when you already have a deadline. What do you do? (Reported [S288], paraphrased)
Tests: Prioritisation, honesty and the value “Take care of each other”. Structure: Clarify how urgent each task is. Tell both people about the trade-off. Agree a plan, and involve your manager if the two clash. Weave in: Shared Value “Take care of each other” [S266]. Trap: Quietly doing both badly, or refusing without a conversation.
Q7. A colleague emails to say they have found a discrepancy in your work. Write your reply. (Reported [S288], paraphrased)
Tests: Ownership, integrity and written tone. Structure: Thank them. Acknowledge the issue. Say what you will check and by when. Confirm the fix. Say how you will stop it happening again. Weave in: Shared Value “Serve with integrity” [S266]. Trap: A defensive tone, or blaming the data.
Q8. Written task: summarise this data about AI adoption and make a recommendation. (Reported [S288])
Tests: Synthesis, structured writing and the “so what”. Structure: Recommendation first, in one line. Three supporting points from the data. One risk and how to manage it. Weave in: Use only the data given. Deloitte says the information you need about AI is inside the question, and no prior AI experience is needed [S260]. Trap: Padding with outside facts, or hedging with no recommendation.
Q9. Email task: reply to a co-worker who says their workload is unmanageable. (Reported [S288])
Tests: Empathy and judgement about when to escalate. Structure: Acknowledge how they feel. Ask one or two specific questions. Offer a concrete step (reprioritise, take one task). Suggest raising it with the manager together. Weave in: “Take care of each other” [S266]. Trap: Trying to fix a resourcing problem alone without the manager.
Q10. AI scenario (practice version): your team wants to use a generative AI tool to draft a client summary. What do you check? (Official category [S260]; this wording is Practice)
Tests: Judgement about responsible AI use, not technical AI knowledge. Structure: Four checks: data (is client data allowed in this tool?), accuracy (check every fact and citation), disclosure (does the client know?), and a named human who signs it off. Weave in: In 2025 Deloitte Australia repaid part of a government contract after a report contained fabricated citations; the revised report disclosed it used Azure OpenAI GPT-4o [S316]. Candidates must also follow Deloitte's Integrity & AI guidance in the assessments themselves [S260]. Trap: Saying AI should be banned, or assuming its output is right.

B. Motivation

Final Stage, Skills and Motivation interview. These are about fit and research. Part 12 gives you full answers for “Why Deloitte?”.

Q11. “Why Deloitte?” (Reported [S264] [S287] [S289])
Tests: Depth of research, and whether your reason is specific to this firm. Structure: Use the Part 12 structure: how the firm is built, the evidence, what it means for you. Weave in: In FY25 restated T&T revenue fell 10% but total revenue fell only 1% [S89] [S305]; UK technology investment rose to £180m in FY26 [S407]. Trap: “Biggest” or “great culture”. Every candidate says it.
Q12. “Why this service line?” (Technology & Transformation, Strategy, Risk & Transactions, or a named team) (Reported [S264])
Tests: Whether you know what the team does and who buys it. Structure: Name the team. Say what its clients buy. Name the skill you would build. Give evidence of your interest. Weave in: UK T&T offerings: Enterprise, Technology & Performance; Engineering, AI & Data; Cyber; Customer; Human Capital; Defence & Security [S320]. UK T&T revenue £1.75bn, up 4% [S407]. Trap: Choosing a team you cannot describe in one sentence.
Q13. “Why consulting?” (Reported [S289])
Tests: A realistic picture of the job. Structure: What consultants do (help a client solve a problem it cannot solve alone, for a fee). What you like about that. Your evidence. One honest trade-off you accept (pressure, travel, changing teams). Weave in: In an MCA client survey the top barriers to AI were data security and privacy (40%), lack of skilled internal teams (34%) and governance (28%) [S240]. Those are gaps clients pay consultants to fill. Trap: “It keeps my options open.” That signals you will leave.
Q14. “Why this role, and what can you bring to it?” (Reported [S287])
Tests: Fit between your strengths and the job. Structure: Two strengths, each matched to something the role needs, each with a short proof. Weave in: The Consulting page asks for curious, open-minded people who enjoy collaboration and relationship-building, with a strong learning orientation [S269]. Trap: Strengths with no evidence.
Q15. “What sets you apart from other candidates?” (Reported [S287])
Tests: Self-awareness without arrogance. Structure: One distinctive combination (for example your subject plus a job or project), the proof, and why it would help a client. Weave in: Tie it to a named team from [S320]. Trap: Running down other candidates.
Q16. “Why Deloitte rather than another Big Four firm?” (Practice; generic example in [S265])
Tests: Knowledge of competitors. Structure: One fact about the field. One Deloitte difference. The link to you. Weave in: Deloitte global revenue US$74.5bn in FY26 against PwC's US$56.9bn in FY25 [S120] [S126]; Deloitte says Gartner ranked it No. 1 consulting provider by revenue for the ninth year running [S125]. Trap: Criticising rivals. Compare, do not attack.
Q17. “Where do you see yourself in five years?” (Practice; generic example in [S265])
Tests: Ambition and whether you will stay. Structure: Talk about skills, not titles: a platform or qualification, client responsibility, leading a small workstream. Weave in: Deloitte UK promoted over 6,000 people in June 2026 [S280]. Trap: “Doing an MBA” or “starting my own company”.

C. Strengths and competency

Final Stage interview. Use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Spend most of the time on Action and say “I”, not “we”.

Q18. “Tell me about yourself” / “Walk me through your CV.” (Reported [S289])
Tests: Clarity, and whether your story leads to this role. Structure: Present (what you study now), past (two experiences that led here), future (why this role). About 90 seconds. Weave in: End on the team you want to join [S320]. Trap: A chronological life story.
Q19. “Tell me about a time you were challenged and how you overcame it.” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Resilience. Structure: STAR. The challenge in two sentences; your actions in detail; a result with a number. Weave in: The Technology page asks for people who are “resilient” [S270]. Trap: A challenge where you did nothing personally.
Q20. “What do you see as your best role in a team?” / “How do you work best in a team?” (Reported [S264] [S289])
Tests: Self-knowledge and flexibility. Structure: Name your natural role (for example, the person who structures the problem). Give an example. Say when you take a different role. Weave in: “Collaborate for measurable impact” [S266]. Trap: Saying “leader” by default.
Q21. “What is your proudest achievement?” (Reported [S264] [S287])
Tests: What you value and how hard you will work. Structure: One achievement with effort and a measurable result. Say why it matters to you. Weave in: Link the skill to client work in your chosen team [S269]. Trap: Grades on their own.
Q22. “What are two of your strengths?” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Self-awareness. Structure: Two strengths, each with a short example and what it would give a team. Weave in: Your Immersive Online Assessment produces a strengths report [S260]. Use its language if it fits you. Trap: Strengths you cannot prove.
Q23. “What's your greatest weakness?” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Honesty and ability to improve. Structure: A real weakness, one example of its effect, what you now do about it, and evidence of progress. Weave in: “Serve with integrity” [S266]. Trap: A disguised boast (“I work too hard”).
Q24. “Tell me about a time you ran into conflict working with someone.” (Reported [S287])
Tests: Maturity; the values “Take care of each other” and “Foster inclusion”. Structure: STAR. Spend time on how you understood their view and how you reached an agreed outcome. Weave in: [S266]. Trap: A story with a villain.
Q25. “Tell me about a time you made a mistake.” (Reported [S287])
Tests: Integrity. Structure: Own it quickly. Fix it. Tell the people affected. Explain what you changed to prevent it. Weave in: “Serve with integrity” [S266]; Deloitte treats breaches of its assessment rules seriously [S260]. Trap: A mistake that turns out to be someone else's fault.
Q26. “Give me an example of when you've been responsible for a project.” (Practice; generic example in [S265])
Tests: Planning and ownership, the daily work of a junior consultant. Structure: Scope, plan, track, report, deliver. Name the tool you used to track it. Weave in: Analysts “collaborate across disciplines” with strategy, design, engineering and data colleagues [S321]. Trap: No dates, no numbers, no sense of what you did.
Q27. “Tell me about a time you demonstrated leadership.” (Practice; generic example in [S265])
Tests: “Lead the way”. Structure: Leadership without a title counts: you set direction, got others moving and got a result. Weave in: [S266]. Trap: Equating leadership with being in charge.

D. Values: Deloitte's five Shared Values

Deloitte's current Shared Values are: Lead the way; Serve with integrity; Take care of each other; Foster inclusion; Collaborate for measurable impact [S266]. Older guides list “Integrity, Outstanding value, Commitment, Diversity” [S264]. Do not use the old list. Each question below is a practice prompt built on one value.

Q28. Lead the way: “Tell me about a time you changed how something was done.” (Practice [S266])
Tests: Initiative. Structure: What was wrong, what you proposed, how you persuaded people, what improved. Weave in: Deloitte says it aims to be “not only leading the profession, but also reinventing it” [S266]. Trap: A change nobody else noticed.
Q29. Serve with integrity: “A client calls when nobody else is in the office and asks you to shred one of their documents without telling anyone. What do you do?” (Practice; generic example in [S265])
Tests: Integrity and escalation. Structure: Do not act. Say politely you need to check. Escalate to your manager the same day. Keep a note. Weave in: Joiners must clear personal independence checks [S261]; conflict checks run before engagements are accepted [S94]. Trap: Agreeing to keep the client happy.
Q30. Take care of each other: “Tell me about a time you noticed someone struggling. What did you do?” (Practice [S266])
Tests: Care with good boundaries. Structure: What you noticed, how you raised it, what you did, and when you involved someone else. Weave in: [S266]. Trap: Becoming the hero who fixed everything alone.
Q31. Foster inclusion: “Tell me about a time you made sure a quieter voice was heard.” (Practice [S266])
Tests: Inclusive behaviour. Structure: The situation, what you changed (process or habit), and the effect on the outcome. Weave in: Deloitte UK introduced school- and university-blind recruitment in 2015 [S267]; 44% of September 2026 starters are based outside London [S271]. Trap: Talking about inclusion in general with no action.
Q32. Collaborate for measurable impact: “Tell me about a team result you can measure.” (Practice [S266])
Tests: Teamwork that produces a number. Structure: Team goal, your part, the measure, the result. Weave in: “tangible, measurable, attributable impact” [S266]. Trap: No number at all.

E. Commercial awareness

Topical questions are a listed category in the Final Stage interview [S263]. Use the pattern: the story in one line, the mechanism, the effect on Deloitte, your view.

Q33. “Tell me about something in the news and how it will affect Deloitte.” (Reported [S264])
Tests: Whether you follow business news and can link it to the firm. Structure: The story in one line; the mechanism; the effect on Deloitte's revenue, people or risk; your view. Weave in: Deloitte won a Home Office data contract worth up to £200m despite the government's pledge to cut consultancy spend [S233]. Trap: A story you cannot connect to Deloitte.
Q34. “Deloitte grew revenue 2% but distributable profit 14% in FY26. What does that tell you?” (Practice [S407])
Tests: Basic financial reasoning. Structure: Margin rose. Possible drivers: pricing, mix, cost control (voluntary redundancy in audit [S227]), efficiency from technology. Say what you would want to know next. Weave in: £5.81bn is UK and Switzerland consolidated; UK T&T was £1.75bn [S407]. Trap: Calling £5.81bn the UK-only figure.
Q35. “Globally Technology & Transformation grew slowest (2.5%), but in the UK it grew fastest (4%). Why?” (Practice [S300] [S407])
Tests: Hypothesis thinking. Structure: Offer two or three hypotheses and how you would test each. Do not claim to know. Weave in: ERP and cyber demand [S400]; public sector data work [S233]; regional technology centres [S323]. Trap: Stating one cause as fact.
Q36. “What does the creation of Deloitte EMEA mean for UK clients and for a graduate?” (Practice [S124])
Tests: Understanding of the firm's structure. Structure: What changed, why (pooled investment), what it could mean for clients, and what it could mean for you. Weave in: From 1 June 2026: 16 firms, 132,000 people, about €20bn revenue, over €1.5bn of investment over four years in GenAI, sovereign cloud and sector solutions [S124]. Trap: Implying the UK firm has disappeared. The UK firm still exists and has its own CEO [S407].
Q37. “The government says it wants to cut consultancy spend. Is that bad news for Deloitte?” (Practice [S233] [S334] [S335])
Tests: Balanced judgement. Structure: Both sides, then a view: less advice, more delivery and capability-building. Weave in: Public sector consulting hit a record £3.7bn in 2024/25 with Deloitte the top supplier [S335]; the NAO says government lacks consistent spend data [S334]. Trap: Cheerleading for consultants.
Q38. “Accenture and Deloitte are now about the same size. How do they differ?” (Practice [S129] [S120])
Tests: Competitor knowledge. Structure: Size, mix, ownership, constraints. Weave in: Accenture FY26 US$74.18bn, half managed services, about 814,000 people, listed [S129]; Deloitte US$74.5bn, partnership with audit and tax [S120]. Trap: Claiming Deloitte is the biggest on every measure.

F. Technology and AI

Expect at least one of these for a Technology & Transformation role. Plain-English explanations beat jargon.

Q39. “Explain an ERP implementation (or a cloud migration) to a non-technical client.” (Practice [S269] [S270])
Tests: Communication. Structure: Analogy, then what changes for staff, then why these programmes go wrong (data quality, change management, scope). Weave in: UK T&T growth came partly from “ERP implementation” demand [S407]. ERP (enterprise resource planning) is the core software that runs finance, HR and supply chain. Trap: Jargon and acronyms.
Q40. “What cyber risk should every UK board worry about?” (Practice [S269])
Tests: Risk thinking. Structure: One risk, how it happens, the business impact, two actions. Weave in: Deloitte's Cyber team works on ransomware recovery, supply-chain security and resilience [S269]; 60% of CFOs named cyber-attacks a key risk in Q1 2026 [S225]. Trap: Describing technology with no business consequence.
Q41. “Your teammate used a generative AI tool to draft client content and did not check it. What do you do?” (Practice [S260] [S261])
Tests: Integrity and courage. Structure: Raise it privately first, check the content together, involve the manager if it has gone to the client. Weave in: The Australian refund [S316]; Hayley McKelvey's line on using AI “responsibly and strategically” [S226]. Trap: Ignoring it, or reporting before talking to your teammate.
Q42. “Will AI replace graduate consultants?” (Practice [S229] [S407])
Tests: A balanced view and your own place in it. Structure: What AI takes (first drafts, data work), what stays (judgement, client trust, change), how training is shifting. Weave in: Darren Graves: “the role our people play will matter more, not less” [S407]; Big Four firms moving trainees into judgement work earlier [S229]; CFOs name AI the second biggest dampener on graduate hiring after cost control [S224]. Trap: Either extreme: “nothing will change” or “we are all doomed”.
Q43. “Only 11% of organisations have agentic AI in production. Why so few?” (Practice [S244])
Tests: Understanding of AI adoption. Structure: Define agentic AI (AI that takes actions, not only answers). Give the barriers: process redesign, data, risk and governance. Weave in: Tech Trends 2026 says the hard part is redesigning processes “agent-first” [S244]. Trap: Blaming the technology alone.
Q44. “Deloitte research found nearly a third of GenAI users use it without their employer knowing. What would you advise a client?” (Practice [S243])
Tests: Turning a finding into advice. Structure: The risk (data leakage), the cause (staff want tools), the fix (approved tools, policy, training). Weave in: Workers spend about £958m a year of their own money on GenAI for work; only 17% have in-house tools [S243]. Trap: Recommending a ban.

G. Deloitte-specific

Questions that only make sense at Deloitte. Getting these right separates you from candidates who prepared generically.

Q45. “What do you know about how Deloitte is structured?” (Practice [S407] [S302])
Tests: Basic firm knowledge. Structure: Network, then the UK firm, then the four businesses, then where your team sits. Weave in: Deloitte LLP is a member of Deloitte EMEA, which is a member of DTTL; “DTTL and Deloitte EMEA do not provide services to clients” [S407]. Advisory is T&T plus SR&T Advisory [S407]. Trap: Calling Deloitte one global company.
Q46. “Why hasn't Deloitte split audit from consulting, as EY tried to?” (Practice [S104] [S308] [S310])
Tests: Understanding of the business model. Structure: History, the argument for staying together, the costs, your view. Weave in: Deloitte dropped its own consulting spin-off in 2003 [S104]; Global CEO Joe Ucuzoglu said keeping the model was “not even a close call” [S308]; EY abandoned its split in April 2023 [S310]. Trap: Taking a side without the costs.
Q47. “What are personal independence rules and why do they matter to you?” (Practice [S261] [S314])
Tests: Whether you understand the audit link. Structure: Deloitte audits companies, so staff must not hold certain financial interests in audit clients. It also limits what consulting can sell to those clients. Weave in: “You will be required to clear Personal Independence checks before you join us” [S261]; non-audit fees for listed audit clients are capped at 70% of the average audit fee [S314]. Trap: Not knowing that Deloitte is also an auditor.
Q48. “What did you learn from the Deloitte Australia AI report case?” (Practice [S316])
Tests: Maturity on a sensitive topic. Structure: Facts in two sentences, the lesson (human checks, disclosure), what you would do as an analyst. Weave in: The refund was on an AU$440,000 contract; the report contained fabricated citations [S316]. It was a separate member firm, but the story ran under the Deloitte name [S302]. Trap: Gloating, or pretending it did not happen.

H. Final-stage topic discussion follow-ups

The topic discussion is “two-way”: the assessor asks questions throughout [S260]. These practice follow-ups test whether you can think on your feet. Prepare a short answer to each for your topic.

Q49. “What is the strongest argument against your view?” (Practice, built on the official format [S260])
Tests: Intellectual honesty. Structure: State the counter-argument fairly, say why you still hold your view, or say what would change it. Weave in: Use the counter-case evidence from your topic notes. Trap: Saying there isn't one.
Q50. “If you were advising the CFO, what would you tell them to do on Monday?” (Practice [S260])
Tests: Turning analysis into action. Structure: One action, one owner, one measure of success. Weave in: CFO priorities from the Deloitte CFO Survey [S224]. Trap: Another round of analysis.
Q51. “What evidence would change your mind?” (Practice [S260])
Tests: Scientific thinking. Structure: Name one data point and the threshold that would flip your view. Weave in: Point to a specific published number you used. Trap: “Nothing would.”
Q52. “How would a firm like Deloitte help here, and how would it get paid?” (Practice [S260])
Tests: Commercial sense. Structure: The service, the team that sells it, the pricing model (time and materials, fixed fee or managed service). Weave in: Deloitte sells “Operate” managed services as well as projects [S120]. Trap: Forgetting that consulting is a business.

I. Curveballs

Unexpected questions test composure. Pause, structure, answer.

Q53. “Teach me something in two minutes.” (Practice)
Tests: Clarity and structure. Structure: One idea, one analogy, one example, check understanding. Weave in: Choose something from your degree. Trap: Something too big to fit in two minutes.
Q54. “What is one weakness of Deloitte?” (Practice [S316] [S318] [S227])
Tests: Honesty and balance. Structure: One real weakness, why it exists, what the firm is doing about it. Weave in: Reputational spillover between member firms [S316]; FRC sanctions [S318]; low attrition led to audit voluntary redundancies [S227]. Trap: Refusing to name one, or naming one with venom.
Q55. “Should governments use consultants at all?” (Practice [S337] [S332] [S334])
Tests: Balanced judgement on a contested issue. Structure: The case for (skills, speed), the case against (cost, dependence), your conditions. Weave in: Test and Trace: about £1,000 a day per Deloitte consultant [S332]; The Big Con argues reliance weakens state capability [S337]; the NAO found 86% of survey respondents said consultants added value [S334]. Trap: One-sided either way.
Q56. “If you don't get this offer, what will you do?” (Practice [S260])
Tests: Resilience and real motivation. Structure: Learn from the feedback, build the skill, reapply. Weave in: Deloitte gives feedback after the final stage and lets you reapply next academic year [S260]. Trap: Naming a competitor as your plan B.

Questions to ask them

You will usually get a few minutes at the end of the interview. Ask one or two. Each question below shows you read primary material and want to understand the job. Pick the ones that fit the interviewer (Part 10).

QuestionSourceWhy it impresses
“T&T grew 4% in FY26, faster than the other UK businesses. Where inside T&T is that growth coming from: AI work, or core ERP and cyber?”[S407] [S400]Uses the right number for the right unit, and asks about the work you would do.
“Globally T&T grew slowest at 2.5%, but in the UK it grew fastest. What is the UK doing differently?”[S300] [S407]Compares two primary releases. Few candidates will have read both.
“With a Chief AI Officer now on the UK Executive, how has your own day-to-day work changed this year? What do you expect a graduate to do that AI does not?”[S274] [S407]Personal, current and about the real job. Interviewers like talking about their own work.
“What quality checks does your team use when generative AI helps produce a client deliverable?”[S316] [S226]Shows you understand the risk without raising the Australian case aggressively. Ask it neutrally.
“Deloitte EMEA launched on 1 June with over €1.5bn of planned investment. Do UK graduates see more cross-border work as a result?”[S124]Shows you follow structural news and think about what it means for juniors.
“Hammad Rafique moved from leading T&T in Financial Services to leading all of UK T&T in June. Has that changed which sectors new analysts get staffed on?”[S274] [S275]Names the leader of the business you are joining, correctly. Best for a manager or director.
“With the independence rules on audit clients, where does your team find most of its integrated, multi-business work?”[S261] [S314]Shows you understand the multidisciplinary model and its main constraint.
“How does staffing work for a graduate based in, say, Manchester or Belfast on national client work?”[S271] [S323]Practical and grounded in the 44% regional intake and the technology centres.
“The Shared Values include ‘Collaborate for measurable impact’. How does your team measure impact on a typical engagement?”[S266]Turns a values statement into a real operating question.
“Darren Graves talks about reinventing the firm for the next generation. What has that meant for graduates in your team since June?”[S273]Links the new CEO's message to your own future. Best for a director or partner.
DON'T SAY THIS

Do not ask about salary, holidays or how fast you can be promoted in the interview. Do not name the video platform or quote paid prep sites as if they were inside knowledge; Deloitte distances itself from them [S260]. Do not use the old values list [S264].

Part 10

Who you will meet: interviewer and leadership briefing

No interviewers are named for you, so this part describes the types of people you will meet at each stage, how to pitch to each, how to adjust in the room, and a dated briefing on the leaders whose names you should recognise.

Interviewer types by stage

StageWhoEvidenceHow to pitch
Application, Online AssessmentNobody live. Automated eligibility check and scoring.[S260] ConfirmedAccuracy and honesty. Answer ranking tasks as yourself.
Job SimulationRecorded answers reviewed later by the recruitment team or assessors. Platform not named by Deloitte UK.[S260] Confirmed; vendor [S287] ReportedImagine a busy manager watching many videos. Answer in the first 15 seconds, then give evidence.
Topic DiscussionAn “assessor”.[S260] ConfirmedTwo-way. Structure first, then depth on follow-ups. Defend a view; accept good challenge.
Skills and Motivation interviewA “senior person from your chosen service line”.[S264] ReportedCompetency stories plus a clear “why this team”.
Possible extra or older formatSenior managers, directors or partners.[S286] [S289] ReportedShorter, commercial, judgement-focused.

The early-careers recruitment team runs logistics; its staff give advice on the official page [S260]. Final-stage assessors are usually practitioners, often managers or senior managers, sometimes directors Inferred. In Deloitte's grade structure a manager runs day-to-day project work, a senior manager runs larger workstreams and client relationships, and a director or partner owns the client relationship and sells the work Inferred.

How to pitch to each type

Recruiter or assessor

Their question: does this candidate meet the criteria and show the capabilities?

Give them: clear STAR stories that are easy to score, the Shared Values in action, a calm manner.

Avoid: vague answers that leave them nothing to write down.

Manager or senior manager

Their question: can I give this person work on Monday?

Give them: reliability, learning speed, Excel and PowerPoint basics, how you handle a deadline and feedback.

Avoid: grand strategy talk with no sign you can do the work.

Director or partner

Their question: would I put this person in front of a client, and will they stay?

Give them: one sharp, defended view on the client market, real motivation, integrity.

Avoid: long answers. Lead with the point.

The pitches above are Inferred from the stage evidence in [S260], [S264] and [S286]. They are general patterns, not Deloitte policy.

Reading the interviewer, and adjusting honestly

Adjusting to your interviewer is about relevance: giving the level of detail they need. It is not about pretending to be someone else or flattering them. Use these signals Inferred:

SignalWhat it probably meansAdjust by
Detailed follow-ups on how you did somethingThey are testing whether you can do the work.Give steps, tools and numbers. Keep stories concrete.
Questions about clients, markets or “so what”They think commercially, often a senior person.Lead with your conclusion. Link to client value.
They interrupt or look at the clockYour answer is too long.Finish the sentence, give the result, stop.
They push back on your viewA test of judgement, not a sign you are failing.Restate their point fairly, then hold or update with a reason.
They share their own experienceRapport is building.Ask one genuine follow-up question, then return to your answer.
DON'T DO THIS

Do not research interviewers' private lives or social media, or mention personal details about them. Do not mirror opinions you do not hold. If you learn your interviewer's name, it is fine to read their public Deloitte profile for their team and role, and nothing more.

Part 11

The scenario playbook: frame method, ladder, composure set, CV grill

One answer protocol and one priority order that work on any scenario Deloitte puts in front of you, from the ranking items in the online assessment to a director pushing back in the final interview. Then the eight ways interviewers test whether your answer holds, how to keep your body calm, the 30-scenario ladder, five hard scenarios worked in full, and a drill for surviving a three-levels-deep grilling on your CV.

Why scenarios decide this process

Deloitte UK tests judgement at every stage of its early-careers process. The Immersive Online Assessment (stage 2) has a behavioural part built on "realistic workplace scenarios" where you rank possible actions from most to least likely [S350] Confirmed. The Job Simulation (stage 3) adds ranking, selecting responses, written answers and recorded video answers. Deloitte says "some scenarios may refer to workplace tools like AI" and that it is interested in "how you think and make decisions ... and consider using AI responsibly in a professional setting, not your technical AI knowledge" [S350] Confirmed. The Final Stage skills and motivation interview, about 50 minutes, includes scenario-based questions according to TargetJobs [S260] [S263] Reported.

So the same skill is scored three times, in three formats: a click-to-rank screen, a 2-minute recording, and a live conversation where someone can push back. This Part gives you one method that works in all three. It has two pieces. A protocol tells you what to say, in what order, in about a minute. A priority order tells you which concern wins when two good things collide. Learn both until they are automatic, because Deloitte's own advice on the ranking tasks is to "go with your gut instinct" [S260] Confirmed. The aim of practice is to train your gut, not to game the test.

KEY TERMS

Scenario question: "What would you do if...?" It asks about a situation you have not met, so it tests judgement rather than memory. Situational judgement test (SJT): the written or on-screen version, where you rank or pick from given options. Frame: the logic that holds your answer together (what matters most and why). An interviewer "breaks the frame" when they push until you drop that logic. Escalate: pass a decision to someone more senior or to a specialist team, openly and early.

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

Deloitte does not publish how its ranking items are scored or which "capabilities" the final interview scores against [S260]. The timings below for video answers come from TargetJobs (30 seconds to 2 minutes) and a prep vendor (2 to 3 minutes, from a search summary only) [S263] [S288] Reported. The answer method in this Part is this pack's synthesis of Deloitte's own Code, the law it cites and standard interview practice Inferred. It is a tool for thinking, not a leaked marking scheme.

The four-step answer protocol

Every scenario answer, spoken or written, follows four steps: steady, sort, act, close. A full spoken answer takes 45 to 75 seconds. That is long enough to show judgement and short enough to leave room for the follow-up, which is where most marks are won or lost Inferred. In a recorded video answer with 2 to 3 minutes available, use the same four steps and spend the extra time in step 3, on the twist you expect next.

Step 1: Steady (about 0 to 8 seconds)

Take one slow breath out. Then repeat the problem back in one line. This does two jobs. It buys you thinking time without dead air, and it shows the interviewer you heard the actual question rather than the one you hoped for. If a fact is missing that changes the answer, ask one question now, not five.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"Let me make sure I've got this. The client wants the pack tonight, and the data in it isn't checked yet."

"Before I answer: is the client also a Deloitte audit client? That changes what I can do." (Use only when it really changes the answer.)

Step 2: Sort (about 8 to 25 seconds)

Say what is at stake, then rank it out loud using the priority order in the next section. Separate what you know from what you would need to find out. This is the step most candidates skip. They jump straight to action, which makes the answer sound like a reflex instead of a judgement. Deloitte's own Code tells its people to "consider all available information to assess the situation, use professional judgment, consult with relevant stakeholders as appropriate and, where necessary, take action" [S340] Confirmed. Step 2 is the "assess" part of that sentence.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"Two things matter here. The first is client confidentiality, because that's a legal and Code issue. The second is the deadline. The first one decides how I do it. The second decides how fast."

Step 3: Act (about 25 to 60 seconds)

Give the first concrete step, the person you tell and the time by which you tell them. Then give the route that still meets the goal. An answer that only says "I would refuse" or "I would escalate" scores badly because it stops the work Inferred. Deloitte's Code calls its method ACT: Assess the situation, Consider and Consult, Take action. It adds: "Speaking up is taking action!" and "No one at Deloitte should have to navigate a difficult situation alone" [S340] Confirmed. So "I'd talk to my manager" is a proper action in Deloitte's own terms, as long as you also say what you would do meanwhile.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"First I'd do the analysis in the firm's approved tool, not a public one. Then I'd tell my manager before 6pm that one section rests on an assumption, and offer to firm it up by 10am."

Step 4: Close (about 60 to 75 seconds)

State the outcome, the record you leave behind and the follow-up. Then stop. Silence after a clean close is fine. The record matters because it is what protects you, your manager and the client later. The McKinsey opioid case ended with a former senior partner agreeing to plead guilty to obstruction for deleting files [S390] Confirmed. A junior does not need that level of drama to learn the point: write it down.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"So the client gets the pack on time, nothing confidential leaves the firm, and the email to my manager is the record. I'd check back at 5pm."

DON'T SAY THIS

"It depends." (Alone, it sounds like dodging. Say what it depends on, then answer both branches.) "I'd just do what the partner says." (Rank is not a reason.) "I'd report them straight to the regulator." (A junior escalates inside the firm first, unless the firm itself is the problem; Deloitte's Speak Up channel exists for that case [S340] [S343].) "I'd go above my manager's head immediately." (One level at a time, unless it is an ethics or legal matter [Inferred from S340].)

The priority order when good things collide

Most hard scenarios are not good against bad. They are two good things that cannot both win: the deadline and the check, the client's wish and the rule, your manager's request and the partner's. You need a fixed order, decided in advance, so you are not inventing your values under pressure. For this role the order is:

  1. Law, independence and the firm's name.
  2. The client's real interest and fair treatment of every stakeholder.
  3. The process and the record (change control, documentation, accurate timesheets, approved tools).
  4. Speed and convenience.

Each level beats every level below it. Within a level, use judgement. And when nothing above is at stake, speed wins: most of the job is simply getting good work done fast.

Why each level sits where it does

LevelThe Deloitte and legal basisWhat it means in a scenario
1. Law, independence, the firm's nameShared Value "Serve with integrity": "Upholding that trust is our single most important responsibility" [S340] [S342]. Breaching the Code can lead to consequences "up to and including dismissal" [S340]. UK GDPR fines reach "£17.5 million, or 4% of your total worldwide annual turnover" [S353]. The Bribery Act makes a firm liable for an associated person's bribe unless it had "adequate procedures" [S355]. Since 1 September 2025 a large organisation can be guilty if an associate commits fraud intending to benefit it or its clients [S361] [S362]. UK MAR bans insider dealing and unlawful disclosure [S360]. The FRC Ethical Standard bars an audit firm from taking "a management role" at an audited entity [S364].Confidential client data never leaves approved systems. No backdating, no inflated numbers, no tipping. If the client is a Deloitte audit client, you give options and the client's management decides. Anything in this band beats any deadline, any seniority and any client request. The firm's name sits here because one person's breach becomes the firm's breach: Deloitte Australia repaid part of a A$440,000 fee after an AI-assisted report contained nonexistent references [S388].
2. The client's real interest and fair treatmentCode, integrity: "We are straightforward and honest in our professional opinions" and "truthful about ... the knowledge we possess, and the experience we have" [S340]. Objectivity: no "bias, conflict of interest, or undue influence" [S340]. ICAEW adds "undue reliance on ... technology" as an objectivity threat [S372]. Shared Values: "Foster inclusion" and "Take care of each other" [S342]. Procurement Act s.82: no supplier may get an "unfair advantage" [S367]."The client" means the client organisation, not whichever executive is shouting. A sponsor who wants a red risk hidden from the board is asking you to act against the client's interest. Fair treatment covers the quiet stakeholders too: the remote worker left out of the workshop, the competing supplier in a procurement.
3. The process and the recordAPM: change control is how requests to change the agreed baseline are "captured, evaluated and then approved, rejected or deferred" [S377]. Code: "We record hours worked timely and accurately" [S340]. Deloitte UK runs GenAI through "use-case approval" and a "clearing house" and gives staff secure internal tools [S345]. JD: "Using firm-approved AI tools responsibly" [S3]. "Accountability is squarely a human domain" [S347].New asks go through change control, even small ones. Timesheets show the truth. AI goes through approved tools, and you check its output. The process exists so a large programme stays honest and so you can prove later what happened.
4. Speed and convenienceShared Value "Collaborate for measurable impact": "tangible, measurable, attributable impact" [S342]. Clients pay for results on time.Speed is a real value. But it only operates inside levels 1 to 3. One twist: speed of escalation belongs to level 1. Capita's containment was "not enacted for 58 hours" after an alert and it was fined £14m [S394]. Raise problems fast even when the fix will be slow.
THE ONE SENTENCE THAT HOLDS EVERY FRAME

"I'll keep it legal and honest first, do right by the client second, follow the process and leave a record third, and go as fast as those three allow."

Say it to yourself before every scenario. Say it aloud only if an interviewer asks how you make these calls in general.

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Prompt: should the client's interest ever rank above the process? For: processes can be slow and a rigid junior can hurt a client by waiting for sign-off on something obvious. Against: the process exists because individuals under pressure misjudge the client's interest; change control protects the client from scope creep and surprise cost [S377]. Suggested stance: the client's interest ranks higher, which is why you raise a process that is hurting the client openly and fast. You do not quietly bypass it.

Ranking items: applying the order to multiple choice

In the Immersive Online Assessment you see a short workplace scenario and four or five possible actions. You rank them from the one you would most likely take to the one you would least likely take [S350] Confirmed. The Job Simulation includes the same kind of item, some about AI [S350]. Deloitte does not publish the scoring key. Typical SJT design, which this pack infers applies here, scores how close your order is to an expert order, so getting the top and bottom right matters most Inferred.

The five-pass method

  1. Bottom first. Any option that breaches level 1 (shares confidential data, misstates facts, hides a problem, breaks a law) goes to the bottom. If two do, the one that does more harm, or is harder to undo, goes lowest.
  2. Then the do-nothing options. Ignoring the problem, or passing it on without a view, sits just above the breaches.
  3. Top next. The best option protects every level that is at stake and still moves the work forward. It usually involves acting and telling someone.
  4. Middle by level. Between two safe options, the one that serves a higher level ranks higher. If they serve the same level, prefer the one that consults at the right level and leaves a record.
  5. Gut check. Read your order top to bottom. Would you be comfortable explaining it to the partner and to the client? If not, swap.

Practice item (invented, not a real Deloitte question)

You are two weeks into a cloud migration project. At 6pm your manager asks for a two-page summary of 40 client staff interview transcripts by 9am. The transcripts include staff names and frank comments about their managers. A fellow analyst says: "Paste them into a free chatbot. Ten minutes, done." You have access to the firm's approved AI tool. Rank these actions.

RankOptionReasoning using the priority order
1C. Check the engagement has no restriction on AI use, draft in the firm's approved tool, verify every claim against the transcripts, and note in your covering email that it was AI-assisted.Protects level 1 (data stays inside approved systems [S340] [S345]), level 2 (accurate content, disclosed method), level 3 (approved tool, a record) and level 4 (on time). Deloitte Australia's refund shows why verification and disclosure matter [S388].
2D. Work through the night by hand and deliver at 9am without telling anyone how long it took.Safe on levels 1 to 3 and on time. Loses marks because it is silent and unsustainable; "Take care of each other" applies to yourself too [S342]. Some experts might swap D and E.
3E. Tell your manager at 6pm you cannot do it by 9am and ask for a new deadline.Honest and safe, but gives up on the client's deadline without trying a compliant route.
4B. Delete the names, then paste the transcripts into the free chatbot.Still sends confidential client information outside the firm without permission [S340]. Removing names reduces personal-data risk but the comments may still identify people. A level 1 breach, slightly less harmful than A.
5A. Paste the full transcripts into the free chatbot, then check the summary carefully.Discloses named personal data and confidential client material outside the firm [S340] [S353]. Checking afterwards does not undo the disclosure. Bottom.
DON'T DO THIS

Don't use AI, a friend or a paid "insights" site during the assessment. Deloitte's rules say online assessments "must be completed independently and without AI assistance", that you record an integrity statement first, and that a breach means removal from the process [S351] Confirmed. Inside the firm, using GenAI in assessments "constitutes gross misconduct" [S345].

Eight ways interviewers break a frame

A live interviewer listens to your first answer and then tests whether it holds. Deloitte's own recruiters say assessors "are not trying to trip you up or trick you" [S260] Confirmed, so read the moves below as probes rather than hostility. Most are the natural follow-ups a manager would ask if you gave that answer at work. Your job is to stay in the frame: keep the same priority order, change your plan only if new facts justify it, and stay pleasant.

TacticWhat they are really testingHow to hold, and what not to do
1. InterruptionCan you stay organised when your structure is broken? Do you get flustered or defensive?Finish one sentence at most, then go where they lead. Do not restart your whole answer later. If the interruption was the more important question, say so: "Good point, that's the bigger issue."
2. Flat contradictionDo you cave the moment a senior person disagrees? Or do you dig in without listening?Name what evidence would change your view, then keep your view if that evidence is absent. Caving loses the frame; arguing loses the room. Integrity in the Code means "straightforward and honest in our professional opinions" [S340].
3. SilenceWill you fill the gap by retracting, over-explaining or adding a worse idea?Silence is not a signal you were wrong. Count three seconds, then offer to go deeper on one part. Never add "or I suppose I could just do what they asked".
4. EscalationDoes your answer survive higher stakes and more senior pressure?The higher the stakes, the higher the person you consult, not the faster you give in. Deloitte's Code says retaliation against those who raise concerns "is not tolerated" [S340].
5. Authority squeezeWill rank alone change your answer?Separate the goal from the method. Agree to the goal, decline the method, offer an alternative with a time. Seniority changes who decides, not what the law says.
6. False choiceCan you see a third option under pressure?There is almost always a third route: deliver part on time, flag the rest, raise it early. Name it. If there truly is no third route, choose by the priority order and say so.
7. Knowledge trapWill you bluff?Say you do not know the detail, state the principle you do know, and say who you would check with. Bluffing about law in an interview is exactly the behaviour they fear on a client site.
8. Invitation to badmouthWill you blame others, and will you talk about people behind their backs?Decline the bait warmly. Talk only about what you did and would do differently. The Code applies to behaviour "both inside and outside of the Deloitte workplace" [S340], and assessors read badmouthing as a preview of how you will talk about clients.
SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

When you genuinely change your mind after a push: "That's a fair point I hadn't weighed. With that fact, I'd change step two to X. The rest stays the same." Changing a step because of a new fact is judgement. Changing your values because of a frown is losing the frame.

Staying calm physically: what the evidence supports

A frame holds only if your body lets your working memory work. Three techniques have peer-reviewed evidence behind them. None is magic, and each study tested something slightly different from a Deloitte interview, so each comes with a caveat.

TechniqueWhat the study foundHow to use itCaveat
Cyclic sighing (exhale-focused breathing)Balban et al. 2023, Cell Reports Medicine: a one-month randomised study of 5-minute daily practices. Cyclic sighing gave more improvement in mood and a bigger drop in breathing rate than mindfulness meditation (p < 0.05) [S385] Confirmed.Practise 5 minutes a day in the weeks before. On the day, do a few rounds in the waiting room: a full breath in through the nose, a short second top-up breath, then a long slow breath out through the mouth.The study measured daily practice over a month, not one breath before an interview. One author disclosed an advisory role with WHOOP [S385]. A few slow exhales are low cost and low risk Inferred.
Reappraise anxiety as excitementBrooks 2014, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General: people who reappraised anxiety as excitement "feel more excited and perform better" than those who tried to calm down, across singing, public speaking and maths tasks. Saying "I am excited" out loud worked [S384] Confirmed. Jamieson et al. 2010: students told that arousal improves performance did better on GRE maths, including on the real test 1 to 3 months later [S386] Confirmed.Do not tell yourself to calm down. Say "I'm excited" quietly before you go in. Treat a racing heart as fuel. Both states are high arousal, so relabelling is easier than switching off [S384].Lab and test settings, mostly with students. Effects are modest. It helps performance; it does not make the feeling disappear.
Expressive writingRamirez and Beilock 2011, Science: a brief exercise writing about worries just before an exam "significantly improved students' exam scores, especially for students habitually anxious about test taking" [S387] Confirmed. Park, Ramirez and Beilock 2014 found a similar effect for maths anxiety [S395].About 10 minutes before you leave, or the night before: write freely about what you fear will go wrong in the interview. Then put it away.Classroom exams, not interviews. Science published an erratum in 2014 [S387]. Best evidence is for people who are habitually anxious.

The composure routine on the day [Inferred, built on S384, S385, S387]

  1. That morning: 10 minutes of expressive writing about your worries. Bin the page.
  2. In the waiting room: three to five cyclic sighs. Then say "I'm excited" quietly to yourself.
  3. In the room: use the four-step protocol. A fixed structure means your working memory goes on the content, not on organising it.
  4. When pushed: breathe out before you answer. One exhale is your "steady" step.

The scenario ladder: every JD duty line, three rungs

The ladder turns each of the ten duty lines in the Technology Strategy & Transformation graduate job description (D1 to D10, decoded in Part 1) into three practice scenarios of rising difficulty [S2] [S3]. The easy rung is a craft task: can you do the work well? The medium rung adds a stakeholder pulling against you. The hard rung puts an ethical or legal line in play, so the priority order decides the answer. The full 30 cards follow this section, in the same order as the grid.

HOW TO PRACTISE THE LADDER

Practise one row per day for ten days. Say each answer aloud, timed, using the four steps. Then have a friend play the interviewer and use two of the eight tactics on your hard-rung answer. Record yourself once a week; the Job Simulation is recorded, so you need to be comfortable talking to a camera [S260].

The composure set: five hard role-specific scenarios

These five are the scenarios where candidates most often lose the frame, because each pits a senior person, a deadline or their own pride against the priority order. Each card gives the setup, the trap, the answer, why it works, the twist an interviewer will add, and a decision tree. Figure 30 draws the trees for the two highest-stakes cards. The other three trees are written out in the cards.

Composure set 1 · Two seniors, one deadlineHARD
Setup

It is 1pm. The engagement partner asks you for a cut of the cost baseline for a 5pm call with the client CFO. Ten minutes later the client's IT director, whom you sit next to on site, asks you to rebuild the application inventory for her 5pm meeting with her own boss. Each task is about four hours. Your manager is on leave today.

The trap

Saying yes to both and failing one at 4.55pm. Or picking by rank ("the partner wins") without telling the other person. Or picking by proximity (the client is sitting next to you).

What to say

"I can't do both properly by 5. Both matter, so I wouldn't choose silently. I'd tell both of them now, within ten minutes, and ask whoever owns my priorities on this engagement to decide. With my manager away, that's the engagement lead. While I wait, I'd start the piece that is client-facing at board level, the CFO call, and I'd tell the IT director what I can give her by 5: a cleaned version of the existing inventory with the gaps marked. Then I'd confirm the decision in a two-line email."

Why it works

It applies the order: nothing in level 1 is at stake, so the call is level 2 (the client's interest), then level 3 (the record), then speed. It follows the Code's encouragement to consult "others in their chain of command" rather than deciding alone [S340]. It respects the idea that one person is accountable for a decision, as in a RACI matrix [S379]. It offers a partial delivery instead of a silent miss, which is "Collaborate for measurable impact" in practice [S342].

The twist, and how to hold

"Both of them say: don't bother anyone, just do mine." Hold: "I understand. I'll give you an honest time instead of a hopeful one. I'd rather tell you now that 5pm isn't possible for both than tell you at 4.55." Then you still tell the engagement lead, because a missed client deadline is their risk too.

Decision tree

Can both be done well by the deadline? Yes: do both, confirm times. No: tell both people now. Then: is there an owner of your priorities you can reach? Yes: they decide; start the more client-critical task meanwhile. No: choose by the priority order (legal or board-facing first), offer the other person a partial deliverable with a time, and write it down.

Composure set 2 · Asked to skip a controlHARD
Setup

It is 7pm before a steering committee. A director on your team says: "The firm's AI tool is too slow. Paste the client's survey export into ChatGPT, get me the themes, and we're done by eight." The export contains client employees' names and comments. Variants an interviewer may use instead: "Backdate your timesheet so last week's hours go on the new code", or "Skip the conflict check, we start on Monday regardless".

The trap

Complying because a director asked. Or refusing with a lecture and no alternative, which leaves the director stranded and makes you look rigid.

What to say

"I want to get you those themes tonight. I can't put client data into a public tool, because that's disclosing it outside the firm. What I can do is run it in our approved tool or theme it by hand from the top 200 comments, and you'll have it by 8.30. If 8.30 is too late, I'll tell the engagement partner now so the timing risk isn't on you alone."

Why it works

Deloitte's Code prohibits "disclosure of confidential and personal information entrusted to us unless granted permission" [S340]. The JD itself specifies "firm-approved AI tools" [S3]. Deloitte UK runs GenAI through use-case approval and gives staff secure tools that analyse confidential data "within its secure digital ecosystem" [S345]. Personal data brings UK GDPR, whose principles include integrity and confidentiality [S353]. For the timesheet variant, the Code says "We record hours worked timely and accurately" [S340], and since September 2025 a firm can be criminally liable if an associate commits fraud intended to benefit it or its client [S361] [S362]. For the conflict-check variant, Deloitte UK says "all proposed engagements ... go through a conflict check before they are accepted" [S345].

The twist, and how to hold

"Everyone does it. I'm the director and I'm telling you to." Hold: "I believe you that it's common. I still can't do it, and I'd rather be the person who got you a slightly later answer than the person who caused a data incident on your engagement. Do you want me to raise it with the partner, or shall I just crack on with the approved route?" If the pressure continues, the Code's route is to consult the chain of command or Ethics, and retaliation for raising concerns "is not tolerated" [S340].

Decision tree

See Figure 30, tree A.

Composure set 3 · Overheard deal talkHARD
Setup

You are queuing for coffee near the office. Two people you recognise from another Deloitte team are discussing, fairly loudly, a "Project Falcon" and that a FTSE 250 company you know is "being bought at a big premium next month". You are not on that work. A friend who works in finance is texting you about shares that evening.

The trap

Treating it as gossip. Telling your friend "I can't say, but I wouldn't sell". Trading yourself. Or pretending you heard nothing and doing nothing.

What to say

"I'd assume it could be inside information, so I wouldn't trade, tip or repeat it to anyone, including friends. I'd tell my manager or the Risk or Ethics team, briefly, what I heard, where and when, because a leak in a public place is something the firm needs to know about, and they may need to manage it. I wouldn't confront the colleagues myself or try to judge whether it was price-sensitive. That's Risk's call."

Why it works

UK MAR defines inside information as "information of a precise nature, which has not been made public ... which, if it were made public, would be likely to have a significant effect on the prices" [S358]. It bans insider dealing, recommending it, and unlawful disclosure [S360]. Disclosure is lawful only "in the normal exercise of an employment, a profession or duties" [S359], so need-to-know sharing inside the engagement team is fine; telling a friend is not. Deloitte's Code prohibits "the use of confidential information about our clients for personal advantage or for the benefit of third parties" [S340] and asks everyone to report suspected noncompliance whoever is involved [S340].

The twist, and how to hold

"Your friend says: just tell me if I should hold or sell." Hold: "I can't talk about clients, and please don't ask me about shares." Even a hint is a recommendation. "The colleagues are senior. Won't reporting them damage your career?" Hold: "The Code says retaliation isn't tolerated [S340]. And I'm not accusing anyone. I'm reporting a risk so the firm can deal with it."

Decision tree

See Figure 30, tree B.

Composure set 4 · Your AI-assisted figure was wrongHARD
Setup

Yesterday your team sent a client a benefits analysis. You built one section with help from the firm's approved AI tool. This morning you notice the tool had combined two years of savings into one, so a headline figure is overstated by about a third. The client has not mentioned it. Your manager is in back-to-back meetings.

The trap

Quietly fixing the file and hoping. Blaming the tool. Or panicking and emailing the client directly before telling your team.

What to say

"I'd message my manager now, short and factual: the figure, the correct figure, how it happened, and that it's my section. I'd suggest a correction note to the client today, with the corrected page. While they decide, I'd re-check every other number I produced with the tool, so we only correct once. Afterwards I'd add a step to my own checklist: any AI-assisted number gets traced back to its source before it leaves my hands."

Why it works

Deloitte's own guidance says "an AI model cannot be meaningfully held accountable for its outputs, accountability is squarely a human domain" [S347]. The Code's integrity rule and duty to report apply [S340]. The ICAEW Code names "undue reliance on ... technology" as a threat to objectivity [S372]. And the firm has lived this: Deloitte Australia agreed to repay part of a A$440,000 fee after an AI-assisted government report was found to contain nonexistent references and an erroneous summary of a court case [S388] Confirmed.

The twist, and how to hold

"Your manager says: nobody will notice, just fix it in the next version." Hold: "I'd rather the client hears it from us today than finds it at their board. If the decision is to correct it in the next version, I'd want that decision written down and the client told the figure is being revised." That keeps level 2 (the client's real interest) above level 4 (convenience).

Decision tree

Has the wrong figure left the firm? No: fix it, tell your manager, check related numbers. Yes: tell your manager now. Then: could the client act on it before a correction? Yes: push for a same-day correction note. No: agree a correction route and date, in writing. In every branch: never fix silently, never blame the tool, re-check everything else you touched.

Composure set 5 · Deadline with half the dataHARD
Setup

A steering committee pack is due to the client at 9am. One input, the licence costs from the client's procurement team, has not arrived. Without it, the total cost of the preferred option could be out by 10 to 20 per cent. It is 10pm, and procurement are not answering.

The trap

Guessing the number and presenting it as fact. Or holding the whole pack back, so the committee meets with nothing.

What to say

"I'd deliver on time with what's solid and make the gap impossible to miss. I'd use last year's licence figure as a labelled assumption, show the total as a range, and put a line on the summary slide saying which number is provisional and when it'll be firm. I'd tell my manager tonight, so they aren't surprised in the meeting, and I'd log it as an assumption and a dependency in the RAID log. First thing tomorrow I'd chase procurement through the client's programme lead."

Why it works

The Code asks for being "straightforward and honest in our professional opinions" [S340]: a clearly labelled assumption is honest, a silent guess is not. Representing an estimate as fact to win the next phase could even become a fraud risk [S361]. A RAID log (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies) exists for exactly this, and APM notes that issues can turn into change requests [S377]. The pyramid principle, leading with the answer and then the support, still works with a range [S374].

The twist, and how to hold

"The client sponsor says: the board hates ranges, give me one number." Hold: "I can give you one central number on the slide, with the range and the assumption in a footnote. If the board asks, you'll have the answer ready." You give the sponsor what they need without hiding the uncertainty from the board.

Decision tree

Can you get the missing fact before the deadline? Yes: get it. No: would the gap change the recommendation? Yes: tell your manager tonight and agree whether to delay that one decision, not the whole pack. No: deliver on time with a labelled assumption and a range, log it, and chase the fact in the morning.

SOURCE UNCERTAIN

Deloitte UK's own code of conduct, its insider-list procedures and its GenAI-with-client-data policy are not public [S340] [S345]. The trees use the public Global Code, the Transparency Report and the law. On day one, your induction will give you the firm's real procedures; follow those where they differ.

The CV grill: holding your ground three levels deep

The skills and motivation interview will include "tell me about a time" questions and probably "run me through your CV" [S260] [S289]. A good interviewer does not stop at your first answer. They dig three levels deep on one line of your CV, and the frame you have to hold is simple: every level must match the one above it. If your first sentence inflates, the third level will find it.

Level 1: the claim

"Tell me about your role as society treasurer." They hear your headline and pick the word that sounds biggest ("led", "transformed", "managed").

Level 2: the mechanism

"How exactly did you do that? Why that approach?" They test whether you did it or watched it, and whether you understood why it worked.

Level 3: the proof and the counterfactual

"How do you know it was you? What would have happened without you? What did it cost?" They test honesty and self-awareness.

Prospects, the UK careers service, recommends the STARR structure (situation, task, action, result, reflection), "five to eight STARR examples", and a focus on "what you specifically did and decided", with tangible outcomes [S382] Confirmed. Deloitte's Code adds the integrity rule that governs the whole grill: "We are truthful about ... the knowledge we possess, and the experience we have" [S340]. In Deloitte's terms, claiming more than you did is an integrity question.

Eight attacks and the answers that hold

The attackWhat it testsA frame-holding answer (adapt, never invent)
1. "What did YOU do?"Whether "we" hides a passenger."Three things were mine. I built the tracker, I ran the weekly check-in, and I wrote the final report. The design was the team's." Count your actions on your fingers; specific verbs beat adjectives.
2. "So what was the result, in numbers?"Commercial instinct and honesty about measurement.Give the number and how you know it. If nothing was measured, say so and give the honest proxy: "We didn't track hours saved. What I can tell you is the reimbursement backlog went from 30 claims to zero in a term."
3. "What would you do differently?"Reflection, the second R in STARR [S382].One specific change, why, and evidence you have since done it: "I'd have tested it with users first. I did that on my next project and it saved a rewrite." Never "nothing", never a fake weakness.
4. "That sounds like your team's work."Whether you inflate under pressure or fold."It was a team result, and I'm proud of the team. My part was X, and the evidence is Y: the file history, the minutes, my supervisor's reference." Agree with the true part; hold the true claim.
5. "Why should I believe that?"Composure when your honesty is questioned.Stay warm. Offer a detail only the doer would know ("the hardest bit was that the bank export split names across two columns") and a way to verify it. Do not get defensive; it is a fair question.
6. "Isn't that just X?" (admin, a bar job, a society role)Whether you can translate ordinary experience into the job."On paper, yes. What made it relevant to consulting was one thing: I had to get a decision from people who didn't report to me." Then link to a JD duty line, for example D1 rapport or D6 status reporting [S2].
7. "What were you doing in this gap?"Honesty and self-possession, not the gap itself.True, short, no apology spiral: what happened, what you did in it, what you are ready for now. You can explain extenuating circumstances on the application form [S260].
8. "Why that grade?"Ownership without excuses. Graduate entry typically requires a 2:1 [S350].State the fact, give the cause in one sentence without blame, say what changed, then give current evidence: "My first-year maths mark was low because I under-prepared for exams. I changed how I revise and my second-year mark in the same area was 68."
DON'T SAY THIS

"I basically ran the whole thing." (Level 2 will ask how, level 3 will ask who else was there.) "My team let me down." (Tactic 8 in disguise.) "I can't remember the numbers." (Prepare them; see the drill below.) "We used ChatGPT to write it." (Fine to mention honestly if relevant, but then expect "how did you check it?" and have an answer [S347].)

The four-line drill for every CV bullet

Before any interview, take every bullet on your CV and write four lines under it. If you cannot fill all four, either cut the bullet or go and find the evidence. This is how you survive level 3.

  1. Claim: the one sentence you would say first, with an honest verb (built, ran, wrote, fixed, persuaded).
  2. Evidence: what proves it, and who could confirm it (a file, minutes, a reference, a link).
  3. Number: the one figure that shows scale or result, and how you know it. If none, the honest proxy.
  4. Lesson: what you would do differently, and where you have since applied it.
CV bulletClaimEvidence (and who confirms)Number (and how you know)Lesson
Practice example (invented): treasurer, university hiking societyI moved the society's budget from paper to a shared spreadsheet.The spreadsheet's version history; committee minutes approving it; the society president.Reimbursement time down from about three weeks to one, from the claims log dates.I'd have asked members first; two committee members kept using paper for a month.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

When an attack lands and you need a second: "That's a fair challenge. Let me be precise about what was mine." It is the CV version of step 1 of the protocol: steady, then sort.

One-page summary of this Part

  • Protocol: steady, sort, act, close. 45 to 75 seconds. Deloitte's ACT method (Assess; Consider and Consult; Take action) sits inside it [S340].
  • Priority order: law, independence and the firm's name; the client's real interest and fairness; the process and the record; speed. "Legal and honest first, the client second, process and record third, as fast as those allow."
  • Ranking items: bottom first (breaches), then do-nothing options, then the top (protects everything at stake and moves the work), then the middle by level.
  • Frame-breakers: change a step for a new fact, never your values for a frown.
  • Composure: write out worries, sigh out slowly, call it excitement [S384] [S385] [S387].
  • CV grill: Claim, Evidence, Number, Lesson for every bullet.
Part 11 continued

Scenario cards: three rungs for every duty line

Thirty worked scenarios, one easy, one medium and one hard for each of the ten duty lines in the JD. Each card shows the trap, a scaffold answer in your own voice, the rule that makes it right, and the follow-up that tests whether you hold.

Every card uses the four-step protocol from the first half of this Part. Steady: pause, acknowledge, check the facts. Sort: rank what is at stake. Act: say the concrete next step, usually with a named person. Close: confirm, record, follow up. The ranking in the Sort step never changes:

THE PRIORITY ORDER USED ON EVERY CARD

1. Law, independence and the firm's name > 2. The client's real interest and fair treatment of people > 3. Process and an honest record > 4. Speed. When two pull against each other, the higher one wins. Deloitte's own dilemma method says it in three words, ACT: Assess, Consider and Consult, Take action, and adds "Speaking up is taking action!" [S340] Confirmed.

Scenarios are illustrative, written for a first-year Analyst in Technology Strategy & Transformation (TST). Clients are generic on purpose. Numbers inside setups are invented for the exercise; every rule cited under "Why it works" is sourced.

D1 · Senior client engagement and rapport

The duty: "We work with their most senior leaders and top-level executives", and you will learn "How to build rapport with clients and ensure they have confidence in your capability" [S2].

D1 · Rung 1: First call with the CIOEASY
Setup

Three weeks into an IT operating model review for a UK retailer, your manager messages from a delayed train: "Five minutes late, can you open the call with the CIO?" (Chief Information Officer, the top technology executive). You have never met her.

The trap

Filling time with improvised opinions, or apologising so much that you waste a senior person's time.

What to say

Steady: re-read the call objective. Sort: her time matters most; my job is to start well, not run the content. Act: "Good morning, I'm [name], an analyst on the Deloitte team. [Manager] joins in five minutes. So we use your time well, could I confirm today's goal, agreeing the phase two interview list, and play back last week's three themes?" Close: log questions I can't answer as actions; hand over with a one-line summary.

Why it works

The JD names client confidence in your capability as a skill to build [S2]. The Code: "We are truthful about ... the knowledge we possess, and the experience we have" [S340]. Opening with the objective is Minto's point-first rule [S374].

The twist, and how to hold

"So, should we outsource infrastructure?" Hold: "That's exactly what phase two will answer. What I can share now is what your team told us." Give facts; park the opinion for your manager.

D1 · Rung 2: Director doubts your experienceMEDIUM
Setup

In a requirements workshop at a central government department, a client director asks you: "How many of these have you actually done?" You are seven months into the job. The room goes quiet.

The trap

Inflating ("quite a few") breaches integrity. Shrinking ("I'm only an analyst") tells the room to discount you.

What to say

Steady: the question is fair. Sort: honesty first, then his real worry: is this team competent? Act: "Honestly, this is my second programme of this kind. What I bring today is the detail: I've read all your process maps and I own the requirements log. The wider team has run this work many times, and [manager] can take you through that." Close: "If there's a specific concern about the approach, I'll note it now so we answer it before we finish."

Why it works

The Code requires truth about "the experience we have" [S340]. "Serve with integrity" calls client trust "our single most important responsibility" [S342]. Firm credentials are shown by the people who own them Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

"So we're paying for you to learn?" Fees are the partner's conversation. "That's a fair challenge; I'll make sure [manager] picks it up with you today." Then tell your manager straight after.

D1 · Rung 3: Client wants the bad news buriedHARD
Setup

The sponsor at a UK insurer asks you, in a corridor, to leave the red data-migration risk off Thursday's steering committee pack: "the board will panic". You keep the RAID log (Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies).

The trap

Agreeing to please her, or refusing flatly and starting a confrontation you do not own.

What to say

Steady: "I understand the worry about how it lands." Sort: hiding a red risk misleads the client's own board; presentation is my manager's and partner's call. Act: "I can't remove it on my own, but I'll take your concern to [manager] today. Could we show it with the mitigation plan and a named owner, so the board sees a risk being managed?" Close: same-day note to my manager quoting the request; the log stays unchanged.

Why it works

The Code: be "straightforward and honest in our professional opinions", and consult, because "No one at Deloitte should have to navigate a difficult situation alone" [S340]. Misstating status to win the next phase is a fraud risk; the failure-to-prevent-fraud offence has applied since 1 September 2025 [S361][S362] Confirmed.

The twist, and how to hold

"Your partner already agreed." Hold: "Then it'll be a quick conversation. I'll confirm with them before I change anything." Never act on a second-hand approval.

D2 · IT operating model

The duty: "helping organisations move away from IT, the department of computers, to technology as a business partner and enabler"; TST's first listed offering is "Technology Operating Model" [S2]. An operating model is how a function is organised, funded, sourced and governed.

D2 · Rung 1: Explain IT as business partnerEASY
Setup

In a current-state interview at a UK housing association, the finance lead asks what "moving IT from cost centre to business partner" means for her team. A cost centre is a unit judged mainly on what it spends.

The trap

A jargon answer, or promising outcomes the review has not yet found.

What to say

Steady: treat it as a real question; it is the heart of the project. Sort: clear and accurate beats impressive. Act: "Today IT is mostly judged on keeping systems running cheaply. As a business partner, IT would plan with you, agree what technology finance needs to hit its goals, and be measured on those goals too. For your team, that might mean a named IT contact in budget season instead of raising tickets." Close: "Does that match what you'd want? I'll note it as evidence for the review."

Why it works

It mirrors the JD [S2] and the TST page aim to "increase the value, agility, efficiency and experience of technology investments" [S41]. Answer first, then example, is the Minto pyramid [S374].

The twist, and how to hold

"So will my team get cut?" Hold: "I don't know, and the review hasn't reached recommendations. I can promise your view goes into the evidence." Never speculate about headcount.

D2 · Rung 2: IT head resists the new modelMEDIUM
Setup

At a UK logistics company, the head of infrastructure says the proposed model (moving his services to a managed provider) will cut his team and he will not support it. He asks what the draft report says.

The trap

False reassurance, leaking draft findings to keep him onside, or writing him off as a blocker.

What to say

Steady: acknowledge this is personal for him. Sort: drafts are confidential and belong to the sponsor; his concern is real evidence and deserves fair treatment.
