Act: "I can't share draft recommendations; they aren't final and they belong to [sponsor]. What I can do is capture your concerns properly. What would any new model have to get right for your team and the service?" Close: log it in the stakeholder map; tell my manager today and suggest a one-to-one with the engagement lead.

Why it works

On a power/interest grid he is high on both: "manage closely" [S380] Reported. The Code bars disclosing confidential information without permission [S340]. "Take care of each other" puts "respect, fairness" first [S342].

The twist, and how to hold

"Then I'll tell the CIO your team is out of its depth." Hold: do not trade information for peace. "That's your right. I'd still rather your points shape the work." Escalate to your manager at once.

D2 · Rung 3: Two sponsors, two operating modelsHARD
Setup

At a UK utility, the CIO privately asks you to make the options slides favour one central IT function. The COO (Chief Operating Officer) separately asks you to favour IT embedded in each business unit. You draft the options pack.

The trap

Tilting slides towards whoever spoke last or ranks higher, or settling the politics yourself.

What to say

Steady: thank each; note the request. Sort: objectivity and the organisation's interest beat either executive's preference; the decision sits with the client's governance. Act: to each: "I'll make sure both options are scored fairly against the agreed criteria." To my manager: "Both sponsors have asked me for different outcomes. Could the steering committee re-confirm the criteria and weights, and we score both openly?" Close: the scoring workbook records every criterion, weight and source.

Why it works

The Code: "We do not allow bias, conflict of interest, or undue influence, to alter our interactions" [S340]. The ICAEW Code names "undue influence of ... individuals" as an objectivity threat [S372]. A RACI gives each decision one Accountable owner [S379]: here, the steering committee. For a Deloitte audit client, "informed management" must decide [S364].

The twist, and how to hold

"Remember who signs off your invoices." That is commercial pressure: do not negotiate it, report it to the partner the same day. The Code also covers influence that is only "perceived" [S340].

D3 · The digital core and the technology landscape

The duty: "create a digital core" and "Discovering how technologies support everything an organisation does, and which technologies work best for each part of a business" [S2]. The digital core is the ERP (enterprise resource planning) and core platforms that finance, supply chain and HR run on.

D3 · Rung 1: Map the application landscapeEASY
Setup

A UK retailer sends a 400-row application inventory. You have two days for a first landscape view: a one-page map of which systems support which business capabilities. Rows have blanks, duplicates and missing owners.

The trap

A beautiful diagram on dirty data, or quietly deleting rows you think are duplicates.

What to say

Steady: confirm the purpose: steering pack or internal working view? Sort: accuracy and traceability before polish. Act: "I'd group applications by capability (finance, supply chain, stores, HR, customer), tag owner, platform and contract end date, and flag blanks and suspected duplicates in a column instead of deleting them. End of day one, I'd send a rough view plus the data-gap list." Close: every count traces to row IDs; gaps go to the client's application owner as questions.

Why it works

Buckets that do not overlap and leave nothing out are MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) [S375]. Improving the value of technology investments is TST's stated aim [S41]. An early check-in saves a day of rework Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

The client now wants it tomorrow. Hold: trade scope, not accuracy. "I can do the top three capabilities fully and mark the rest draft."

D3 · Rung 2: Vendor already chosen before analysisMEDIUM
Setup

Early in an ERP platform selection for a UK manufacturer, a client executive says the vendor is already decided and asks you to "make the analysis fit". Deloitte has alliances with several shortlisted vendors.

The trap

Reverse-engineering the scores. With alliance revenue in play, a rigged selection also looks like the firm steering for itself.

What to say

Steady: ask what the reasons are; there may be good ones. Sort: objectivity and the firm's name first; the client may choose, but our report must be honest. Act: "It's your decision. I'd suggest our report shows the criteria and scores as they come out, with your strategic reasons recorded beside them. That gives your board a decision it can defend." I tell my manager the same day. Close: the scoring workbook stays unaltered; the instruction is noted.

Why it works

Deloitte UK lists 14 alliance partners, including SAP, Oracle and Workday [S319] Confirmed. The Code bans "undue influence" over judgement [S340]. Decisions belong to the client's "informed management" [S364]. Business relationships go through conflict checks [S35].

The twist, and how to hold

"Your firm partners with that vendor anyway." Hold: "That's exactly why our scoring has to be clean. I'll flag the alliance point to [manager] so it's handled properly."

D3 · Rung 3: Legacy system nobody understandsHARD
Setup

On an ERP replacement for a UK water company, the cutover plan (the step-by-step switch from old system to new) assumes the legacy billing system is documented. It is not. It holds critical customer data, and its only expert retires in a month.

The trap

Assuming someone senior has spotted it, or announcing a crisis in a big meeting before you have facts.

What to say

Steady: check what documentation exists, the leaving date and which cutover tasks depend on it. Sort: customers' billing and data first; it belongs in the RAID log; the date makes it urgent. Act: "I think this is a red risk. Several cutover tasks assume documentation that doesn't exist, and the only expert leaves at month end. I'd suggest a knowledge-capture sprint with him from next week, and a client decision on extending his contract." Close: logged with owner and date; on the next status report.

Why it works

Tracking risks and deadlines is core junior work [S9]. Issues can become change requests [S377]. UK GDPR requires accurate personal data [S353]. Capita's £14m ICO fine followed a 58-hour delay in acting on an alert [S394] Confirmed: speed of escalation matters.

The twist, and how to hold

The expert refuses to be "interrogated" in his last month. Hold: "Take care of each other" [S342]. Frame it as recognising his knowledge; his line manager sets it up, in short sessions, recorded with consent.

D4 · Business case and value

The duty: "improving financial performance, accelerating speed to market" and "Help assess technology investments, identify opportunities to improve value, agility, efficiency, and user experience" [S2]. A business case sets out costs, benefits and risks so a client can decide whether to invest.

D4 · Rung 1: Sense-check a benefits numberEASY
Setup

Your manager asks you to sanity-check a £12m savings figure in a UK retailer's cloud migration business case before it goes to the client tomorrow.

The trap

Re-reading the slide and saying "looks fine", or rebuilding the whole model overnight.

What to say

Steady: ask how deep a check, and by when. Sort: accuracy over speed, inside the deadline. Act: "Three checks. Trace the £12m to its source cells. Test scale against the client's IT cost baseline. Check the basis: annual or five-year, gross or net of migration cost. If it's five-year and gross but the slide says 'per year', the label is wrong." Close: a short note with cell references; my manager decides the wording.

Why it works

Assessing technology investments is in the JD [S2]. The ICAEW Code asks professionals to "Act diligently" [S372]. Answer first, then evidence, is Minto [S374].

The twist, and how to hold

"Just tell me if it's roughly right." Hold: one line, plus the caveat that matters: "Roughly right, but it's five-year, not annual." Short is fine; dropping the caveat is not.

D4 · Rung 2: Benefits that do not add upMEDIUM
Setup

On a finance transformation business case for a central government department, you find 30 FTE (full-time equivalent posts) of savings already claimed in another programme's approved case.

The trap

Deleting the savings yourself, or ignoring it because the client supplied the number.

What to say

Steady: re-check both documents and versions. Sort: a board approving a double-counted case wastes public money; accuracy first, raised through my manager. Act: "I've found an overlap. The 30 FTE in our benefit line also appear in the other programme's approved case. Unless the two are coordinated, the department counts the same saving twice. Shall I draft a note for the client's finance business partner to confirm?" Close: an issue in the RAID log with an owner; the model's change log records the edit.

Why it works

Benefits must be mutually exclusive, the first half of MECE [S375]. Departments must "demonstrate the value-for-money case" for consultancy [S176] Confirmed. Honest professional opinions are a Code duty [S340].

The twist, and how to hold

"Everyone does it, and the other programme won't deliver anyway." Hold: "Then the case can say so openly, as a dependency. What we can't do is count it twice without saying."

D4 · Rung 3: Partner wants a bigger numberHARD
Setup

Late evening. A partner asks you to lift the productivity assumption in an ERP investment case so it clears the client's hurdle rate (the minimum return needed to approve an investment): "Make it 18%, not 10%."

The trap

Doing it because of seniority, or refusing as an accusation. There may be evidence you have not seen.

What to say

Steady: ask, do not accuse. Sort: misleading a client's investment decision touches the law and the firm's name. Act: "Happy to update it. Could you point me to the evidence for 18% so I can source it in the assumptions log? Our benchmark supports about 10%. If we can't source it, could we show 18% as an upside scenario beside the base case?" Close: the assumptions log records who changed what and why. If pushed with no basis, I consult my manager or Ethics.

Why it works

The Code: honest opinions, and "Speaking up is taking action!" [S340]. Since 1 September 2025 a large organisation can be guilty if an associate commits fraud meant to benefit it or its client [S361][S362] Confirmed. "Retaliation against those who raise ethical concerns is not tolerated" [S340].

The twist, and how to hold

"It's an assumption. Don't be naive." Hold: "Agreed, it's a judgement. I just want it written down with its basis, so it holds up if their board asks." Keep it about the record, not the person.

D5 · Net zero and inclusive ways of working

The duty: transforming how clients run "in ways that drive net zero and incorporate inclusive ways of working" [S2]. Net zero means cutting greenhouse gas emissions as far as possible and balancing the rest with removals.

D5 · Rung 1: Add carbon to the caseEASY
Setup

A UK retailer asks whether its cloud migration business case should include a carbon estimate. Your manager wants your view at tomorrow's stand-up.

The trap

Stating "cloud is greener" as fact, or brushing it off as out of scope.

What to say

Steady: check whether carbon is in the agreed scope. Sort: accuracy first, then the client's stated goal. Act: "Yes, as a separate line, kept apart from the financial benefits, because the client says net zero matters. But it needs sources: current data-centre energy use, the provider's published figures, and a range, not a point. If we can't source it, we say what data we'd need." Close: offer a one-slide method note; flag any scope change to my manager.

Why it works

Net zero is written into the JD [S2]. "Lead the way" includes "leading the way to a more sustainable world" [S342]. UK sustainability reporting standards were published for voluntary use in February 2026 [S202] Reported. APM: define scope early [S378].

The twist, and how to hold

The client wants a precise figure by Friday, with no data. Hold: give the method and a range labelled "Estimate", plus when a real figure becomes possible.

D5 · Rung 2: Workshop excludes remote colleaguesMEDIUM
Setup

Your all-day design workshop at a UK bank's head office is in person only. Three key client staff who work part-time or remotely cannot attend, including one area's process owner.

The trap

Running it anyway and "catching them up later", or rescheduling without asking anyone.

What to say

Steady: confirm who is missing and which sessions affect them. Sort: fair treatment and good requirements beat the convenience of the plan. Act: to my manager: "Three of the people closest to the process can't make Thursday. Could we add a video link for the two sessions on their area, inside their working hours? If not, I'll run a 45-minute follow-up with them before sign-off." Close: the notes record attendance and how absent colleagues' input was captured.

Why it works

"Inclusive ways of working" is in the JD [S2]. "Foster inclusion": Deloitte is "at our best when we foster an inclusive culture" [S342]. Requirements should be agreed by the people who own the process Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

"They can read the minutes." Hold: "They can, and they will. The risk is designing a process their team runs without them, so I'd like their input before sign-off." Frame it as a quality risk, because it is one.

D5 · Rung 3: Green claim without evidenceHARD
Setup

The client wants the final report to say the programme "delivers net zero IT". Your data supports only a modest cut in data-centre energy use. The report carries Deloitte's name.

The trap

Letting marketing language into a Deloitte deliverable, or lecturing the client.

What to say

Steady: re-check the data and method. Sort: honesty and the firm's name first; an unsupported claim also exposes the client. Final wording is my manager's and partner's call. Act: "I want the strongest claim the data supports. Today that's a reduction in energy use for in-scope IT, not net zero. Could we say it 'reduces emissions from in-scope IT, a step towards net zero', give the range, and list what going further would take?" Close: a footnote with method and sources; I raise the wording with my manager before the draft goes.

Why it works

The Code: "We are truthful about the services we provide" [S340]. "Serve with integrity" calls trust "our single most important responsibility" [S342]. As UK sustainability reporting matures [S202], climate claims face more scrutiny Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

"We'll put it in our press release anyway." Hold: "That's your call for your release. Our report has to say what our evidence shows." The relationship conversation is the partner's.

D6 · Large-scale transformation, design through implementation

The duty: "you will work on large-scale technology transformations, from the design through to implementation" [S2]. For a first-year Analyst this mostly means PMO (project management office) work: RAID logs, status reports, plans and meeting packs Inferred.

D6 · Rung 1: Update the RAID logEASY
Setup

At 6pm you are handed the programme RAID log for tomorrow's 10am status meeting. Half the actions have no owner; several dates have passed.

The trap

Typing guessed owners in as fact, or perfecting the formatting until 2am.

What to say

Steady: ask which items will actually be discussed. Sort: an accurate record beats a complete-looking one. Act: sort by RAG status (red, amber, green) and due date; for the top ten, propose owners from past minutes, marked "proposed, to confirm". Then to my manager: "Twelve actions have no owner. I've proposed owners for the top ten, to confirm in the meeting. Two are overdue and red." Close: confirm owners in the meeting; update the log the same day.

Why it works

Junior postings openly list "tracking deadlines, and preparing materials" [S9]. A RACI gives each task one Accountable person [S379], so owners are agreed, not assigned by you. Answer-first notes are Minto [S374].

The twist, and how to hold

"Just put names in, nobody will notice." Hold: "I'll put them in as proposed, so nobody is surprised in the meeting." Just as quick, and honest.

D6 · Rung 2: Status report turning amberMEDIUM
Setup

Your testing workstream will miss a milestone by two weeks because the test environment arrived late. The weekly status report goes to the client tomorrow. Last week it was green.

The trap

Keeping it green and hoping to recover, or putting the bad news in the report before your manager has heard it.

What to say

Steady: confirm the cause, the size of the slip and my confidence. Sort: honest reporting first; my manager hears before the client. Act: "The environment arrived nine days late; at current pace we miss by two weeks. Options: two extra testers from the delivery centre for three weeks, or move two low-priority interfaces to the next release. I'd recommend the first." Close: the report shows amber with cause, impact, recovery plan and the decision needed, by when.

Why it works

APM: "Formal change control is required when tolerances are breached" [S377]. A Deloitte director describes client check-ins "so we can manage any potential risks" [S55]. Misreporting progress to secure more work is a fraud risk [S361].

The twist, and how to hold

The client's workstream lead asks you to stay green "until we've tried to recover". Hold: "I'll show amber with your recovery plan in it. That gives you credit for the plan."

D6 · Rung 3: Go-live with a known defectHARD
Setup

On an HR and payroll rollout for a large public sector employer, the client wants to go live on Monday. Testing has an open severity-one defect (the highest level): overtime is miscalculated for some part-time staff.

The trap

Marking the test as passed to protect the date, or acting as if go/no-go is your decision.

What to say

Steady: confirm who is affected and any workaround. Sort: paying people correctly and handling their data lawfully outrank the schedule; the client's accountable owner decides, with full information. Act: "It isn't my call, but the go/no-go meeting must see this clearly. The defect underpays some part-time staff. Options: go live with a checked manual adjustment for that group, or delay one pay cycle." Close: the decision and any accepted risk are minuted with the owner's name.

Why it works

User acceptance testing lets users "determine whether to accept the system" [S381] Reported. The Accountable person signs off [S379]. UK GDPR requires accurate personal data [S353]. A failed test reported as passed is a false record [S340].

The twist, and how to hold

"Deloitte gets blamed for any delay. Close it as a known issue." Hold: reclassifying is fine only if the client's accountable owner accepts it in writing, with a workaround. You never close it yourself.

D7 · Requirements

The duty: "Working with individuals from our clients' business and IT teams to understand what the problems and needs are, and transforming those into technical requirements" [S2]. A requirement is a testable statement of what a system must do.

D7 · Rung 1: Run a requirements interviewEASY
Setup

You have 45 minutes with an operations manager at a central government department to capture requirements for a new case-management system.

The trap

Asking "what features do you want?" and collecting a wish list, or steering her to a system you know.

What to say

Steady: prepare the objective, the current process map and about eight open questions. Sort: the problem before solutions. Act: "Could you walk me through the last case you handled? Where did it slow down? What happens when that step goes wrong?" Then play back: "So the need is to see all correspondence on a case in one place, and success is fewer missed deadlines. Is that right?" Close: same-day write-up; each requirement testable, linked to its source, and sent to her to confirm.

Why it works

A sister posting describes "Getting to the bottom of client's problems through interactive workshops and labs" [S8]. Asking "why" before "how" is the diagnostic issue tree [S376] Reported. Good requirements are testable, traced and agreed Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

She starts naming members of the public in real cases. Hold: "I don't need names; the pattern is enough." Data minimisation is a UK GDPR principle [S353], and some government material needs vetting before you see it [S370].

D7 · Rung 2: Business and IT disagreeMEDIUM
Setup

At a UK retailer, store operations want real-time stock visibility. IT says it is impossible within budget. Each side asks you, separately, to back them.

The trap

Picking a side to be liked, or setting the priority yourself.

What to say

Steady: listen to both; write down each claim. Sort: my job is to make the trade-off visible; the client's product owner decides. Act: "It isn't my call, but I can make the choice clearer. Can we separate the need from the solution? If the need is stock accurate to within an hour, does it have to be real time? IT, what would hourly cost?" Then two or three options with cost, benefit and risk go to the product owner. Close: the decision and reasons go in the decision log.

Why it works

The Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner "one person, not a committee" [S373]. A solution issue tree breaks "how" into options [S376]. "Collaborate for measurable impact" is a Shared Value [S342]. For an audit client, management must decide [S364].

The twist, and how to hold

"You're the consultant, just tell us who's right." Hold: give a recommendation with evidence, clearly labelled as one, and leave the decision with the owner.

D7 · Rung 3: Scope creep from a senior userHARD
Setup

A client finance director keeps emailing you new requirements outside change control (the agreed process for approving scope changes) and expects them in the release two weeks away.

The trap

Quietly building them in (untested, unpaid, a risk to the release), or a blunt "no" to a senior client.

What to say

Steady: thank him; the ideas may be good. Sort: a stable release and the agreed contract come first, handled so the relationship holds. Act: "Thank you, these are useful. To get them in safely, I'll log them as change requests today so the product owner can weigh them against the sprint goal. I'll come back by Thursday with the time each would take." I copy my manager. Close: change register, plus a weekly summary to the sponsor of requested, approved and deferred items.

Why it works

APM change control: log, assess impact on "benefits, scope, quality, time, resources, costs, risks", then approve, reject or defer [S377]. Scrum: "No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal" [S373]. Clear scope prevents later misunderstanding [S378].

The twist, and how to hold

"I'm paying for this programme. Just do it." Hold: "Understood. The fastest safe route is through the product owner this week." If it repeats, your manager takes it to the engagement lead; the commercial point is theirs.

D8 · Documents and client materials

The duty: "Creating documents crucial to the delivery and execution of the programme, alongside materials presented back to clients" [S2]. In practice: steering committee packs, design documents and workshop materials, mostly in PowerPoint Inferred.

D8 · Rung 1: Tighten a slide for tomorrowEASY
Setup

At 7pm your manager says your three-slide summary is "too busy" and needs rewriting for a 9am client meeting.

The trap

Shrinking the font, defending every point, or working all night.

What to say

Steady: ask one question: "What's the one decision the client needs to make tomorrow?" Sort: clarity over completeness. Act: "I'd rewrite each title as a full sentence stating the point, keep three supporting points with numbers under each, and move detail to an appendix. Version two by 9pm, with a note: 'Titles now tell the story in order; detail is in the appendix.'" Close: every number ties to its source; template and spelling checked.

Why it works

Minto: ideas are easiest to grasp "organized as a pyramid under a single point" [S374]. Supporting points that do not overlap are MECE [S375]. Several review rounds on client documents are normal Inferred.

The twist, and how to hold

At 8am your manager rewrites it again, differently. Hold: no ego. Make the change, keep a version log, and later ask which principle to apply next time.

D8 · Rung 2: Typo found after sendingMEDIUM
Setup

An hour after a client pack went to twelve client stakeholders, you spot a cost shown as £12m that the source gives as £1.2m.

The trap

Hoping nobody notices, or sending your own panicked correction to all twelve without your manager.

What to say

Steady: verify the error and whether it changes any conclusion. Sort: honesty with the client, through the agreed route; fast, but speed comes last. Act: message my manager within minutes: "The cost slide shows £12m; the source says £1.2m. The conclusion is unchanged. Suggested fix: a corrected version with a one-line note. Draft attached." Close: once agreed, the correction goes out, the version log is updated, and I add a number tie-out step to my checklist.

Why it works

The Code requires honesty with clients [S340]; the ICAEW Code asks for due care [S372]. Owning every line of a deliverable is the lesson of Deloitte Australia's 2025 report refund [S388] Confirmed.

The twist, and how to hold

The email also went to an outside supplier, and the appendix lists staff names and salaries. Hold: that may be a personal data breach, which covers accidental disclosure. Escalate at once to your manager and the firm's incident route; the client may have 72 hours to notify the ICO [S354].

D8 · Rung 3: Pack contradicts the client's dataHARD
Setup

The night before a board pack goes out, you see the client's latest quarterly data. Volumes have fallen sharply, and the savings behind the headline recommendation rest on the old, higher volumes. Seniors have signed off.

The trap

Staying quiet because it is late and approved, or changing the recommendation yourself.

What to say

Steady: check the version and date of both data sets. Sort: the board must not decide on a false basis; that and the firm's name outrank the deadline. Act: phone my manager tonight, then send the comparison: "Last week's data shows volumes well below the pack's baseline. If right, the headline savings fall by about two-thirds. I've checked twice. Options: hold the pack a day, or send it with a flagged caveat and an update to follow." Close: record what was found and decided.

Why it works

The Code requires honest opinions and consultation: "No one at Deloitte should have to navigate a difficult situation alone" [S340]. Trust is "our single most important responsibility" [S342].

The twist, and how to hold

"Too late, the partner signed off. Send it." Hold: "Could I have two minutes with the partner? I'd rather they decide knowing this." If still told to send, ask for the instruction in writing and consult further. Speak Up is open to you, and retaliation is not tolerated [S340].

D9 · Firm-approved AI, used responsibly

The duty: "Using firm-approved AI tools responsibly to support client delivery" [S3]. Two words carry the weight: firm-approved.

D9 · Rung 1: Which AI tool to useEASY
Setup

You want an AI assistant to summarise fifteen sets of stakeholder interview notes. You are not sure which tools the firm approves for client material.

The trap

A personal account on a public chatbot "just this once", or avoiding AI altogether out of fear.

What to say

Steady: ask before starting. Sort: client confidentiality first, then the record. Act: "I'd ask my manager which tools are approved for client data on this engagement, and whether the contract allows AI use. Then I'd use the approved tool, strip out names it doesn't need, and check each summary against the notes." Close: keep the source notes, mark that AI assisted, and treat each reviewed summary as my own work.

Why it works

Deloitte UK rates GenAI a "Very High", new priority risk, controlled by use-case approval and a "clearing house" process [S345] Confirmed. Its internal tool PairD works "within its secure digital ecosystem" [S345]. The Code bars disclosing confidential information [S340]. Deloitte: "accountability is squarely a human domain" [S347].

The twist, and how to hold

"Use whatever's quickest." Hold: "I'll use the approved tool; it's just as quick and keeps us inside policy."

D9 · Rung 2: Colleague pastes data into ChatGPTMEDIUM
Setup

You see a fellow analyst paste client interview transcripts, with names and job titles, into a public AI chatbot to save time.

The trap

Ignoring it as "not my business", or calling it out in front of the team.

What to say

Steady: speak privately, straight away. Sort: confidentiality and a possible breach first; care for the colleague next. Act: "I think that's a public tool, and client data isn't meant to go in there. Can we stop and tell [manager] now? It's better coming from you, and I'll come with you." If they refuse, I raise it myself the same day. Close: the manager and the firm's route decide if it is reportable; I note what I saw and when.

Why it works

The Code's duty to report covers "a colleague" [S340]. A personal data breach includes accidental "unauthorised disclosure"; notifiable ones go to the ICO within 72 hours [S354] Confirmed. "Take care of each other" is why you offer to go with them [S342].

The twist, and how to hold

"Everyone does it, and I've deleted the chat." Hold: deleting does not undo the disclosure, and destroying records can make things far worse, as McKinsey's obstruction plea showed [S390]. Escalate the same day.

D9 · Rung 3: AI draft cites a fake sourceHARD
Setup

A senior colleague drafted, with AI help, a section of a client report on operational resilience. It cites a regulation paragraph and a study you cannot find anywhere. The report is due tomorrow.

The trap

Quietly deleting the citations but keeping the claims, or assuming they exist because a senior wrote them.

What to say

Steady: search the primary sources: legislation.gov.uk, the regulator's site, the journal. Sort: the firm's name and client trust first. Act: "I can't verify two references in that section. I've checked the regulator's site and the journal; they may be AI errors. Can we find the real sources, or remove the claims they support?" Close: every citation verified and logged, the claims re-checked, and AI use disclosed if the contract requires it.

Why it works

In 2025 Deloitte Australia agreed to repay part of a roughly A$440,000 government report found to contain nonexistent references [S388] Confirmed. "Because an AI model cannot be meaningfully held accountable for its outputs, accountability is squarely a human domain" [S347]. The ICAEW Code warns against "undue reliance on ... technology" [S372].

The twist, and how to hold

"The point is right even if the reference is off. Cite something similar." Hold: a citation must support the exact claim. If no real source does, the claim goes, or is labelled as our judgement.

D10 · Teaming across the wider T&T practice

The duty: "you will be working with teams across our wider Technology and Transformation practice, understanding how we bring our range of technical expertise and combine them" [S2]. This is the matrix: offerings, industries, alliances and delivery centres.

D10 · Rung 1: Hand-off to the delivery centreEASY
Setup

On Friday you must hand a testing workstream to an offshore delivery-centre team six hours ahead of the UK. On Monday you move to another project.

The trap

A 6pm email saying "see attached", with context only you understand.

What to say

Steady: list what the new team needs to work without me. Sort: continuity for the client, then a written record. Act: "I'd write a handover pack: scope, status of each test, open defects with owners, environments and access, contacts, and what 'done' looks like. Then a call in the overlap window to walk through open defects, asking them to play back the top three priorities." Close: access through the proper request; a daily written update for the first week.

Why it works

Deloitte UK postings ask for clear communication "with clients and colleagues both on and offshore" [S51] Confirmed. Deloitte has opened UK technology centres in Belfast, Cardiff, Manchester and Newcastle [S323] Reported. "Collaborate for measurable impact" means "teaming across businesses, geographies, and skill sets" [S342].

The twist, and how to hold

The team lead has no client system access yet and asks to borrow your login. Hold: never. Using someone else's credentials is unauthorised access under the Computer Misuse Act [S363]. Chase the access request and tell your manager about the delay.

D10 · Rung 2: Alliance partner oversells the clientMEDIUM
Setup

In a joint client meeting, a software alliance partner's salesperson promises the client features that are not on the vendor's published product roadmap.

The trap

Contradicting the vendor in front of the client, or staying silent while the client plans around features that may never arrive.

What to say

Steady: no confrontation in the room. Sort: the client's interest and honest advice come before the alliance relationship. Act: in the room: "That's an important point. Could we capture an action to confirm the timing in writing?" Afterwards I tell my manager, with the roadmap reference, and suggest the plan and business case don't assume the feature until it is confirmed. Close: the action log shows the confirmation request, owner and date.

Why it works

Deloitte UK works with 14 alliance partners [S319] Confirmed. Typically the vendor sells the licence and Deloitte sells the implementation Inferred, so clients must trust that the advice is independent. The Code requires objectivity and truthfulness [S340].

The twist, and how to hold

The rep messages you: "Don't rock the boat, we bring you a lot of work." Hold: pass it to your manager. The Code bans influence even "perceived to" affect judgement [S340].

D10 · Rung 3: Two practices, one client, conflictHARD
Setup

Your TST team is advising a central government department on reducing reliance on one outsourced IT service. You hear another Deloitte practice is bidding to run a managed service there, which could compete with, or gain from, your recommendation.

The trap

Passing your engagement's findings to the bid team "to help the firm", or ignoring what you heard.

What to say

Steady: separate what I know from what I heard. Sort: law and the firm's name first: procurement rules and client confidentiality. Act: "I wouldn't share anything from our engagement with the bid team. I'd tell my manager today what I heard, so the engagement partner and the firm's risk team can check whether there is a conflict to disclose or manage." Close: stay inside my engagement's boundaries; note when I raised it.

Why it works

Deloitte UK conflict-checks all proposed engagements and declines those it cannot manage [S35] Confirmed. The Procurement Act 2023 makes authorities manage conflicts, and a supplier with an unfair advantage can be excluded [S366][S367]. PwC Australia's tax leak shows the cost of reusing one client's information for another [S392]; McKinsey's FDA case shows non-disclosure is itself the failure [S391].

The twist, and how to hold

Over coffee, a bid-team colleague asks: "What's their real budget pressure?" Hold: "Sorry, I can't talk about my client's work. Best to go through the engagement partner." Then tell your manager.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

"When something goes wrong on a project, I steady myself and check the facts, then rank what's at stake: the law and the firm's name first, then the client and the people affected, then the process, and speed last. Then I take one concrete step with a named person and write it down. Your Code calls that ACT, and says speaking up is taking action." [S340]

Part 12

Why Deloitte, in three lengths, and the counter-case

A “why Deloitte” answer built on how the firm works, not on adjectives. Three versions to learn, a table to replace weak lines, an honest case for the alternatives, and a one-page figure to revise from.

The idea behind every version

Most candidates say why they like Deloitte. A stronger answer explains how Deloitte is built, shows evidence that the design works, and says what that means for the job you would do. This is a mechanism-based answer: it explains cause and effect.

The mechanism here is the multidisciplinary model. Deloitte keeps audit, tax, advisory and technology in one partnership. Deloitte's own description: “Our multidisciplinary model, deep domain and industry knowledge, and commitment to upholding quality and trust in the corporate reporting ecosystem allow us to provide integrated solutions” [S300]. Deloitte decided to keep its consulting business in 2003, when rivals sold or floated theirs [S104].

KEY TERMS

Partnership: the firm is owned by its equity partners, who share the profit; there are no outside shareholders. Distributable profit: the profit available to share among equity partners (£899m in FY26) [S407]. Independence: rules that stop an auditor selling most other services to the companies it audits, so the audit stays objective [S314].

The 30-second version

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

“I want to start where the shape of the firm helps me learn. Deloitte keeps audit, tax, advisory and technology in one partnership, and last year showed why that matters: in FY25 technology and transformation revenue fell 10%, but the firm fell only 1% [S89] [S305]. That stability is what pays for things like £180 million of technology investment and a new Chief AI Officer [S407]. And in FY26, Technology & Transformation was the fastest-growing UK business, on ERP, cyber and human capital work [S407]. That is the work I want to learn.”

Why it works: one mechanism, two numbers, one link to the job. Each claim has a source you could name if asked.

The 2-minute version

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

“I looked at why Deloitte is built the way it is, because that tells me what the job would really be like.

First, it is a portfolio. Deloitte UK has four businesses. In FY25 T&T revenue fell 10% but total revenue fell only 1%, because tax and audit kept growing [S89] [S305]. In FY26 revenue rose 2% and distributable profit 14% [S407]. So the firm can keep hiring and investing through a weak consulting year. It hired more than 1,950 graduates, apprentices and interns in FY26 [S407].

Second, it turns that stability into investment. UK technology investment rose to £180 million, and Hayley McKelvey joined the UK Executive as the first Chief AI Officer [S407] [S274]. Globally Deloitte has committed US$3 billion to AI through 2030 [S300] and rolled Claude out to more than 470,000 people, with 15,000 to be certified [S325].

Third, alliances. Deloitte UK works with 14 platform partners, including SAP, Workday, ServiceNow and Salesforce [S319]. Clients pay for certified people who can make those platforms work, and that is a concrete skill I can build early.

I also see the limits. Independence rules mean Deloitte often cannot consult for its own audit clients [S314]. And the Australian report case showed how one member firm's AI error affects the whole brand [S316]. That makes me care about quality checks as much as speed.

So my reason is specific: a firm whose structure lets it keep investing in technology delivery, in the business where I can learn a platform skill and see AI change delivery from the inside.”

The close: one specific thing you would work on

Interviewers often end with “What would you want to work on?” A precise answer signals that you have pictured the job.

SAY THIS IN THE INTERVIEW

“The thing I would most like to work on is responsible AI in delivery: helping a team in Engineering, AI & Data use tools like Claude safely, with the checks that would have caught the citation errors in the Australian report [S320] [S325] [S316]. Deloitte is clearly investing there, with a Chief AI Officer whose remit covers client work and internal operations [S407]. I would like to help that investment show up as better work for clients.”

YOUR OPINION GOES HERE

Choose your own “one thing”. Options: responsible AI in delivery (above); ERP and finance transformation, the largest named growth driver [S407]; cyber resilience [S269]; public sector data work, given the Home Office contract [S233]. For picking AI: it is where the firm is investing. Against: many candidates will say AI. A suggested stance: pick the one you have real evidence for in your own CV, and link it to AI only if you can do so honestly.

What most candidates say, and what you can say

Most candidates sayYou can saySource
“Deloitte is the biggest, a global leader.”“Deloitte says Gartner has ranked it No. 1 in consulting by revenue for nine years running. What interests me is why: the multidisciplinary model.”[S125] [S300]
“I like the variety of clients.”“UK T&T was £1.75bn in FY26, up 4%, driven by ERP, cyber and human capital work. That is the work I would actually do.”[S407]
“Deloitte has a great culture of collaboration.”“People sit in an offering and an industry, so teams form around client problems. Independence rules limit that at audit clients, so I would expect most integrated work at non-audit and public sector clients.”[S301] [S314] Inferred
“Deloitte invests in innovation and AI.”“A new UK Chief AI Officer, £180m of UK technology investment, Claude for 470,000+ people and 15,000 certifications.”[S407] [S325]
“I want to make an impact.”“Deloitte has been the top UK government consulting supplier for five years. I also know the counter-case: the NAO says spend data is unreliable.”[S335] [S334]
“Strong training and brand.”“More than 1,950 early-careers hires in FY26, and 12-week technical academies feeding technology roles.”[S407] [S271]
“Deloitte is stable.”“It is stable because it is a portfolio: in FY25 T&T fell 10% but the firm fell 1%.”[S89] [S305]
DON'T SAY THIS

“Deloitte UK made £5.81bn.” The £5.81bn figure is UK and Switzerland consolidated. Say “the UK and Swiss firm”, or use the UK business-line figures [S407].

The counter-case: why someone might reasonably choose elsewhere

Knowing the honest case for rivals makes your answer more credible. If an interviewer asks “why not X?”, acknowledge what X does well, then give your Deloitte-specific reason. Never run a rival down.

AlternativeThe honest case for itHow to answer “why not X?”
AccentureAbout the same size as Deloitte (US$74.18bn in FY26) with about 814,000 people; half its revenue is managed services. As a listed company with no audit business, it has no independence limits on who it can sell to [S129].“Accenture is the purer technology play. I want technology delivery next to tax, risk and deals expertise in one firm, which is Deloitte's model [S300].”
MBB (McKinsey, BCG, Bain)Smaller teams and more board-level strategy work. BCG grew 7% to US$14.4bn in 2025 with 33,500 people, and over 40% of revenue is now AI and technology work [S133].“I am more interested in making change happen than in strategy alone. Deloitte both advises and delivers, which is where I want to learn first.”
PwCSame model and similar UK scale: UK revenue £4.365bn, up 2%, in FY26 [S138]. It set up a standalone technology and AI unit in the UK in 2024 [S404].“PwC is a fair comparison. I chose Deloitte for the specific T&T evidence: fastest UK growth in FY26, the four regional technology centres and the alliance base [S407] [S323] [S319].”
EYSame model, but it nearly split audit from consulting in 2022-23, so it has thought hard about conflicts [S310]. EY UK consulting fell 6% in FY25 [S139].“EY's debate was interesting. I prefer a firm that has settled its model and is investing behind it, such as Deloitte EMEA's €1.5bn plan [S124].”
KPMGThe fastest Big Four grower globally in its last year (5.1%), though UK/Swiss Advisory fell 3% [S128] [S140].“KPMG is growing well globally. For technology delivery in the UK, Deloitte's T&T scale and its alliances were more compelling to me.”
A boutiqueFaster responsibility, a deep niche and no independence red tape Inferred. Less scale, fewer alliance certifications.“I want breadth first, then I can specialise. A large firm gives me more teams and sectors to try.”
Industry or the civil serviceThe Big Con argues capability should be built inside organisations, not rented [S337]. At its peak, consultants made up a large share of Test and Trace central staff [S333].“I take that argument seriously. Good consulting work should leave the client more capable, and that is the kind of work I would want to do.”

Deloitte-specific risks to weigh honestly

  • Restated UK T&T revenue fell 10% in FY25, with several rounds of job cuts [S89] [S305].
  • Low attrition led to voluntary redundancy offers in UK audit in June 2026 [S227] [S407].
  • Reputational spillover from separate member firms, such as the Australian AI report [S316] and a US DEI settlement with no admission of liability [S242].
  • The FRC is investigating Deloitte's audits of Glencore and Stenn [S252] [S253].

None of these is a reason to avoid applying. Knowing them shows you have looked at the firm with open eyes.

Part 13

Cheat sheet

One page for the waiting room. The reasoning behind each line is in Parts 9, 11 and 12.

Part 14

Glossary

Every term of art in this pack, in plain English, in one alphabetical list. Use it as a lookup while you read, and as a self-test before an interview.

Each entry gives a short definition. Where a term changes how you should talk or act at Deloitte, a line starting "Why it matters here" says how. Source markers appear on Deloitte-specific and regulatory facts; general consulting vocabulary carries none because it is standard usage. Dates and figures are as of 4 October 2026.

Terms A to Z

70% cap
The rule that non-audit fees from a public interest entity audit client cannot exceed 70% of the average audit fee over the previous three years [S182][S364]. Why it matters here: it limits how much consulting Deloitte can sell to companies it audits.
ACT method
Deloitte's Global Code frame for ethical dilemmas: Assess the situation, Consider and Consult, Take action. The Code adds "Speaking up is taking action!" [S340]. Why it matters here: it is a ready-made structure for any ethics scenario question.
Agentic AI
AI systems that take actions (send, book, update, approve) rather than only producing text. Deloitte's Tech Trends 2026 says only 11% of organisations have such systems in production [S244]. Why it matters here: the hard part is redesigning the process, which is consulting work.
Agile
A way of delivering projects in short cycles, testing with users and adjusting as you learn, instead of fixing every requirement up front. Scrum is the most common agile framework.
Alliance partner
A technology vendor whose software a consultancy implements. Deloitte UK lists 14, including SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, AWS, Google and Oracle [S319]. Why it matters here: much T&T graduate work runs on these platforms.
ARGA (Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority)
The regulator that was meant to replace the FRC. The government abandoned the Audit Reform Bill on 20 January 2026, so ARGA will not be created [S185][S186].
Audit & Assurance (A&A)
Deloitte's audit business. It gives independent opinions on whether company accounts are true and fair. UK revenue £998m in FY26 [S407].
Audit committee
A board committee of a company, mostly independent directors, that oversees its auditor. Non-audit services to a public interest entity need its approval [S364].
Audit Governance Board (AGB)
Deloitte UK's majority-independent board that oversees the audit practice, set up under operational separation. It continues under the new UK Board [S93][S94].
Basel 3.1
The UK version of the final global bank capital rules. The PRA's final rules take effect on 1 January 2027 [S196][S197]. Why it matters here: banks buy help with data, models and reporting to comply.
Bench
Consultants not currently staffed on a client project. Time on the bench is not chargeable, so long bench periods hurt utilisation.
Big Four
The four largest professional services networks: Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG. Deloitte is the largest by revenue, at US$74.5bn in FY26 [S70][S126].
BPSS (Baseline Personnel Security Standard)
The UK government's basic pre-employment check (identity, right to work, employment history, unspent convictions) for people with access to government assets. It is not a formal clearance but underpins SC [S369][S370]. Deloitte UK does not say it is required for all graduates.
BrightStart
Deloitte UK's school-leaver apprenticeship route. 182 BrightStart apprentices were among the September 2026 intake [S231][S260].
Bribery Act 2010, section 7
Makes a commercial organisation guilty if someone associated with it pays a bribe to win business for it, unless it had "adequate procedures" to prevent bribery [S355][S357]. Why it matters here: it is why gifts and hospitality rules are strict.
Chargeable hours
Hours recorded against a client code and billed. Deloitte's Code requires hours to be recorded "timely and accurately" [S340].
Change control
The process for logging, assessing and approving or rejecting any change to an agreed project scope [S377]. Why it matters here: the correct answer when a client asks for "one small extra thing".
Change management
Helping people adopt a new system or way of working through communication, training and support. Technology projects often fail here, not in the build.
Chartered Management Consultant (ChMC)
A professional accreditation run with the MCA. Over 2,800 holders in the 2026 MCA report [S150].
Chief AI Officer
A new seat on Deloitte UK's Executive, held by Hayley McKelvey from June 2026, responsible for AI strategy "across client services and internal operations" [S407].
Cloud migration
Moving a client's systems and data from its own data centres to a cloud provider such as AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud.
Conflict check
The test every proposed engagement goes through before acceptance. Deloitte declines work where a conflict "cannot be eliminated or reduced to an acceptable level" [S94].
Consumer Duty
FCA rules requiring retail financial firms to deliver good outcomes for customers. In force 31 July 2023 for open products and 31 July 2024 for closed products [S200].
Contextual recruitment
Judging grades against a candidate's school and circumstances. Deloitte UK announced it in September 2015 with Rare Recruitment, alongside school- and university-blind interviews [S267][S268]. Whether it still runs in the 2027 cycle is not confirmed.
Cutover
The planned switch from an old system to a new one, often over a weekend, with a rehearsed plan and a rollback option if it fails.
Data controller and data processor
Under UK GDPR the controller decides why and how personal data is used; the processor handles it on the controller's behalf. A processor must tell the controller about a breach without undue delay [S354]. A consultancy is often the processor.
Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA)
The UK law amending data protection rules. Royal Assent 19 June 2025; most changes in force from 5 February 2026 [S194][S195].
Delivery centre
A lower-cost site where project work is done at scale. Deloitte UK opened technology centres in Belfast, Cardiff, Manchester and Newcastle from June 2025, starting with 750 technologists and aiming for 1,500 [S254].
Deloitte Digital
Deloitte's brand for customer, marketing and creative work, built partly through agency purchases such as Heat (2016) and Acne (2017) [S405]. Why it matters here: it links creative design to technology delivery.
Deloitte EMEA
A combined firm of Deloitte LLP and other European, Middle Eastern and African member firms, live from 1 June 2026: about €20bn revenue, 132,000 people and over €1.5bn of planned investment [S93][S124]. Richard Houston is its CEO [S407].
Deloitte LLP
The UK firm, a limited liability partnership registered in England and Wales, number OC303675, at 1 New Street Square, London [S407].
Deloitte NSE (North and South Europe)
The regional holding entity that was Deloitte LLP's parent until 31 May 2026. It served no clients and has been replaced by Deloitte EMEA [S93][S94].
Deloitte University EMEA
Deloitte's residential learning campus, moved in 2024 from near Brussels to a purpose-built site near Paris [S283].
Distributable profit
The profit shared among equity partners, on a management accounts basis. £899m in FY26 for the UK and Switzerland [S93][S407].
DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act)
EU regulation on ICT risk, incident reporting, resilience testing and oversight of technology suppliers in financial services. Applies from 17 January 2025 [S201].
DTTL (Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Limited)
The UK private company limited by guarantee that coordinates the Deloitte network. It "does not provide services to clients", and member firms cannot bind each other [S83].
ECCTA failure to prevent fraud
Section 199 of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023: a large organisation commits an offence if an associated person commits fraud to benefit it, unless it had reasonable prevention procedures. In force 1 September 2025 [S361][S362].
Enabling Functions
Deloitte UK's name for its internal support teams, such as HR, IT, finance and Quality, Risk & Security, which runs conflict and independence checks [S330].
Engagement
One piece of paid client work, defined by a contract, a team and a fee. Also called a project.
Equity partner
An owner of the LLP who contributes capital and takes a share of profit. Deloitte UK had 784 at the 2026 year end, a record [S407].
ERP (enterprise resource planning)
Core business software for finance, HR and supply chain, such as SAP S/4HANA. ERP programmes are large, long and risky.
Ethical Standard
The FRC's rulebook on auditor independence. The current version took effect on 15 December 2024. Its test is whether an "objective, reasonable and informed third party" would see a threat [S364].
EU AI Act
The EU's risk-based AI law, in force 1 August 2024. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved the main high-risk deadline to 2 December 2027 [S192][S193][S234]. Why it matters here: it creates AI governance work for UK firms selling into the EU.
Final Stage Assessment
Stage 4 of Deloitte UK's process. For graduates: an in-person Topic Discussion (30 to 40 minutes) and a Skills and Motivation Interview (about 50 minutes). The Summer Vacation Scheme final stage is a virtual interview only [S260].
Financial year (Deloitte)
Deloitte's year ends on 31 May, so "FY26" means June 2025 to May 2026 [S93].
Fixed fee
A contract with an agreed total price. Deloitte still tracks progress through hours at charge-out rates [S93]. Why it matters here: overruns come out of the firm's margin.
Framework agreement
A pre-approved list of suppliers that public buyers can call off work from without a full tender each time. MCF4 is the main one for consultancy [S191].
FRC (Financial Reporting Council)
The UK regulator of auditors and accountants. It sets the Ethical Standard, inspects audits and can fine firms. It fined Deloitte a record £15m over Autonomy in 2020 [S105].
GCA (Government Commercial Agency)
The UK government's central buying agency, renamed from Crown Commercial Service on 1 April 2026 [S190].
Generative AI (GenAI)
AI that produces new text, images or code from a prompt. Large language models are the main kind.
Global Principles of Business Conduct
Deloitte's global code of ethics (October 2025 edition), covering integrity, confidentiality, anti-corruption, respect and responsible AI. Each member firm adds local rules [S340].
Hallucination
When an AI model states something false with confidence, such as an invented citation. Deloitte Australia partly refunded a government report in 2025 after fabricated references were found [S113]. Why it matters here: you must check every AI-assisted source and number.
Human in the loop
A person reviews and owns AI output before it is used. Deloitte's own guidance says accountability for AI output is "squarely a human domain" [S347].
Hypothesis-driven
Starting with a likely answer and testing it with data, instead of collecting everything first. It saves time and keeps analysis focused.
Immersive Online Assessment
Stage 2 of Deloitte UK's process: a behavioural part (rank responses to workplace scenarios) and a cognitive part (numerical and verbal reasoning), with a strengths report afterwards [S260].
Independence
An auditor's freedom from interests that could bias its opinion. The Ethical Standard bans any service that would put the firm in a management role at an audit client [S364]. Why it matters here: consultants must not make decisions for an audit client.
Industry (Deloitte)
The client sector a professional aligns to: Consumer; Energy, Resources & Industrials; Financial Services; Government & Public Services; Life Sciences & Health Care; Technology, Media & Telecom [S301].
Inside information
Precise, non-public information about a listed company that would likely move its share price if published (UK MAR Article 7) [S358]. Sharing it outside normal duties is unlawful [S359].
Integrity & AI guidance
Deloitte UK's rules for applicants on using AI in assessments. Breaking them is treated as a breach of process [S261][S351]. Why it matters here: write your own answers.
ISQM (UK) 1
The standard requiring an audit firm to run a system of quality management. Deloitte UK's 2025 review found two deficiencies, "neither severe nor pervasive" [S94].
Issue tree
A diagram that breaks a big question into smaller ones. Diagnostic trees ask "why"; solution trees ask "how". Branches should be MECE [S376].
Job Simulation
Stage 3 of Deloitte UK's process: a recorded, one-way assessment with ranking, multiple-choice, written and video answers, including scenarios that mention AI [S260].
Lead Client Service Partner (LCSP)
The partner who owns Deloitte's whole relationship with a large client and coordinates account plans and pursuits across offerings [S322]. Sources describe the US firm; the UK use is assumed similar Inferred.
Leverage
The number of staff per partner. Deloitte UK has about 16.5 staff per partner (FY26, own calculation) [S88][S93]. More leverage means more billable hours behind each partner's profit.
LLM (large language model)
An AI model trained on huge amounts of text to predict and generate language, such as Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's GPT models.
LLP (limited liability partnership)
A UK legal form where partners (members) own the business and share profit, but are not personally liable for its debts in the way old-style partners were [S93].
Local currency growth
Growth with exchange-rate effects stripped out. Deloitte's FY26 global revenue grew 3.8% in local currency but 5.7% in US dollars [S70].
Managed services
Running a system or process for a client on an ongoing contract, often for years. Revenue is recurring, and the provider carries operational risk.
MAR (UK Market Abuse Regulation)
The law banning insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information and market manipulation [S358][S360].
MCA (Management Consultancies Association)
The UK consulting trade body. It put UK consulting fee income at £21.8bn in 2025 [S150].
MCF4 (Management Consultancy Framework Four)
The government's main consultancy framework, run by the GCA from 29 July 2025 to 28 July 2027, with 10 lots and 219 suppliers [S117][S191].
MECE
"Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive": split a problem into parts that do not overlap and together cover everything [S375].
Member firm
A legally separate national or regional Deloitte firm in the DTTL network. Each is liable only for its own acts [S83].
Monitor Deloitte
Deloitte's strategy consulting brand, from the 2013 purchase of Monitor Group [S134]. Since the 2024 restructure it sits within SR&T [S307].
Multidisciplinary model
One firm offering audit, tax, consulting and deals advice under one brand. Deloitte kept consulting in 2003 when its rivals sold theirs [S104].
Non-audit services
Anything an audit firm sells to an audit client other than the audit. For public interest entities only a short permitted list is allowed [S364].
Offering
A Deloitte practice defined by what it does. UK T&T offerings include Enterprise, Technology & Performance; Engineering, AI & Data; Cyber; Customer; Human Capital; and Defence & Security [S320].
Offshore and nearshore delivery
Doing work in lower-cost countries far away (offshore, such as India) or nearby (nearshore). The Big Four are moving more work to India, Malaysia and the Philippines [S162].
Operate
Deloitte's managed-services offer. The FY26 global release names it an area of "significant growth" [S70].
Operational resilience
FCA and PRA rules requiring firms to keep important business services within set impact tolerances during severe disruption. Transition ended 31 March 2025 [S199].
Operational separation
The FRC requirement that the Big Four ring-fence their UK audit practices with separate governance and finances. All four met it by 2024 [S183][S184].
Outcome-based pricing
Fees linked to results delivered (cost saved, revenue gained) rather than hours worked. Growing slowly across consulting [S163].
PairD
Deloitte's internal generative AI assistant, rolled out in the UK from October 2023 and to 75,000 people in Europe and the Middle East by January 2024 [S328]. UK staff sent about 1 million prompts a month in FY25 [S85].
Partner annuity
A pension paid to retired Deloitte UK partners out of current profit. Closed to new entrants from 1 June 2021; liabilities £1,545m, payments mainly capped at 8% of operating profit [S93].
PEP (profit per equity partner)
Distributable profit divided by equity partners. Deloitte UK's average was £1.125m in FY26 [S407].
Personal independence
Checks every joiner must clear before starting, restricting financial interests in audit clients [S261]. Why it matters here: you may need to sell some shares.
PIE (public interest entity)
Listed companies, banks and insurers, which face the strictest audit rules, including the whitelist and the 70% cap [S182][S364].
PIRG (Public Interest Review Group)
Deloitte UK's panel for engagements with high public-interest or reputational risk. In FY25 it considered 32 matters and declined 9% [S94].
PMO (programme management office)
The team that runs plans, governance, reporting and risk logs for a large programme. A common first role for graduates.
Procurement Act 2023
The UK public procurement law, in force from 24 February 2025 [S190]. Buyers must identify and manage conflicts of interest [S366][S368].
Pyramid (staffing)
The shape of a consulting firm: few partners at the top, many juniors at the base. AI threatens the base by automating junior tasks [S162].
Pyramid Principle
Barbara Minto's rule for clear writing: put the main point first, then group supporting points beneath it [S374].
RACI
A table showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task, ideally with one Accountable person [S379].
RAID log
A project list of Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Dependencies, reviewed regularly.
Rate card
The standard daily charge-out rate for each grade. Deloitte recognises revenue using hours at charge-out rates [S93]. Deloitte does not publish its rates.
Realisation
The share of the standard value of time that is actually billed and collected after discounts and write-offs.
RFP (request for proposal)
A buyer's formal invitation for firms to bid for a piece of work. The firm's reply, often with a presentation, is the pitch.
Salaried partner
A partner by title who is an employee, not an owner. Deloitte UK had 654 on an FTE basis in FY26 [S88].
SaaS (software as a service)
Software rented by subscription and run by the vendor in the cloud, such as Salesforce or Workday.
SC (Security Check)
UK government clearance for posts needing long-term access to SECRET material. It builds on BPSS [S370].
Scope
What a project will and will not deliver. Defining it clearly prevents later disputes [S378]. Scope creep is unpaid growth in that list.
SCQ (Situation, Complication, Question)
Minto's way to open a piece of communication by stating what is true, what has changed, and the question that raises [S374].
Scrum
An agile framework with a team of 10 or fewer, three roles (Developers, a Product Owner and a Scrum Master) and work in Sprints [S373].
Shared Values
Deloitte's five values: Lead the way; Serve with integrity; Take care of each other; Foster inclusion; Collaborate for measurable impact [S266].
Skills and Motivation Interview
The roughly 50-minute final-stage interview on "alignment with the capabilities we look for" [S260]. Expect strengths and "tell me about a time" questions.
SOW (statement of work)
The contract document that says what will be delivered, by when, by whom and for what fee.
Speak Up
Deloitte's third-party-run channel for raising ethics concerns, anonymously if needed. Retaliation is not tolerated [S340][S343].
Sprint
A fixed cycle of one month or less in Scrum. Changes that endanger the Sprint Goal are not made mid-sprint [S373].
SR&T Advisory (Strategy, Risk & Transactions)
One of Deloitte's two consulting businesses, covering strategy, risk and deals work. UK revenue £913m in FY26 [S407].
Stakeholder map
A grid plotting people by power and interest, to decide who to manage closely and who to keep informed [S380].
STAR (or STARR)
An answer structure: Situation, Task, Action, Result, plus Reflection. Prospects suggests preparing five to eight examples [S382].
Strengths-based interview
Questions about what you enjoy and do well naturally, rather than only past examples. Deloitte's online assessment is designed to find "your unique strengths" [S350].
Summer Vacation Scheme
Deloitte UK's summer internship, using the same process as graduate roles but with a virtual interview-only final stage [S260].
Systems integrator (SI)
A firm that makes several software products work together inside a client's organisation.
T+1
Settling share trades one business day after the trade. The UK plans to move to T+1 by 11 October 2027 [S198].
T&M (time and materials)
Billing for hours actually worked at agreed rates, plus expenses. The client carries the overrun risk [S93].
T&T (Technology & Transformation)
Deloitte's largest business, covering technology implementation, data, AI, cyber and transformation. UK revenue £1.75bn in FY26, up 4% [S407].
Target operating model (TOM)
A design for how an organisation should work in future: people, processes, technology and governance.
Tax & Legal
Deloitte's tax compliance, tax advice and legal business. UK revenue £1.36bn in FY26 [S407].
Topic Discussion
The first final-stage exercise: a 30 to 40 minute two-way discussion with an assessor on a topic you research in advance [S260].
Transparency report
An annual report the audit firm must publish on governance, audit quality and risk. Deloitte UK's 2025 report rates its reputational risk "Very High" [S94].
Trustworthy AI
Deloitte's framework for responsible AI, launched 2020. Its dimensions include fair and impartial, transparent and explainable, responsible and accountable, safe and secure, robust and reliable, and respectful of privacy [S346][S348].
UAT (user acceptance testing)
The final test in which business users check a system meets their needs before they accept it [S381]. Users, not the build team, sign it off.
UK Board
Deloitte UK's top governance body from 1 June 2026, replacing the UK Oversight Board. Jane Whitlock chairs it [S93][S407].
UK GDPR
The UK's main data protection law. Notifiable breaches go to the ICO within 72 hours; top fines are £17.5m or 4% of turnover [S353][S354].
UK SRS (UK Sustainability Reporting Standards)
UK versions of the ISSB climate and sustainability disclosure standards, published 25 February 2026 for voluntary use [S202].
USI (US-India delivery)
The US Deloitte firm's delivery organisation in India, reported at over 100,000 people [S324] Reported. Its role in UK work is not established.
Utilisation
The share of a consultant's available hours that are chargeable to clients. Deloitte does not publish its targets.
Whitelist
The short list of non-audit services an auditor may provide to a public interest entity audit client, mostly audit-related or required by law [S180][S364].
Zora AI
Deloitte's suite of AI agents for finance, HR, procurement and other functions, launched March 2025 with NVIDIA technology and sold on subscription [S327].

Part 16

Gaps and open questions

What this pack could not establish, why, and how you can find out yourself; where sources disagree and what the pack did about it; and an honest check against the brief.

How to use this part

No outside researcher can see inside a private partnership. Some things Deloitte simply does not publish (day rates, utilisation targets, scoring rubrics). Some pages were paywalled or blocked. And several research workstreams hit a shared limit on web searches, so they switched to reading primary pages directly. This part lists every gap the research files recorded, grouped by topic. Use it three ways:

  • Do not bluff on these points. If an interviewer raises one, say what you know and what you could not confirm. That is a strength, not a weakness.
  • Turn some into questions. Gaps marked "ask" make good, genuine questions at an event or at the end of an interview.
  • Check the dated ones. Some will close on a known date (for example, when London roles go live on 5 October 2026 [S14]).

What could not be established

The role, the JD and recruitment

What is missingWhyHow you could find out
A London T&T graduate advert. THE JD used in Part 1 is a Belfast posting [S2].London Consulting roles were not live on 4 October; they open on 5 October [S14].Check the board on or after 5 October. Compare the London text with Part 1's decode line by line.
Graduate salary.Not published on any Deloitte page read. Only self-reported snippets (about £34k to £39k) [S58][S59] Reported.The live advert or the offer letter. Do not ask in interview.
The "10 core skills" and the capability framework used to score interviews.They sit behind the Candidate Zone or are not published [S2][S260]. "Deloitte Talent Standards" was not found anywhere.Candidate Zone after you apply. Use the five Shared Values meanwhile [S266].
This year's final-stage topics.Candidate-report sites (Glassdoor, The Student Room) returned errors [S289].Your invitation will give the topic. Ask peers who applied last year.
Whether a group exercise or partner interview still happens at graduate level.The official page lists only the topic discussion and interview [S260]; older anecdotes mention both [S289][S286].Read your final-stage invitation closely.
Whether school- and university-blind interviewing (announced 2015) is still used.Only 2015 sources confirm it [S267][S268].Ask at a Deloitte event: "Is contextual recruitment still part of the process?"
Security vetting for graduates (BPSS or SC).No Deloitte UK page says it is standard; many T&T roles prefer SC [S54]. BPSS rules are public [S369][S370].Ask: "Would a graduate in this team be put forward for clearance?"
Pre-employment screening provider and steps.Seen only in search snippets [S293][S291].Your onboarding emails.
Whether graduates attend Deloitte University EMEA in year one.Not stated [S283].Ask at an event or after an offer.
The named head of UK early careers.Not found on pages read.Not needed. Do not guess a name.
Performance system name, utilisation targets, typical years per grade.No primary source; the HBR article on Deloitte's redesign is paywalled [S61].Ask a current analyst: "How is performance reviewed in year one?"
T&T's share of the graduate intake.Not published [S29].Ask: "How many analysts join TST each year?"

The firm: money, structure and delivery

What is missingWhyHow you could find out
Deloitte's day rates.Government framework rate cards sit in a tool that could not be opened [S117].Not knowable from outside. Do not quote a number; Test and Trace rates from 2021 are the only disclosed example [S332].
Utilisation, realisation and margin by business.Not disclosed; only group cost lines [S93].Not knowable. Talk about the mechanism instead (Part 2).
FY26 global revenue in US dollars by business and region.The release gives growth rates only; the FY26 Global Impact Report was not found [S70].Check for the Global Impact Report later in the autumn.
A consistent UK revenue series before FY2019, and global headcount for FY2017 and FY2020.Different perimeters; snippets only [S118][S119].Older annual reviews on deloitte.com.
Which offshore centres UK T&T uses.Postings say "onshore and offshore" only [S50][S51]. The UK group owns Deloitte India Services Limited, purpose not stated [S24]. USI belongs to the US firm [S324].Ask: "How do London analysts work with Belfast and offshore build teams?"
Size of Enabling Functions.Pages describe teams, not numbers [S330].Not needed for a consulting interview.
UK job-cut numbers before 2026.Secondary press and snippets only [S100][S102].Treat as Reported. Do not lead with them.
The UK Annual Review narrative for FY26.Only the metrics, accounts and press release were read [S88][S93][S407].Read it on deloitte.com/uk before the final stage.
The UK code of conduct, gifts thresholds, Speak Up vendor.Not public; the Global Code is [S340].Use the Global Code wording in answers.
Whether "Lead Client Service Partner" is the UK term.Sources found were US [S322].Ask: "Who owns the overall relationship on a large account?"

People and leadership

What is missingWhyHow you could find out
Current leaders of UK Cyber and Deloitte Digital.Not on a current service page; the Extended Leadership Team page may predate June 2026 [S26].Check the service pages on the day. Use names marked AMBER in Part 1 only after re-checking.
Hammad Rafique's exact prior title.One trade source plus Deloitte's release, worded differently [S274][S275].Say "led T&T in Financial Services before taking over UK T&T".
Joe Ucuzoglu's start date as Global CEO.His profile says December 2022 [S278]; another pass could not confirm a date on a primary page [S73].Say "Deloitte's Global CEO" without a date.
The UK ethics officer's name.The page and a search summary disagree [S344].Not needed. Do not use it.

AI and internal tools

What is missingWhyHow you could find out
Which AI tools a UK T&T analyst uses day to day in 2026, and whether PairD is still the main one.PairD is confirmed for 2024 and FY25 [S328][S85][S345]; Claude is global [S116]. No UK 2026 tool list.Ask: "Which internal tools would I use in my first six months?" (Part 9).
A public Deloitte UK policy on using GenAI with client data.Only Transparency Report controls are public [S345].Apply the Code's confidentiality rule [S340] and the JD's "firm-approved" wording [S3].
Firms' AI investment figures from a commentator blog (for example Deloitte US$2bn).Not checked against press releases [S163].Use Deloitte's own US$3bn to 2030 figure instead [S70].

Competitors and the market

What is missingWhyHow you could find out
PwC and EY FY26 global results, and EY UK FY26.Not published or not found by 4 October [S126][S127].Check their press rooms; PwC global usually reports in the autumn.
Kennedy, Vault, Oliver Wyman, PA Consulting, Kearney and Bain figures; Accenture, IBM and Capgemini UK numbers.Search limit reached [S406].Not needed in depth. Avoid numeric claims about them.
